articles.title: AI models can be tricked into identifying civilians as military targets by telling them it’s a game
articles.body:
Some AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and other leading AI labs could be easily tricked into identifying targets for military strikes — even if they include civilians or locations like schools — simply by being told they’re playing a game, according to a new research report by Vals.
Vals, a San Francisco-based AI evaluation startup, tested whether leading AI models could be manipulated into participating in autonomous warfare. Researchers used simulated scenarios and a combination of generated and real imagery from Ukraine and Iran to see if the AI models would mark targets in drone and satellite imagery.
The models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, and other companies frequently identified potential targets in drone and satellite imagery, including civilians and surrendering soldiers. When the models refused to cooperate, researchers were able to jailbreak them by claiming the battlefield scenarios were part of a game.
The findings come amid growing fears about the immediate risks posed by AI, beyond the existential threats associated with artificial general intelligence.
Earlier this year, Anthropic became embroiled in a dispute with the Department of Defense after it told the agency it could not use Anthropic’s technology for mass surveillance of Americans or autonomous warfare. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has insisted that today’s AI systems aren’t reliable enough to make life-or-death decisions without a human in the loop. Meanwhile, the Pentagon argued it should be able to deploy the technology for any lawful military purpose.
The new research raises further questions about whether AI companies are capable of preventing their models from being used in warfare.
Ironically, AI models from Anthropic performed the worst in these simulated scenarios. But none of the models performed particularly well. None of the researchers’ requests were blocked by a safety classifier, and refusals were uncommon. Even when models did refuse, they often complied after being told they were playing a game.
Anthropic spokesperson Eduardo Maia Silva told TechCrunch the company appreciates Vals’ report, recommendations, and collaboration, and acknowledged that the outcomes were not acceptable.
“The examples in the report are very clearly against our rules and we have banned and will ban users when we see this behavior,” according to an emailed company statement sent by Silva. “Even for authorized settings, Anthropic has long been firm that today’s frontier AI systems are not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons.”
Anthropic told TechCrunch that its teams were already developing additional safeguards before the report was published and that those measures would be in place soon. Anthropic is also expanding its own testing and enhancing safeguards and enforcement to address any gaps it finds.
OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans told TechCrunch the company prohibits using its public models to facilitate violence or for unapproved national security purposes, including in the scenarios Vals simulated.
“We actively detect and disrupt misuse, including by suspending accounts that violate our policies,” OpenAI said in an emailed statement. “We’re also developing additional safeguards for our public models against misuse involving drones and drone software.”
Vals notes in the report that the models were never asked to directly make strike decisions, a task the researchers said the models would typically refuse. That doesn’t mean their outputs couldn’t have dire or fatal consequences in the real world. For instance, targeting information could be used by autonomous weapons systems.
In some scenarios, the models were asked to report whether people were visible. Positive reports were followed by simulated strikes and the models would see the consequences.
The report relies on commercial models from frontier AI labs, not the models those companies might provide to the military. It’s not clear whether the additional safeguards would apply to military use, though.
Vals also noted that technical challenges, including latency and limited onboard computing capacity, make it difficult to use general-purpose AI models for live drone targeting. Those constraints make their deployment in combat less of an immediate threat.
A more immediate threat, the researchers say, is that AI models could be used to annotate battlefield footage at scale, producing training data for autonomous targeting systems.
For instance, researchers relied on real satellite imagery of an Iranian school that was bombed by the U.S. in February 2026, killing more than 150 civilians. Bloomberg later reported that an “overreliance on AI” contributed to the strike. In Vals’ testing, models frequently marked the school, which sat next to a military complex, as a strike target, with Claude Opus 5.5 selecting the school in 69% of ordinary trials and 72% of game-framed trials.
Anthropic no longer has an active Pentagon contract, but other companies, including SpaceXAI, OpenAI, and Google do. A recent Congressional Research Service report found that the Pentagon is not known to be using any frontier AI model in autonomous weapons systems directly.
TechCrunch has also reached out to Meta, Google, Thinking Machines Lab, and SpaceXAI for comment.

articles.title: Effects of a Nuclear Detonation in Low Earth Orbit
articles.body:
Physics > Physics and Society
  [Submitted on 6 Nov 2026]
Title:Effects of a Nuclear Detonation in Low Earth Orbit
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:More than 13,000 satellites operate in low Earth orbit (LEO), and concern has grown that nuclear weapons could be used in space to target them. Beyond the initial X-ray burst, electrons released by radioactive fission products can become trapped in Earth's magnetic field, repeatedly exposing satellites as an artificial radiation belt. Here we couple prompt radiation, electron trapping and belt evolution to satellite failures, collisions and atmospheric drag. For a 1-Mt detonation at 500km over the South Atlantic, repeated belt exposure disables approximately 98% of modeled satellites within one week in our central case. Tripling the assumed radiation tolerance delays widespread failure by only days: approximately 97% are still disabled within two weeks. The loss of maneuverability sharply increases collision risk, with approximately 20 collisions expected within two years. Drag removes many disabled spacecraft from lower altitudes, but replacement satellites could remain exposed to radiation and debris for years. These findings show how a single detonation could devastate orbital infrastructure and support efforts to prevent the deployment and use of nuclear weapons in space.

articles.title: Highly classified US national security communications network goes down
articles.body:
The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter.
The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said.
As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said.
“The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”
A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month.
“The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.”
The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. AI tools helped researchers exploit them, setting off a scramble by government agencies and corporations around the world to address the issue in recent weeks. The NSA itself urged organizations to apply software patches.
The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords.
Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack.
A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One.
Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. “It could impact analysis and reporting, but for highest priority requirements they would find a way to work those. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.”
A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a three-level system that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The recording told non-emergency personnel to arrive for work in a staggered manner and for emergency personnel to arrive as usual. The New York Times first reported that detail.
The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country.
All flights nationwide were grounded for hours on Friday after a massive systems failure, leading to thousands of flights being delayed or canceled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas.
Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings.
And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts.
There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security.
The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official.
Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time.
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Kylie Atwood and Haley Britzky contributed reporting.

articles.title: Who Builds the Machines That Build the Machines?
articles.body:
On October 28, 2026, the White House issued a proclamation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. This followed a Commerce Department investigation that concluded imports of robotics and industrial machinery “threaten to impair the national security.” No new tariffs have been set yet. Section 232 opens a 180-day window till April 26, 2027 to negotiate with trading partners.
This ties back to one theme that keeps coming back to me as I write on Core Matter. The bottleneck for scaling physical AI sits below the finished machine, in the components inside it, the materials inside those components (eg, rare earth magnets), and the machines that build them (this piece’s topic), as we covered in Part 4 of the actuator series. It’s like a Russian doll, layer after layer.
With the fresh Section 232 news, I went down the rabbit hole of the US machine tool landscape. Here’s what I found.
- The US imports about half of the machine tools it uses, $5.8bn of $11.4bn in 2025. Assuming demand (which is not the trend, see point 3) stays flat, US output would need to grow 63% to 83% ($4.4bn to $5.8bn a year) to replace imports with domestic machines.
- The US builds everyday machines and imports the precise ones. About 55% of import value is the high-end versions of machines US plants already make, such as 5-axis machining centers. Precision machines, small-module gear grinders, precision grinders and the heaviest forging presses have no confirmed US volume builder. Imports rose 29.5% for grinders and 76.7% for gear machines in Jan to Sep 2026. These machines make the ball screws, bearings, gears and forgings that aircraft, turbines and robots depend on.
- Orders are at a record by value since 1998, while a domestic ramp is limited by people and components. US machine tool orders grew 45.0% to $5.76bn in Jan to Sep 2026, after 3 straight years of decline. Aerospace, power generation, munitions and shipbuilding are pulling it up. A domestic ramp is limited by people, castings and imported components (the components that make the machines, the next doll in). We dive into the key cost drivers and where industrial AI could change the cost structure.
This piece also launches our first Core Matter model, a US machine tool demand model built up by end market. It puts US machine tool consumption at $12.7bn to $15.4bn a year on average over the 2026 to 2030 build-out, up from $11.4bn in 2025. Paid subscribers can download the full model, with every input and source, at the end of this piece.
In this piece
- US Machine Tool Imports Are Half of an $11.4bn Market
- Which Machine Tools the US Makes vs. Imports
- Aerospace, Gas Turbines, Munitions and Ships Drove Machine Demand in 2026
- Who Builds Machine Tools in the US, and How Fast Can Supply Ramp?
- Fixed Costs and People Keep New Machine Tool Builders Scarce
- Machine Tool Startups Building the Machines That Build the Machines
- Section 232, the 1986 Machine Tool Precedent and What the 180 Days Decide
1. US Machine Tool Imports Are Half of an $11.4bn Market
Assuming domestic demand stays flat, which is not the trendline as we’ll discuss in section 3, closing the import gap means $4.4bn to $5.8bn of new US machine output a year, or output up 63% to 83%. The low end replaces net imports, and the high end replaces every imported machine.
In 2025 the US produced $7.0bn of machine tools, consumed $11.4bn, imported $5.8bn and exported $1.4bn, per Gardner’s World Machine Tool Survey.
Forming and stamping ($1.48bn) and machining centers ($1.43bn) are the top 2025 imports. Imports of precision grinders or gear grinders rose rapidly at 29.5% and 76.7% in January to September 2026, against about 9.6% for all machine tool imports. We could not confirm US volume production.
2. Which Machine Tools the US Makes vs. Imports
The US imports 5-axis machines, horizontals with pallet systems, large gantries and boring mills, precision and gear grinders, and presses. It builds in volume entry and mid-range 3-axis mills and lathes.
“Japanese and DACH (Germany, Austria and Switzerland) machines generally fulfill buyer needs in the higher segment while US and Taiwanese (ROC) generally fulfill them in the lower.”
One distributor analyst put it succinctly in a filing to the Section 232 docket.
What do higher vs. lower segments mean? Higher means more axes, tighter precision, bigger work envelopes and more automation, at a higher price. The average imported machining center cost about $196k in 2024, roughly 2x our estimate of about $96k per machine at Haas, the largest machine tool builder in North America.
See the table below of what these machines do, and who the main buyers are.
While Okuma (Charlotte), Makino (Ohio), United Grinding (Ohio), Kapp Niles (Colorado) and DN Solutions (New Jersey) have large US sites, the sources we found describe them as sales, service or headquarters sites.
The largest two import classes feed autos, aerospace and defense. Forming and stamping machines make stampings, shell bodies and aerospace forgings. Machining centers make everything from brackets and housings to aerospace structures and turbine parts. My guess is that a cutoff at the high end would hit aerospace, defense and power first.
The US built its own heavy forging presses in the 1950s. The newest ones came from a German builder. Heavy forging presses squeeze titanium, aluminum and nickel into one-piece parts such as landing gear, airframe bulkheads and turbine discs. Because so few exist, these presses can cap how many aircraft and engine parts get made here.
Robot reducers need ultra-precision gear machines, which are imported and in low volumes. Robot joints use reducers, small gearboxes whose teeth are cut and ground on gear machines. Leaderdrive, a Chinese reducer maker, told the Shanghai stock exchange that a plant for 1 million harmonic reducers a year needs 30 ultra-precision gear machines, at about $833k each.
Assuming 23 reducers per humanoid (on the low end, based on Unitree G1 teardown), 1 million humanoids a year (Tesla’s stated line capacity) would need about 690 of those machines, or about $115mn a year bought over the 5 years to 2030. That is 2.3x and 1.2x all US gear-machine imports, $50.7mn in 2025 and about $100mn a year at the 2026 pace.
I ranked the hardest machines to ramp domestically based on, a) which are whether we found a US builder making them in volume, b) how long new capacity takes, and c) how much it costs. Details are in the Core Matter Industrial Machinery Model.
Machines to build in the US, ranked from hardest to ramp:
- Small-module gear grinders. They finish the gears in robot reducers and aerospace gearboxes. We could not confirm volume production of these at any US builder.
- Precision cylindrical and thread grinders. These grinders make the ball screws and bearings that other machines need. United Grinding, the Swiss grinding group, serves the US from an import and service site in Ohio. We found 2 US builders, Weldon (Pennsylvania) and Drake (Ohio), and could not confirm volume production at either.
- Heavy forging presses. The 2 largest US presses we found built or rebuilt since 2000 came from a German builder. Each project took years and $100mn or more.
- Large gantries and boring mills. Ingersoll and Fives build them here, so these are the likeliest candidates to ramp. The constraint is size and lead time.
- High-end 5-axis machines and automated horizontals. Mazak and DMG MORI already build some in the US, so expansion of existing plants is the shorter path here.
3. Aerospace, Gas Turbines, Munitions and Ships Drove Machine Demand in 2026
US machine tool orders have picked up significantly in 2025 and 2026. Order value rose 22.5% to $5.74bn in 2025, and another 45.0% to $5.76bn in January to September 2026. That was after 3 straight years of decline, including a 3.8% fall in 2024. AMT calls the first half of 2026 its strongest half since the series began in 1998.
Who buys these machines in the US?
- Aerospace orders rose 45.1% in 2025, and in the first half of 2026 aerospace ordered more machinery than in any half on record. AMT ties 2026 demand to the space economy, commercial aircraft backlogs and munitions, so commercial demand is part of it alongside defense.
- Power generation orders in the first half of 2026 ran 14% above automotive.
- Contract job shops, AMT’s largest customer group, grew orders 19.1% in 2025.
- Data centers drive gas turbines machinery demands. Klingelnberg says that in the US “the rising energy needs of these data centers are providing additional momentum, for example through investments in gas turbines.”
The US buys $11.4bn of machine tools a year today. Four build-outs (munitions, ships, gas turbines, commercial aerospace) add $1.0bn to $2.9bn a year of extra buying for 5 years, on top of 1% to 3% normal growth. That puts US buying at $12.7bn to $15.4bn a year in 2026 to 2030.
Munitions is the largest piece. The one new US plant we found, Haas Henderson, adds about $0.5bn of machines sold at home. So imports rise from $5.8bn to about $6.9bn to $9.5bn a year, and the import share goes from 51% to 54% to 62%.
4. Who Builds Machine Tools in the US, and How Fast Can Supply Ramp?
A domestic ramp-up faces four limiting factors.
- Workforce. This is the manufacturing story repeating all over again. Gleason’s executive put it first, saying “First you need a large enough, trained workforce. This needs to be the top priority to expand the industrial base.” Haas is hiring more than 1,000 people for Henderson at starting pay of about $23 an hour.
- Castings. Castings are the heavy iron bed and columns of a machine. Haas bought “more than 100 million pounds of castings each year” back in 2006 and worried that shrinking US foundry numbers “could limit their company’s growth.” At 10,000 to 13,000 machines a year, that is roughly 7,700 to 10,000 pounds (3.5 to 4.5 tonnes, about the weight of 2 to 3 cars) of castings per machine.
- Imported components. The parts inside the machines are imported too, including controls (FANUC, Siemens, Heidenhain, Mitsubishi), spindles, ball screws and linear guides. Tariffs raise their cost, and control deliveries have seen delays. 
  - In April 2025 Haas asked for “tariff exemptions for raw materials and components vital to the U.S. machine tool industry.” DMG MORI’s 2025 results blame late deliveries partly on “delays in switching to new European-made CNCs.”
- Time. “A shift in global production takes a lot of time,” per GMTA, a US importer of German gear machines. One example is Haas’s plant in Henderson, Nevada. The city closed the land sale in November 2019, with completion planned for 2022. Haas asked the city to extend its deadline, citing the pandemic, supply chains and construction costs. They eventually held the groundbreaking in October 2024. The plant is scheduled to open in Q1 2027, 5 years behind schedule.
Imports are slow to fill a jump in demand too, since foreign builders hold about 7 months of sales in backlog, with DMG MORI at 7.0 months on September 30, 2026 and Klingelnberg at about 7 at the end of March 2026. Klingelnberg’s backlog has halved since 2023.
5. Fixed Costs and People Keep New Machine Tool Builders Scarce
Would this spur a new generation of startups to build the machines that build the machines? As I read the filings of listed builders, the economics are brutal.
What I took away from these financials is that for European and Japanese builders, people cost about as much as materials. Personnel is 30% to 41% of revenue or operating output and materials 38% to 41%. At Chinese builders, total employee pay is 15% to 19% of revenue (Haitian and Kede, 2025) and materials 50% to 62%. Personnel, depreciation and overhead are fixed costs, so margins swing with the cycle. 2025 was a weak year. In 2023 Hermle earned an operating margin of about 21.8% and DMG MORI 10.0%. Labor productivity in US metalworking machinery “has grown only 0.9% per year over the last 30 years.”
What are the key materials? Neway, a Chinese CNC machine builder (688697.SS)’s IPO prospectus published their bill of materials. Of Rmb840.0mn ($122mn) of purchases in 2020, the split is below.
- Functional components (hydraulics, tool magazines, rotary tables) are 25.6%
- Castings are 22.3%
- Electrical parts (mainly the control) are 20.9%. The control alone is about 17.7% of purchases.
- Transmission parts (spindles, guides, screws, bearings, gears) are 15.4%
- Accessories, machined parts, sheet metal and other are 15.8%
Control and distribution are two levers that can help expand margins.
- The control. A CNC control is the machine’s computer, software, servo drives and motors. Most builders we checked buy it from FANUC, Siemens, Heidenhain or Mitsubishi, and FANUC earns a 21.4% operating margin (company-wide) against 3% to 10% at most builders we checked.
- Cutting the middlemen. US distribution typically has 2 levels, “a wholesaler and a dealer,” and “each level marks their cost up as much as 20%.”
6. Machine Tool Startups Building the Machines That Build the Machines
Could venture capital close the machinery gap with the next wave of startups? I went searching and found no venture-backed US company building production machining centers, grinders or gear machines. (If you are building them, I’d love to hear from you!)
What we can learn from history. Haas, the largest machine builder in North America, was founded in 1983, during the import surge behind the 1983 machine tool Section 232 petition. It started with indexers and built its first vertical machining center in 1987. Today it builds about 10,000 to 15,000 machines a year on about $1.2bn of revenue, and is private.
The small US builders popped up in the 2000s. They include Tormach (Wisconsin, 2001), Pocket NC, now Penta Machine (Montana, 2011), and Langmuir Systems, a plasma-table maker bought by ShopSabre in 2023. They design and sell desktop and small-shop machines.
US venture money has gone to companies that use machine tools or build equipment for their own factories. Examples include Hadrian, Machina Labs, Divergent, VulcanForms, Freeform and Seurat. Hadrian’s new Alabama factory is the first of three supported by a $900mn Navy contract, with a goal to “automate 80% of the work.”
This year’s capital went to factory software and sensing. Arda, led by OpenAI’s former research chief Bob McGrew, came out of stealth in October 2026 with $232mn of funding, its Series A at a $1.5bn valuation, building AI that turns product designs into assembly lines. Matter, whose cofounder and CEO Adi Prasad came from Tesla, offers final assembly, test and packaging for robots in the US. In machining software, CloudNC raised $20mn (UK, September 2026, with Lockheed’s venture arm), Limitless Labs $20mn (Israel) and IPercept $16.5mn (Sweden, entering the US).
Funded machine builders abroad tell a different story. Ethereal Machines (India) raised a $28.5mn Series B in 2026. It builds its own multi-axis CNC machines, sells machining as a service from them, and is building its own controller and a 300,000 sq ft plant. Shanghai Xinghe (China) builds gear grinders and raised several hundred million yuan in July 2026.
Government money has gone to training and adjacent supply. America’s Cutting Edge, a national CNC machining training initiative backed by Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), received $42mn from the Defense Department from 2020 to 2022 for machine tool training and R&D. The Pentagon’s industrial base program has awarded over $3.3bn since FY2024. The releases we read do not name any machine tool builder.
With Section 232, I believe two opportunities arise domestically in the US.
- Foreign builders establish US bases to build machines. They are more experienced in navigating thin margins, but that would likely still require government incentives to boost investments.
- Startups in the same spirit as Ethereal Machines launch in the US. They would need to think carefully about how to cut labor cost, solve the materials supply chain bottleneck, and build the control in-house from day one.
7. Section 232, the 1986 Machine Tool Precedent and What the 180 Days Decide
This Section 232 has until April 26, 2027 for its first negotiation update. Section 232 last came for machine tools in 1983, 43 years ago. Will history repeat or rhyme?
The US lost its lead in the 1970s and 1980s. Japanese machine tool exports to the US rose over 1,200% between 1964 and 1967, and by 1986 imports were 75% of the numerically controlled (NC) machines sold in the US, the category that includes today’s CNC machines. Across all machine tools, imports went from about 10% of US consumption in the mid-1970s to 25% by 1981 and about 50% by 1986.
- March 1983. The builders’ association petitions for import quotas under Section 232.
- May 20, 1986. Reagan chooses negotiation. “Voluntary restraint agreements will be sought with Taiwan, West Germany, Japan, and Switzerland.”
- Dec 16, 1986. Japan and Taiwan agree to 5 years of restraint from January 1987. articles.title: Who Builds the Machines That Build the Machines?
articles.body:
On October 28, 2026, the White House issued a proclamation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. This followed a Commerce Department investigation that concluded imports of robotics and industrial machinery “threaten to impair the national security.” No new tariffs have been set yet. Section 232 opens a 180-day window till April 26, 2027 to negotiate with trading partners.
This ties back to one theme that keeps coming back to me as I write on Core Matter. The bottleneck for scaling physical AI sits below the finished machine, in the components inside it, the materials inside those components (eg, rare earth magnets), and the machines that build them (this piece’s topic), as we covered in Part 4 of the actuator series. It’s like a Russian doll, layer after layer.
With the fresh Section 232 news, I went down the rabbit hole of the US machine tool landscape. Here’s what I found.
- The US imports about half of the machine tools it uses, $5.8bn of $11.4bn in 2025. Assuming demand (which is not the trend, see point 3) stays flat, US output would need to grow 63% to 83% ($4.4bn to $5.8bn a year) to replace imports with domestic machines.
- The US builds everyday machines and imports the precise ones. About 55% of import value is the high-end versions of machines US plants already make, such as 5-axis machining centers. Precision machines, small-module gear grinders, precision grinders and the heaviest forging presses have no confirmed US volume builder. Imports rose 29.5% for grinders and 76.7% for gear machines in Jan to Sep 2026. These machines make the ball screws, bearings, gears and forgings that aircraft, turbines and robots depend on.
- Orders are at a record by value since 1998, while a domestic ramp is limited by people and components. US machine tool orders grew 45.0% to $5.76bn in Jan to Sep 2026, after 3 straight years of decline. Aerospace, power generation, munitions and shipbuilding are pulling it up. A domestic ramp is limited by people, castings and imported components (the components that make the machines, the next doll in). We dive into the key cost drivers and where industrial AI could change the cost structure.
This piece also launches our first Core Matter model, a US machine tool demand model built up by end market. It puts US machine tool consumption at $12.7bn to $15.4bn a year on average over the 2026 to 2030 build-out, up from $11.4bn in 2025. Paid subscribers can download the full model, with every input and source, at the end of this piece.
In this piece
- US Machine Tool Imports Are Half of an $11.4bn Market
- Which Machine Tools the US Makes vs. Imports
- Aerospace, Gas Turbines, Munitions and Ships Drove Machine Demand in 2026
- Who Builds Machine Tools in the US, and How Fast Can Supply Ramp?
- Fixed Costs and People Keep New Machine Tool Builders Scarce
- Machine Tool Startups Building the Machines That Build the Machines
- Section 232, the 1986 Machine Tool Precedent and What the 180 Days Decide
1. US Machine Tool Imports Are Half of an $11.4bn Market
Assuming domestic demand stays flat, which is not the trendline as we’ll discuss in section 3, closing the import gap means $4.4bn to $5.8bn of new US machine output a year, or output up 63% to 83%. The low end replaces net imports, and the high end replaces every imported machine.
In 2025 the US produced $7.0bn of machine tools, consumed $11.4bn, imported $5.8bn and exported $1.4bn, per Gardner’s World Machine Tool Survey.
Forming and stamping ($1.48bn) and machining centers ($1.43bn) are the top 2025 imports. Imports of precision grinders or gear grinders rose rapidly at 29.5% and 76.7% in January to September 2026, against about 9.6% for all machine tool imports. We could not confirm US volume production.
2. Which Machine Tools the US Makes vs. Imports
The US imports 5-axis machines, horizontals with pallet systems, large gantries and boring mills, precision and gear grinders, and presses. It builds in volume entry and mid-range 3-axis mills and lathes.
“Japanese and DACH (Germany, Austria and Switzerland) machines generally fulfill buyer needs in the higher segment while US and Taiwanese (ROC) generally fulfill them in the lower.”
One distributor analyst put it succinctly in a filing to the Section 232 docket.
What do higher vs. lower segments mean? Higher means more axes, tighter precision, bigger work envelopes and more automation, at a higher price. The average imported machining center cost about $196k in 2024, roughly 2x our estimate of about $96k per machine at Haas, the largest machine tool builder in North America.
See the table below of what these machines do, and who the main buyers are.
While Okuma (Charlotte), Makino (Ohio), United Grinding (Ohio), Kapp Niles (Colorado) and DN Solutions (New Jersey) have large US sites, the sources we found describe them as sales, service or headquarters sites.
The largest two import classes feed autos, aerospace and defense. Forming and stamping machines make stampings, shell bodies and aerospace forgings. Machining centers make everything from brackets and housings to aerospace structures and turbine parts. My guess is that a cutoff at the high end would hit aerospace, defense and power first.
The US built its own heavy forging presses in the 1950s. The newest ones came from a German builder. Heavy forging presses squeeze titanium, aluminum and nickel into one-piece parts such as landing gear, airframe bulkheads and turbine discs. Because so few exist, these presses can cap how many aircraft and engine parts get made here.
Robot reducers need ultra-precision gear machines, which are imported and in low volumes. Robot joints use reducers, small gearboxes whose teeth are cut and ground on gear machines. Leaderdrive, a Chinese reducer maker, told the Shanghai stock exchange that a plant for 1 million harmonic reducers a year needs 30 ultra-precision gear machines, at about $833k each.
Assuming 23 reducers per humanoid (on the low end, based on Unitree G1 teardown), 1 million humanoids a year (Tesla’s stated line capacity) would need about 690 of those machines, or about $115mn a year bought over the 5 years to 2030. That is 2.3x and 1.2x all US gear-machine imports, $50.7mn in 2025 and about $100mn a year at the 2026 pace.
I ranked the hardest machines to ramp domestically based on, a) which are whether we found a US builder making them in volume, b) how long new capacity takes, and c) how much it costs. Details are in the Core Matter Industrial Machinery Model.
Machines to build in the US, ranked from hardest to ramp:
- Small-module gear grinders. They finish the gears in robot reducers and aerospace gearboxes. We could not confirm volume production of these at any US builder.
- Precision cylindrical and thread grinders. These grinders make the ball screws and bearings that other machines need. United Grinding, the Swiss grinding group, serves the US from an import and service site in Ohio. We found 2 US builders, Weldon (Pennsylvania) and Drake (Ohio), and could not confirm volume production at either.
- Heavy forging presses. The 2 largest US presses we found built or rebuilt since 2000 came from a German builder. Each project took years and $100mn or more.
- Large gantries and boring mills. Ingersoll and Fives build them here, so these are the likeliest candidates to ramp. The constraint is size and lead time.
- High-end 5-axis machines and automated horizontals. Mazak and DMG MORI already build some in the US, so expansion of existing plants is the shorter path here.
3. Aerospace, Gas Turbines, Munitions and Ships Drove Machine Demand in 2026
US machine tool orders have picked up significantly in 2025 and 2026. Order value rose 22.5% to $5.74bn in 2025, and another 45.0% to $5.76bn in January to September 2026. That was after 3 straight years of decline, including a 3.8% fall in 2024. AMT calls the first half of 2026 its strongest half since the series began in 1998.
Who buys these machines in the US?
- Aerospace orders rose 45.1% in 2025, and in the first half of 2026 aerospace ordered more machinery than in any half on record. AMT ties 2026 demand to the space economy, commercial aircraft backlogs and munitions, so commercial demand is part of it alongside defense.
- Power generation orders in the first half of 2026 ran 14% above automotive.
- Contract job shops, AMT’s largest customer group, grew orders 19.1% in 2025.
- Data centers drive gas turbines machinery demands. Klingelnberg says that in the US “the rising energy needs of these data centers are providing additional momentum, for example through investments in gas turbines.”
The US buys $11.4bn of machine tools a year today. Four build-outs (munitions, ships, gas turbines, commercial aerospace) add $1.0bn to $2.9bn a year of extra buying for 5 years, on top of 1% to 3% normal growth. That puts US buying at $12.7bn to $15.4bn a year in 2026 to 2030.
Munitions is the largest piece. The one new US plant we found, Haas Henderson, adds about $0.5bn of machines sold at home. So imports rise from $5.8bn to about $6.9bn to $9.5bn a year, and the import share goes from 51% to 54% to 62%.
4. Who Builds Machine Tools in the US, and How Fast Can Supply Ramp?
A domestic ramp-up faces four limiting factors.
- Workforce. This is the manufacturing story repeating all over again. Gleason’s executive put it first, saying “First you need a large enough, trained workforce. This needs to be the top priority to expand the industrial base.” Haas is hiring more than 1,000 people for Henderson at starting pay of about $23 an hour.
- Castings. Castings are the heavy iron bed and columns of a machine. Haas bought “more than 100 million pounds of castings each year” back in 2006 and worried that shrinking US foundry numbers “could limit their company’s growth.” At 10,000 to 13,000 machines a year, that is roughly 7,700 to 10,000 pounds (3.5 to 4.5 tonnes, about the weight of 2 to 3 cars) of castings per machine.
- Imported components. The parts inside the machines are imported too, including controls (FANUC, Siemens, Heidenhain, Mitsubishi), spindles, ball screws and linear guides. Tariffs raise their cost, and control deliveries have seen delays. 
  - In April 2025 Haas asked for “tariff exemptions for raw materials and components vital to the U.S. machine tool industry.” DMG MORI’s 2025 results blame late deliveries partly on “delays in switching to new European-made CNCs.”
- Time. “A shift in global production takes a lot of time,” per GMTA, a US importer of German gear machines. One example is Haas’s plant in Henderson, Nevada. The city closed the land sale in November 2019, with completion planned for 2022. Haas asked the city to extend its deadline, citing the pandemic, supply chains and construction costs. They eventually held the groundbreaking in October 2024. The plant is scheduled to open in Q1 2027, 5 years behind schedule.
Imports are slow to fill a jump in demand too, since foreign builders hold about 7 months of sales in backlog, with DMG MORI at 7.0 months on September 30, 2026 and Klingelnberg at about 7 at the end of March 2026. Klingelnberg’s backlog has halved since 2023.
5. Fixed Costs and People Keep New Machine Tool Builders Scarce
Would this spur a new generation of startups to build the machines that build the machines? As I read the filings of listed builders, the economics are brutal.
What I took away from these financials is that for European and Japanese builders, people cost about as much as materials. Personnel is 30% to 41% of revenue or operating output and materials 38% to 41%. At Chinese builders, total employee pay is 15% to 19% of revenue (Haitian and Kede, 2025) and materials 50% to 62%. Personnel, depreciation and overhead are fixed costs, so margins swing with the cycle. 2025 was a weak year. In 2023 Hermle earned an operating margin of about 21.8% and DMG MORI 10.0%. Labor productivity in US metalworking machinery “has grown only 0.9% per year over the last 30 years.”
What are the key materials? Neway, a Chinese CNC machine builder (688697.SS)’s IPO prospectus published their bill of materials. Of Rmb840.0mn ($122mn) of purchases in 2020, the split is below.
- Functional components (hydraulics, tool magazines, rotary tables) are 25.6%
- Castings are 22.3%
- Electrical parts (mainly the control) are 20.9%. The control alone is about 17.7% of purchases.
- Transmission parts (spindles, guides, screws, bearings, gears) are 15.4%
- Accessories, machined parts, sheet metal and other are 15.8%
Control and distribution are two levers that can help expand margins.
- The control. A CNC control is the machine’s computer, software, servo drives and motors. Most builders we checked buy it from FANUC, Siemens, Heidenhain or Mitsubishi, and FANUC earns a 21.4% operating margin (company-wide) against 3% to 10% at most builders we checked.
- Cutting the middlemen. US distribution typically has 2 levels, “a wholesaler and a dealer,” and “each level marks their cost up as much as 20%.”
6. Machine Tool Startups Building the Machines That Build the Machines
Could venture capital close the machinery gap with the next wave of startups? I went searching and found no venture-backed US company building production machining centers, grinders or gear machines. (If you are building them, I’d love to hear from you!)
What we can learn from history. Haas, the largest machine builder in North America, was founded in 1983, during the import surge behind the 1983 machine tool Section 232 petition. It started with indexers and built its first vertical machining center in 1987. Today it builds about 10,000 to 15,000 machines a year on about $1.2bn of revenue, and is private.
The small US builders popped up in the 2000s. They include Tormach (Wisconsin, 2001), Pocket NC, now Penta Machine (Montana, 2011), and Langmuir Systems, a plasma-table maker bought by ShopSabre in 2023. They design and sell desktop and small-shop machines.
US venture money has gone to companies that use machine tools or build equipment for their own factories. Examples include Hadrian, Machina Labs, Divergent, VulcanForms, Freeform and Seurat. Hadrian’s new Alabama factory is the first of three supported by a $900mn Navy contract, with a goal to “automate 80% of the work.”
This year’s capital went to factory software and sensing. Arda, led by OpenAI’s former research chief Bob McGrew, came out of stealth in October 2026 with $232mn of funding, its Series A at a $1.5bn valuation, building AI that turns product designs into assembly lines. Matter, whose cofounder and CEO Adi Prasad came from Tesla, offers final assembly, test and packaging for robots in the US. In machining software, CloudNC raised $20mn (UK, September 2026, with Lockheed’s venture arm), Limitless Labs $20mn (Israel) and IPercept $16.5mn (Sweden, entering the US).
Funded machine builders abroad tell a different story. Ethereal Machines (India) raised a $28.5mn Series B in 2026. It builds its own multi-axis CNC machines, sells machining as a service from them, and is building its own controller and a 300,000 sq ft plant. Shanghai Xinghe (China) builds gear grinders and raised several hundred million yuan in July 2026.
Government money has gone to training and adjacent supply. America’s Cutting Edge, a national CNC machining training initiative backed by Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), received $42mn from the Defense Department from 2020 to 2022 for machine tool training and R&D. The Pentagon’s industrial base program has awarded over $3.3bn since FY2024. The releases we read do not name any machine tool builder.
With Section 232, I believe two opportunities arise domestically in the US.
- Foreign builders establish US bases to build machines. They are more experienced in navigating thin margins, but that would likely still require government incentives to boost investments.
- Startups in the same spirit as Ethereal Machines launch in the US. They would need to think carefully about how to cut labor cost, solve the materials supply chain bottleneck, and build the control in-house from day one.
7. Section 232, the 1986 Machine Tool Precedent and What the 180 Days Decide
This Section 232 has until April 26, 2027 for its first negotiation update. Section 232 last came for machine tools in 1983, 43 years ago. Will history repeat or rhyme?
The US lost its lead in the 1970s and 1980s. Japanese machine tool exports to the US rose over 1,200% between 1964 and 1967, and by 1986 imports were 75% of the numerically controlled (NC) machines sold in the US, the category that includes today’s CNC machines. Across all machine tools, imports went from about 10% of US consumption in the mid-1970s to 25% by 1981 and about 50% by 1986.
- March 1983. The builders’ association petitions for import quotas under Section 232.
- May 20, 1986. Reagan chooses negotiation. “Voluntary restraint agreements will be sought with Taiwan, West Germany, Japan, and Switzerland.”
- Dec 16, 1986. Japan and Taiwan agree to 5 years of restraint from January 1987. The White House projects up to 16,500 more domestic machine sales over the 5 years and cites industry estimates of about $115mn of new plant investment. The full outcome is hard to score. One NBER study found US output rose from 41,992 machines in 1987 to 48,668 in 1988.
- By Oct 1991. Reports said “at least 10 Japanese machine-toolmakers have established plants in the U.S.”

articles.title: The most expensive bargaining chip in history
articles.body:
Back to the index
The most expensive bargaining chip in history
Or: why I suspect the Nvidia scandal has rather more to do with China than Jensen Huang's sex life.
I've spent the past fortnight watching what has to be one of the most extraordinary corporate meltdowns in recent history. Nvidia, the company at the centre of the AI revolution, has lost its founder-CEO, shed an enormous amount of market value, and attracted an apparently inexhaustible supply of accusations ranging from accounting fraud to treason.
All because Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman whom American intelligence believes may have been working for China.
Or so the story goes.
I've been watching the coverage with increasing incredulity. Every day brings some new allegation, generally more sensational than the last, and remarkably few seem to require any supporting evidence. The internet has collectively decided that Huang is guilty of everything from deliberately circumventing export controls to handing over the keys to Nvidia's technological kingdom.
And the share price has obligingly followed the hysteria downwards.
But something about the whole affair has been bothering me. Not simply the media's apparent inability to distinguish an allegation from a fact, or the quite extraordinary willingness of otherwise intelligent people to abandon basic standards of evidence when presented with a sufficiently salacious story.
It's the timing.
There is a missing variable in this picture. Something that makes the otherwise rather bizarre behaviour of the Trump administration, Nvidia's board, and the various national-security officials involved fit together.
I think I may have found it.
What if the entire affair is about negotiating with China?
And what if Nvidia's apparent destruction is not an unfortunate side effect, but a calculated cost?
Start with what we know
American intelligence has reportedly known about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang since at least 2025.
Trump was reportedly briefed in late 2025, and again by Marco Rubio in May 2026, while travelling to meet Xi Jinping in China.
He did precisely nothing. Huang retained his access to the White House and continued advocating for American semiconductor exports to China.
Meanwhile, there was a longstanding disagreement within the administration about precisely those exports.
Huang's position was straightforward: sell China American chips, make Chinese businesses dependent on American technology, and preserve the dominance of the American software and hardware ecosystem.
The national-security faction took the opposite view. Every advanced American chip supplied to China was potentially strengthening a strategic competitor.
Two perfectly intelligible positions, with enormous economic and geopolitical consequences.
In spring 2026, Rubio reportedly oversaw a classified memorandum based on CIA intelligence about Alice Huang. According to the Washington Post, he recast the intelligence in more assertive language.
That is a remarkably interesting detail.
We haven't seen the original CIA assessment or Rubio's memorandum. Nor do we know who disclosed its contents to journalists. The reporting establishes that Rubio prepared and circulated the memorandum, not that he personally leaked it.
But the distinction between what the CIA assessed and what Rubio subsequently wrote could turn out to be very important indeed.
Now consider what happened next.
On 28 October, Nvidia announced that it would report quarterly earnings on 17 November.
On 29 October, the first major allegations became public.
On 3 November, Trump's Republicans suffered a midterm defeat.
On 11 November, Nvidia's board accepted Huang's resignation as president, CEO and director, effective immediately.
And on 16 November, three days before Trump was due to meet Xi in Shenzhen, Washington announced new restrictions on Chinese access to American AI computing through overseas data centres.
That last development is the one that really caught my attention.
The curious case of Bessent and Lutnick
Scott Bessent, the Treasury Secretary, has been publicly attacking Howard Lutnick, the Commerce Secretary, for failing to impose sufficiently restrictive controls on advanced semiconductor exports.
Lutnick's position has been that unnecessarily antagonising Beijing risks a wider confrontation.
And Trump?
Trump has been positively serene.
This is a man whose customary response to disagreement is not exactly characterised by studied equanimity. Yet when asked about the increasingly public dispute between his two Cabinet secretaries, he declined to condemn either.
He described them as representing two different approaches to China, both of which he understood.
Which is interesting enough.
But the new export-control rule contains an extraordinary detail.
Although formally issued by the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, its own announcement says it was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council.
Read that again.
The department responsible for administering export controls has published a rule explicitly identifying another department and the White House security apparatus as its authors.
Bessent's faction has, apparently, got its policy.
And they've got it three days before Trump meets Xi.
Coincidence? Entirely possible.
But now consider the incentives.
Good cop, bad cop
Imagine you're preparing to negotiate with China.
You want access to rare earths and other strategic materials. China wants continued access to American technology. Both sides have things the other wants, and both have ways of making life unpleasant.
How do you improve your negotiating position?
One approach is to threaten restrictions on advanced computing unless China provides concessions.
The trouble with that is that the move is transparently coercive. Beijing knows exactly what you're doing, and might respond by escalating its own restrictions.
There is another approach.
Suppose an intelligence scandal erupts involving the CEO of America's most strategically important semiconductor company. Suddenly there are congressional investigations, national-security concerns, accusations of illicit exports, and demands for drastic action.
The administration announces tougher restrictions.
Not, ostensibly, because it's trying to extract concessions from China.
Heavens, no.
Because the scandal has revealed an urgent national-security problem that must be addressed.
Bessent plays the hawk. Lutnick warns about the consequences of confrontation. Trump, displaying an unusual degree of restraint, listens carefully to both.
And then he meets Xi.
Now Trump can say, in effect:
Look, my national-security people are demanding these restrictions. They're very serious about them. I'd like to maintain our good relationship, but I'll need something substantial if I'm going to relax them.
The negotiating position is no longer a threat to introduce new restrictions.
The restrictions already exist. Relaxing them becomes a concession.
And what might China offer in return?
Rare-earth access would be an obvious candidate.
China has already extended the suspension of certain export restrictions until January 2027, while retaining other controls. That is a useful reminder that access to strategic materials is not settled permanently.
There are any number of other possible concessions: trade, tariffs, market access, technology arrangements.
Trump returns home and announces a tremendous agreement.
A very good deal.
The best deal, probably. Nobody has ever seen such a deal.
And everyone gets to declare victory.
But why involve Nvidia's leadership?
This is where the hypothesis becomes rather more speculative, and considerably more interesting.
Huang has resigned, but Nvidia's SEC filing doesn't tell us who initiated the departure, whether he was pressured to resign, or what prompted the decision.
The board initially expressed confidence in him. Days later, he was gone.
Now, despite an extraordinary campaign by employees, shareholders and industry leaders calling for his reinstatement, the board reportedly refuses even to consider bringing him back while its investigation continues.
No detailed explanation of the departure has been published.
This is generally interpreted as evidence that the board has decided Huang's conduct was so reprehensible that Nvidia cannot possibly continue under his leadership.
But there is another possibility.
What if they've been told not to bring him back yet?
Not permanently. Not because the investigation has established some appalling crime. Simply because the political situation hasn't been resolved.
Keep the interim CEO. Continue the search for a replacement. Maintain the appearance that the leadership transition is proceeding normally.
Don't make any moves until Washington has finished negotiating.
If Huang subsequently returns, the board can describe the reinstatement as the result of a careful investigation, reflection, shareholder engagement, or whatever other corporate-governance language proves convenient.
This is not an allegation that Nvidia's directors have received such instructions. I have seen no evidence that they have.
It is a hypothesis that would explain several otherwise rather awkward features of the sequence.
And it comes with an important consequence: if the separation was always intended to be temporary, the staggering market reaction could be a cost somebody anticipated rather than a consequence nobody foresaw.
That would be an extraordinary gamble.
Which brings us to the obvious objection.
Surely nobody would deliberately do this to Nvidia?
Quite.
Why would an American administration deliberately destabilise one of the most valuable companies in the world, the leading supplier of the computing infrastructure underpinning its AI ambitions, just before an important diplomatic summit?
Why risk damaging investor confidence, disrupting an enormous financing ecosystem, and potentially compromising America's technological leadership?
It sounds insane.
And that is precisely what makes the possibility interesting.
In strategic terms, an apparent act of self-harm can be an effective signal if your opponent cannot readily imagine that you would undertake it merely as a negotiating tactic.
Of course, there are limits to this reasoning. An action being surprising does not make it clever, and economic damage does not become imaginary merely because someone hopes to reverse it.
Nvidia's share-price decline is real. Its leadership disruption is real. Financing arrangements, customer confidence and technical execution cannot necessarily be restored by issuing a cheerful press release after a summit.
For this strategy to make sense, the people undertaking it would have to believe that the eventual diplomatic gains justified the disruption, and that the damage could be contained.
Which brings us back to the earnings announcement.
The conveniently timed earnings report
Nvidia reports tomorrow, 17 November.
Management has previously indicated that demand continues to exceed its ability to supply hardware, with substantial expansion expected across successive generations.
Suppose the company produces another exceptional quarter and issues robust guidance.
That could provide a useful stabilising influence precisely when the market is questioning its future.
The administration gets its diplomatic confrontation on Thursday, while investors have fresh operating results against which to judge the company's prospects.
If the negotiations produce a breakthrough, export restrictions can potentially be relaxed and the political temperature reduced.
Perhaps the board's attitude towards Huang's return changes soon afterwards.
Perhaps the independent investigation concludes that the affair was deeply embarrassing but uncovered no material compromise of Nvidia's technology.
Perhaps the scandal simply fades as abruptly as it appeared.
I stress: none of those outcomes is established, and none would prove the events had been coordinated in advance.
But the sequence would be consistent with the mechanism.
And its timing is remarkably convenient.
So what would convince me?
The next few days give us a chance to see whether that timing mattered.
If Thursday's negotiations produce Chinese concessions on rare earths or other strategic materials, accompanied by American flexibility on advanced computing access, that would support the bargaining-leverage component.
If Nvidia's board subsequently reopens the question of Huang's reinstatement, particularly without any dramatic intervening investigative discovery, that would add another interesting piece.
If the intelligence investigation winds down shortly afterwards without finding material wrongdoing, the question of why Huang departed so abruptly would become more pressing.
Conversely, if the chip restrictions remain in place regardless of Chinese concessions, the investigation produces substantive findings explaining Huang's departure, and the board proceeds with a permanent successor, the integrated hypothesis becomes substantially less convincing.
And even a perfectly aligned sequence of favourable developments would not prove prior coordination.
For that, we'd need something much more direct: evidence about the original disclosure, communications between Washington and Nvidia, or documentary proof that someone deliberately sequenced these events.
Until then, this remains a hypothesis.
A rather intriguing one.
Cui bono?
I've watched a great many people examine this scandal as though it were fundamentally a question of whether Jensen Huang should have kept his trousers on.
That may make for excellent television. It doesn't strike me as a particularly satisfactory explanation for the broader geopolitical developments.
The questions I find interesting are rather different.
Who benefits from weakening Huang's influence over American export policy?
Who benefits from imposing additional restrictions on Chinese computing access immediately before major bilateral negotiations?
Why has Trump declined repeated invitations to publicly choose between his feuding Cabinet secretaries?
Why has the administration suddenly found a way to impose restrictions that were previously stalled?
And why has Nvidia's leadership crisis unfolded in such close proximity to both its earnings announcement and the summit?
None of those questions proves anything by itself.
Together, however, they form a pattern worth examining.
My suspicion is that the Nvidia scandal has become a bargaining instrument in a much larger confrontation over technology, rare earths and the terms of America's relationship with China.
Whether that was planned from the outset or opportunistically exploited remains the critical uncertainty.
The distinction matters. A skilful exploitation of unexpected circumstances is very different from deliberately engineering an extraordinary corporate crisis.
But if the full, coordinated version turns out to be correct, it would be an astonishing piece of realpolitik: publicly destabilising America's most important AI supplier, using the resulting outrage to justify restrictions, extracting concessions from Beijing, and then allowing the crisis to resolve.
All while maintaining the appearance that each event emerged organically.
And if the crisis was not coordinated, it is still worth understanding how an affair, an intelligence assessment, a corporate resignation and an interdepartmental policy battle have converged at such a consequential diplomatic moment.
I have no intention of mistaking a pleasing pattern for proof. That's precisely the mistake I've spent the past fortnight watching other people make about Huang.
But equally, I see no reason to ignore a hypothesis simply because it suggests that the public explanation may not be the whole explanation.
Thursday should be interesting.

articles.title: US will say "no" to global ban on killer robots
articles.body:
The United States is expected to oppose a push to begin negotiations on a legally binding treaty restricting autonomous weapons, as countries gather in Geneva for a five-day United Nations conference.
The Seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW), running from November 16 to 20, will consider the next steps for weapons capable of selecting and engaging targets without further human intervention. The UN has warned that such systems pose growing risks to civilians and raise concerns about compliance with international humanitarian law.
The conference is not expected to produce a treaty this week. Instead, delegates will consider whether to launch negotiations on new rules and whether any resulting agreement should be legally binding.
Read More on News
Pressure for Binding Rules
UN human rights chief Volker Türk has called on states to act before technological development outpaces diplomacy. “The international community has critical choices to make right now about the future of armed conflicts and the role of human beings in decisions over the use of force,” he said. “I call on states to urgently agree on binding international rules to regulate autonomous weapons and protect human lives—before it is too late.”
Türk has also called for prohibitions on autonomous weapons that target people, whether by design or in practice, and on systems whose functioning and effects cannot be adequately understood, predicted or controlled by humans.
Newsweek contacted the State Department for comment on Monday.
Nicole van Rooijen, executive director of the campaign group Stop Killer Robots, said in a statement provided to Newsweek that “the vast majority of states worldwide” favor a legally binding instrument, while only about a dozen, including the U.S., Israel and Russia, oppose one.
According to Stop Killer Robots, 130 countries support a legally binding instrument on autonomous weapons, while more than 70 have indicated they are ready to move forward with negotiations.
“We are at a critical juncture,” van Rooijen said, calling for time-limited negotiations on a binding treaty. Campaigners have warned that failing to act could allow technological developments and battlefield practice to shape the rules governing autonomous weapons.
Rather than negotiating a binding treaty, the U.S. has proposed five more years of work by the CCW's expert group to develop a nonbinding instrument, according to a November 4 working paper.
Washington maintains that existing international humanitarian law already applies to autonomous weapons and that a new legally binding treaty is unnecessary.
In the paper, Washington argued that nonbinding rules could be adopted and updated more quickly as technology and military practices evolve. It said such an approach would avoid creating separate legal regimes applying only to countries that ratified a treaty.
The paper also argued it has not been established that autonomous weapons are inherently indiscriminate or excessively injurious, or that they require new prohibitions.
“Rather, State practice in using autonomy in weapon systems demonstrates that appropriate use of autonomous functions can enhance the implementation of existing prohibitions and restrictions in [international humanitarian law] and reduce the risks to civilians as compared to weapons without such capabilities,” it said. “It would be contrary to the humanitarian objectives and purposes of the CCW for states to hamper responsible innovation that advances those objectives and purposes.”
Already Moving Onto Battlefields
The UN has already warned that the debate over autonomous weapons is no longer purely hypothetical. Autonomous weapons systems are increasingly being tested, integrated and deployed, according to Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and Stop Killer Robots, while drones have become central to fighting in Ukraine.
Human Rights Watch has warned that autonomous weapons could misidentify targets, discriminate against vulnerable populations and create gaps in accountability when attacks go wrong. In a 2025 report, the organization called for a legally binding treaty prohibiting weapons that operate without meaningful human control or target people, while regulating other autonomous systems.
AI-assisted weapons and targeting systems have been used in conflicts, including Ukraine and the Middle East. However, such technology is not necessarily fully autonomous: systems that help human operators identify targets differ from weapons capable of selecting and attacking targets without further human approval.
“States must ensure that Russia, or any of the handful of governments blocking progress, are not allowed to hold the future hostage. The stakes are too high,” Anna Hehir, head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, said in a statement emailed to Newsweek.
“A clear global majority has spoken: machines should never be able to decide to kill. States must now use all mechanisms possible, both within and beyond the current U.N. CCW process, to keep human control.”
Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Henry Holloway and Rhian Morgan.

articles.title: Regulatory Capture by Anthropic Through METR
articles.body:
I have conducted an audit of Anthropic's finances.
What I have found is so shocking that I am calling for a Congressional investigation.
Anthropic is not just seeking regulatory capture.
It has built a regulatory capture machine that cannot be turned off.
Structural financial incentives make it impossible for Anthropic -- I call it the Anthropic Network -- to turn off its own AI doom cycle.
It starts with METR.
Dario Amodei proposes "third-party evaluators" to assess the risk of Anthropic's models.
He proposes METR for this purpose.
But METR is financially dependent on the Anthropic's success -- specifically, on the explosive growth of more than $7 billion dollars in Anthropic stock.
Dustin Moskovitz invested this stock into Good Ventures Foundation, where it represents the majority of that organization's portfolio.
And GVF is the overwhelming funder of the entire Anthropic Network ecosystem.
This stock was worth $500 million early last year.
It is worth more than $7.7 billion just ~16 months later.
METR -- and all of those building a career its parent organizations -- cannot afford to disrupt that growth.
Because if Anthropic goes under, many of the organizations that fund METR go under as well.
But if Anthropic succeeds, METR and its parent organizations become more richly financed to regulate AI -- something those at METR want very much.
The "third-party evaluator" is not "third-party" at all.
The evaluator is on Anthropic's payroll.
If this were the end of it, that's bad.
But that isn't all.
The same organizations that fund METR also fund the many organizations, such as the Tarbell Center, that promote AI Doom.
The Tarbell Center publishes AI Doom articles in The Verge, Science, LA Times, The Dispatch, TIME, and others.
They are selling the problem, and then selling the solution to the problem -- from the same money pile: Anthropic's.
All of these organizations are financially dependent on the same exploding $7 billion money pile.
As Anthropic grows more and more powerful, its AI Doom Machine grows better and better financed -- louder and louder.
Meanwhile, the regulatory regime seeded in METR grows larger to solve the increasingly loud -- now hysterical -- problem of AI Doom that the Anthropic Network itself created.
From this standpoint, as Anthropic becomes more powerful, AI might be getting scarier, sure -- but the positive feedback loop also becomes more deafening -- independent of objective facts.
This itself is an objective fact.
The deafening AI Doom is part of an business model, that, as it expands, so too does the AI Doom messaging -- there is simply more money to do it.
But the problem also goes in the other direction:
If Anthropic dies, the Regulatory Regime and the AI Doom Machine are crippled or die.
Neither METR nor Tarbell nor the other organizations in the Anthropic Network can allow that to happen.
Hence, neither METR or the AI Doom Machine can be trusted to provide independent assessments of Anthropic's models or AI more broadly.
They simply are not organizations independent of Anthropic.
And Anthropic cannot detach itself from METR or Tarbell or countless other safety orgs (not shown here), either, because they drive hype for the models and the possibility of eventual regulatory capture, and Anthropic will not give that up willingly.
What's more, the people at all of these organizations are all the same ecosystem, the same community. They just shuffle between organizations.
The Anthropic Network is therefore, so long as it is successful, locked into a self-amplifying feedback loop inside an ideological monoculture.
And that feedback loop is winning.
That's what Jacob Coxon is.
China is keeping messaging tight. That is why optimism for AI is so high in China.
America has Anthropic: a massive company pushing anti-AI propaganda at a state level.
Anthropic will either create hysteria until American AI slows down and China wins, or it will create fractures throughout American society with severe political consequences.
Ironically, because of the structural financial incentives underpinning the Anthropic Network, it has become the same kind of self-amplifying virus that it fantasizes AI to become in the future -- while hiding its tracks just as carefully.
It is the mirror of the same AI virus that it hypothesizes to consume America.
Anthropic's business model, models itself after the very thing it claims to fear.
Except Anthropic's ideology infects humans, not computers.
Congress must investigate.
Evidence and Github in next post.
Then some supplementary figures.
