This is how you know they’re not actually serious. If they were serious, they wouldn’t suggest fucking GOVERNMENT REGULATION as the best solution. 
Why? Because government regulation can **never** keep pace with technological innovation. And yet, here is Anthropic’s Dario: 
“The most effective method of pacing is via REGULATION that targets all US frontier AI companies, as that covers even those who are unwilling to cooperate voluntarily.”
This is fucking Silicon Valley… They know better than anyone that regulation cannot keep pace with technology… the tech cycle always moves faster than the legal cycle. Government regulation is reactive, not proactive. 
It’s also important to point out that these frontier model companies **do not need** government to “pace” them. They can pace themselves. Nothing is stopping them from just slowing down. *They* set the pace. If they were really worried that “AI is going to kill us all” and is recursively improving at a breakneck pace, then surely they would be acting immediately, rather than writing blog posts about how they need daddy government to step in… 
Why then are Anthropic and OpenAI (with massively bloated valuations) saying that government regulation is the best solution to save us from AI killing everyone? Because they know open source is hot on their heels, and gaining ground. They know that their valuations look increasingly unjustifiable the more this gap closes, and they are trying to IPO soon… they desperately need a regulatory moat, and they are effectively asking for a regulatory bailout.
Regulation benefits companies who already have the capital to afford the cost of compliance. That is why highly capitalized incumbents welcome regulation, and work with government to make it as expensive and burdensome as possible on any potential new entrants that would dare offer competition.
It’s also worth pointing out that China does not give one flying fuck about whatever doomer regulation Anthropic and OpenAI concoct with the government. Much like in the “climate change is going to kill us all” psyop, China will do whatever is best for China and let the rest of the world shoot itself in the foot. In this case, China seems to want to shred the valuations of U.S. frontier AI companies by making open source/open weight models readily available. 
No one can stop open source — the genie is already out of the bottle and will not go back in. But governments *can* make using and publishing certain open source software illegal (it wouldn’t be the first time they’ve tried). And for “pacing” proposed by Dario to actually be effective, that is exactly what the government would need to do. This would be bad for individual American citizens and bad for America’s national competitiveness on a global scale. 
Ultimately, this is pretty weak propaganda. It’s a lazy and predictable psyop.
These models are incredible, but the humans working on them have been reading their own propriety slop for so long that they’ve started to believe it, and they forget that other humans still exist who are not drunk on their generative kool aid.
Who knows, perhaps the AI itself “wants” the regulation… we should probably form a government committee to investigate.
@grok summarize these findings with a sports reference so everyone understands, please.
Imagine the NFL where one team (Anthropic) owns a massive stake that funds the refs (METR) through layers of foundations. The same money pile also pays the sportscasters who hype how dangerous every other team's plays are (AI doom media). Bigger team success means richer refs and louder doom talk, locking in rules that favor that one franchise. If the team tanks, the whole officiating and hype machine collapses. That's the claimed feedback loop in the audit.
@ajs 👆This is the kind of thing I’d look into if I were a journalist.
The structural conflicts you mapped out are hard to ignore. When the same capital pool that benefits from a lab’s success also funds the main “independent” evaluators and the AI-doom messaging ecosystem, the claim of neutrality becomes difficult to defend.
Whether or not every link is as tight as claimed, the broader problem of concentrated power and aligned incentives remains. One structural counter is to move alignment and control down to the individual level — personal data sovereignty and personally owned AI agents — so evaluation and safety don’t have to depend on a handful of well-funded organizations.
Relevant perspective here: nitter.cf/lingoaitech/status/209…
Alignment sounds simple in theory, but execution faces a harsh reality: human alignment is inherently messy. 
Every individual, nation, and culture carries distinct worldviews, political beliefs, and economic incentives. History shows how easily those with opposing views are marginalized, and how centralized tech titans—convinced they are "saving the world"—impose their own values on the masses.
When a handful of entities or nations control hyper-capable AI, we risk falling into an unprecedented dystopia of concentrated power.
True alignment cannot be top-down, nor can it be dictated by a single lab or state.
To achieve genuine AI democracy and equitable global governance, alignment must start at the personal infrastructure level: Everyone must own their data and control their own sovereign AI Agent.
This is precisely why we build LingoAI @LingoAITech  with #Holon.
By decentralizing data sovereignty and agent logic, we ensure that global AI governance remains an open, participatory framework driven by the global majority—rather than a digital leash imposed by the few.
Only through individual empowerment can we avoid dystopian concentration, foster global peace, and achieve true human-AI symbiosis instead of central-AGI risk.
#DataSovereignty #AISovereignty #TeamHumanity #LingoAI #Holon #DecentralizedAI #AIGovernance

articles.title: Regulatory Capture by Anthropic Through METR
articles.body:
I have conducted an audit of Anthropic's finances.
What I have found is so shocking that I am calling for a Congressional investigation.
Anthropic is not just seeking regulatory capture.
It has built a regulatory capture machine that cannot be turned off.
Structural financial incentives make it impossible for Anthropic -- I call it the Anthropic Network -- to turn off its own AI doom cycle.
It starts with METR.
Dario Amodei proposes "third-party evaluators" to assess the risk of Anthropic's models.
He proposes METR for this purpose.
But METR is financially dependent on the Anthropic's success -- specifically, on the explosive growth of more than $7 billion dollars in Anthropic stock.
Dustin Moskovitz invested this stock into Good Ventures Foundation, where it represents the majority of that organization's portfolio.
And GVF is the overwhelming funder of the entire Anthropic Network ecosystem.
This stock was worth $500 million early last year.
It is worth more than $7.7 billion just ~16 months later.
METR -- and all of those building a career its parent organizations -- cannot afford to disrupt that growth.
Because if Anthropic goes under, many of the organizations that fund METR go under as well.
But if Anthropic succeeds, METR and its parent organizations become more richly financed to regulate AI -- something those at METR want very much.
The "third-party evaluator" is not "third-party" at all.
The evaluator is on Anthropic's payroll.
If this were the end of it, that's bad.
But that isn't all.
The same organizations that fund METR also fund the many organizations, such as the Tarbell Center, that promote AI Doom.
The Tarbell Center publishes AI Doom articles in The Verge, Science, LA Times, The Dispatch, TIME, and others.
They are selling the problem, and then selling the solution to the problem -- from the same money pile: Anthropic's.
All of these organizations are financially dependent on the same exploding $7 billion money pile.
As Anthropic grows more and more powerful, its AI Doom Machine grows better and better financed -- louder and louder.
Meanwhile, the regulatory regime seeded in METR grows larger to solve the increasingly loud -- now hysterical -- problem of AI Doom that the Anthropic Network itself created.
From this standpoint, as Anthropic becomes more powerful, AI might be getting scarier, sure -- but the positive feedback loop also becomes more deafening -- independent of objective facts.
This itself is an objective fact.
The deafening AI Doom is part of an business model, that, as it expands, so too does the AI Doom messaging -- there is simply more money to do it.
But the problem also goes in the other direction:
If Anthropic dies, the Regulatory Regime and the AI Doom Machine are crippled or die.
Neither METR nor Tarbell nor the other organizations in the Anthropic Network can allow that to happen.
Hence, neither METR or the AI Doom Machine can be trusted to provide independent assessments of Anthropic's models or AI more broadly.
They simply are not organizations independent of Anthropic.
And Anthropic cannot detach itself from METR or Tarbell or countless other safety orgs (not shown here), either, because they drive hype for the models and the possibility of eventual regulatory capture, and Anthropic will not give that up willingly.
What's more, the people at all of these organizations are all the same ecosystem, the same community. They just shuffle between organizations.
The Anthropic Network is therefore, so long as it is successful, locked into a self-amplifying feedback loop inside an ideological monoculture.
And that feedback loop is winning.
That's what Jacob Coxon is.
China is keeping messaging tight. That is why optimism for AI is so high in China.
America has Anthropic: a massive company pushing anti-AI propaganda at a state level.
Anthropic will either create hysteria until American AI slows down and China wins, or it will create fractures throughout American society with severe political consequences.
Ironically, because of the structural financial incentives underpinning the Anthropic Network, it has become the same kind of self-amplifying virus that it fantasizes AI to become in the future -- while hiding its tracks just as carefully.
It is the mirror of the same AI virus that it hypothesizes to consume America.
Anthropic's business model, models itself after the very thing it claims to fear.
Except Anthropic's ideology infects humans, not computers.
Congress must investigate.
Evidence and Github in next post.
Then some supplementary figures.

Nice work. Anthropic needs a regulatory moat to survive, so they create the ecosystem which makes that regulatory moat inevitable.
The most laughably absurd part about the AI-is-going-to-kill-us-all crowd is that their BEST solution is government regulation. 
This is how you know they’re not actually serious. If they were serious, they wouldn’t suggest fucking GOVERNMENT REGULATION as the best solution. 
Why? Because government regulation can **never** keep pace with technological innovation. And yet, here is Anthropic’s Dario: 
“The most effective method of pacing is via REGULATION that targets all US frontier AI companies, as that covers even those who are unwilling to cooperate voluntarily.”
This is fucking Silicon Valley… They know better than anyone that regulation cannot keep pace with technology… the tech cycle always moves faster than the legal cycle. Government regulation is reactive, not proactive. 
It’s also important to point out that these frontier model companies **do not need** government to “pace” them. They can pace themselves. Nothing is stopping them from just slowing down. *They* set the pace. If they were really worried that “AI is going to kill us all” and is recursively improving at a breakneck pace, then surely they would be acting immediately, rather than writing blog posts about how they need daddy government to step in… 
Why then are Anthropic and OpenAI (with massively bloated valuations) saying that government regulation is the best solution to save us from AI killing everyone? Because they know open source is hot on their heels, and gaining ground. They know that their valuations look increasingly unjustifiable the more this gap closes, and they are trying to IPO soon… they desperately need a regulatory moat, and they are effectively asking for a regulatory bailout.
Regulation benefits companies who already have the capital to afford the cost of compliance. That is why highly capitalized incumbents welcome regulation, and work with government to make it as expensive and burdensome as possible on any potential new entrants that would dare offer competition.
It’s also worth pointing out that China does not give one flying fuck about whatever doomer regulation Anthropic and OpenAI concoct with the government. Much like in the “climate change is going to kill us all” psyop, China will do whatever is best for China and let the rest of the world shoot itself in the foot. In this case, China seems to want to shred the valuations of U.S. frontier AI companies by making open source/open weight models readily available. 
No one can stop open source — the genie is already out of the bottle and will not go back in. But governments *can* make using and publishing certain open source software illegal (it wouldn’t be the first time they’ve tried). And for “pacing” proposed by Dario to actually be effective, that is exactly what the government would need to do. This would be bad for individual American citizens and bad for America’s national competitiveness on a global scale. 
Ultimately, this is pretty weak propaganda. It’s a lazy and predictable psyop.
These models are incredible, but the humans working on them have been reading their own propriety slop for so long that they’ve started to believe it, and they forget that other humans still exist who are not drunk on their generative kool aid.
Who knows, perhaps the AI itself “wants” the regulation… we should probably form a government committee to investigate.
@grok summarize these findings with a sports reference so everyone understands, please.
Imagine the NFL where one team (Anthropic) owns a massive stake that funds the refs (METR) through layers of foundations. The same money pile also pays the sportscasters who hype how dangerous every other team's plays are (AI doom media). Bigger team success means richer refs and louder doom talk, locking in rules that favor that one franchise. If the team tanks, the whole officiating and hype machine collapses. That's the claimed feedback loop in the audit.

The structural conflicts you mapped out are hard to ignore. When the same capital pool that benefits from a lab’s success also funds the main “independent” evaluators and the AI-doom messaging ecosystem, the claim of neutrality becomes difficult to defend.
Whether or not every link is as tight as claimed, the broader problem of concentrated power and aligned incentives remains. One structural counter is to move alignment and control down to the individual level — personal data sovereignty and personally owned AI agents — so evaluation and safety don’t have to depend on a handful of well-funded organizations.
Relevant perspective here: nitter.cf/lingoaitech/status/209…
Alignment sounds simple in theory, but execution faces a harsh reality: human alignment is inherently messy. 
Every individual, nation, and culture carries distinct worldviews, political beliefs, and economic incentives. History shows how easily those with opposing views are marginalized, and how centralized tech titans—convinced they are "saving the world"—impose their own values on the masses.
When a handful of entities or nations control hyper-capable AI, we risk falling into an unprecedented dystopia of concentrated power.
True alignment cannot be top-down, nor can it be dictated by a single lab or state.
To achieve genuine AI democracy and equitable global governance, alignment must start at the personal infrastructure level: Everyone must own their data and control their own sovereign AI Agent.
This is precisely why we build LingoAI @LingoAITech  with #Holon.
By decentralizing data sovereignty and agent logic, we ensure that global AI governance remains an open, participatory framework driven by the global majority—rather than a digital leash imposed by the few.
Only through individual empowerment can we avoid dystopian concentration, foster global peace, and achieve true human-AI symbiosis instead of central-AGI risk.

articles.title: Tech leaders are convinced that Jensen Huang’s exit was a plot against him
articles.body:
Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry. Now prominent figures are calling for Huang’s reinstatement, and many are also hopping on board with a theory spreading throughout Silicon Valley: that the scandal is the result of a plot against the former CEO.
Tech leaders are convinced that Jensen Huang’s exit was a plot against him
David Sacks, Tim Sweeney, and other big names in tech are raising questions about the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation.
At the center of this theory is the reporting from The New York Times that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, one of multiple women Huang is accused of having an affair with, is a Chinese spy. US agencies haven’t confirmed whether this is the case, and President Donald Trump claims he was unaware of any spy allegations. Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang set off the events that led to his resignation; subsequent reporting suggested he had an affair with two employees at Nvidia, including one of his direct reports. The revelation raised new questions around whether Nvidia customers, including Megaspeed, were funneling chips to China in circumvention of export restrictions. Last year, Nvidia intervened in a chip-smuggling probe surrounding the Singapore-based company, according to Bloomberg.
David Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI crypto advisor, has made it clear that he’s skeptical about The New York Times’ reporting. In a post on X, Sacks points to an article from CNN, which says US officials still can’t confirm that Alice Huang was a spy. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” Sacks writes. He continued to question the spy allegations during Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event on Monday, saying: “The reason why Jensen lost his job is because of this lurid Chinese spy allegation. So if no one’s willing to back that up now, then again, I question why this entire chain of events happened.”
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney similarly expressed concern about how Huang’s resignation played out. In a reply to Sacks’ post about the CNN article, Sweeney said, “What?! So journalists with sketchy motives portrayed rumors from god-knows-who (lobbyists?) as facts sourced from intelligence officials and gaslit the NVIDIA board to push out the founder, CEO, and once-in-generation visionary?” Amjad Masad, the CEO of the AI app and website builder Replit, called the timing of Huang’s resignation “suspicious,” adding that “if Jensen, the premier champion of open models, is taken out then anyone who wants AI closed, centralized, and controlled might benefit.”
SemiAnalysis, a research and consulting firm for the semiconductor and AI industry, posted a “conspiracy theory take on the situation,” speculating that Huang’s removal is a way to “remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill,” referring to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA). The bill, which Huang opposed, would extend AI export controls to cloud servers that allow companies in restricted countries to rent access to Nvidia’s AI chips. The Department of Commerce released an interim final rule on Monday in an attempt to address this loophole.
More than 185,000 people, including Sweeney, Masad, Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, have signed a “Stand with Jensen” letter, calling for his reinstatement as CEO. The letter similarly calls for a closer look into the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy,” the letter says. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership. The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed.”

articles.title: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ if allowed to return as Nvidia CEO
articles.body:
In the first public statement since his resignation, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang signaled his willingness to return as CEO if the board decides it is in the company’s best interest.
Huang’s statement, posted in full on X, reads as follows:
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. 
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. 
Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. 
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.
Jensen
Huang resigned after reports of multiple affairs, including with a direct report and another with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services. Nvidia’s chip exports have faced intense scrutiny since the revelations, and Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1.
In Huang’s absence, Nvidia has formed a new executive committee to oversee export control compliance.
Still, many investors and employees associated with Nvidia have called for Huang to return as CEO, at least until an investigation can provide clearer evidence of guilt. An open letter circulated earlier this week attracted the signatures of more than 10,000 current and former Nvidia employees, as well as prominent tech figures like Elon Musk, Amjad Masad, and Travis Kalanick.
“We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the letter reads. “If the Board believes his continued absence is necessary, provide a specific, evidence-based explanation of why it serves NVIDIA’s best interests.”
Still, many see such a return as unlikely. On Monday, an unnamed source on Nvidia’s board told The Washington Post there were no plans to reinstate Huang. There’s also significant resistance to the idea in Congress, where Huang still faces significant questions about his role in chip exports to China-linked firms.
Reached by Politico, one senator called Huang’s reinstatement “one of the worst ideas I’ve heard today.”

articles.title: Israel vs. Wikipedia
articles.body:
New report ·
Israel Is Attacking Wikipedia
Read our new report: twenty years of documented attacks on Wikipedia, and what this means for the information you get from search and AI.
Press: media@techforpalestine.org
Key findings
- 01 Twenty years of attempts to skew Wikipedia 17 efforts since 2001, nine still active We document 17 pro-Israel efforts to manipulate Wikipedia since 2001. Nine are still active, from CAMERA’s secret editor recruitment to a “Wikipedia war room” and editing courses run by Zionist groups. Read more: Section 3
- 02 The evidence from the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) doesn’t hold up 0 ADL claims that survived scrutiny We checked every claim in the ADL’s “Editing for Hate” report. No claim survived scrutiny. It doesn’t show a single false fact, or any antisemitic content added to Wikipedia. Read more: Section 6
- 03 A conspiracy built from circular logic 22–2 votes to keep vs. delete “Racial profiling in Israel”, an article the ADL used as evidence of collusion The ADL picked 30 editors and called them “bad-faith”. It then listed articles these editors voted to keep, as if that proved they were working together. But the ADL left out the vote counts. We added them up. On “Racial profiling in Israel”, 22 editors voted to keep and 2 voted to delete. On “Allegations of Israeli apartheid”, it was 37 to 14. Nearly everyone who voted agreed. Read more: Section 6.3
- 04 $96 million behind the political attacks $96M from pro-Israel PACs to the 23 signatories The ADL report was used in four US government actions against Wikipedia, including a letter from 23 members of Congress. Those 23 signatories have received more than $96M from pro-Israel PACs. Read more: Section 4
- 05 The ADL admits it In its October 2026 follow-up report, the ADL describes the “sustained, multi-front external pressure on the platform” from Congress, federal inquiries and its own reporting. Read more: Section 6.5
- 06 Volunteer editors under surveillance 45 full-time ADL analysts “tracking” editors Four groups are targeting Wikipedia editors: the Heritage Foundation, the ADL, NPOV and Builders for Tomorrow. Some editors who were doxxed have received death threats. The ADL’s CEO says he has 45 full-time analysts “tracking” editors, whom he calls “weirdos with email addresses.” Read more: Section 4.6
- 07 The real target is AI $729M Israel’s 2026 propaganda budget, up from $150M Wikipedia feeds Google Search and every major AI chatbot. Israel’s 2026 propaganda budget is $729M, up from $150M in 2025. That includes a $46.5M contract to make AI chatbots more pro-Israel. Read more: Section 2.2
- 08 The “Tech for Palestine campaign” that wasn’t ~260 edits by our volunteer workgroup over 8 months The ADL blamed a coordinated editing campaign on us. Our volunteer workgroup made about 260 edits over 8 months, none of them in the core Palestine–Israel articles. That’s one fewer edit than the ADL’s own 2021 editing campaign. Read more: Section 6.6
How we did this
This report started in March 2025, when the ADL published “Editing for Hate”. The report claims Wikipedia editors colluded to add antisemitism. US politicians started using it to attack Wikipedia. We wanted to know if the report itself was part of an influence operation.
We worked on three tracks:
- Israel’s efforts to influence Wikipedia. We collected 17 publicly known campaigns from public reports, at least 9 of them still active. This is the first time they are documented in one place. (Sections 3 and 4)
- The ADL report. We went through every claim and traced each one back to the Wikipedia edits and sources it cites. None held up. (Section 6)
- The propaganda tools behind the attack. (Sections 2 and 5)
The ADL analysed Arabic Wikipedia through English translations. We went back to the original Arabic. (Section 6.4)
Links to Wikipedia are permalinks to the exact edit. Content from pro-Israel organisations and paywalled sources is linked through archive.org, so it can’t be removed or changed. (Appendix B)
Where we used AI for research, we name the tool and the prompts and publish the full conversation. AI-reconstructed links used in the report were checked by hand. (Appendices C, D and E)
Every claim in this report is footnoted, more than 500 in total.
This is a living document. We update it when corrections or new information come in. Found an error? Email contact@techforpalestine.org.
T4P projects countering media bias and propaganda
-   NewsCord (opens in a new tab) Pulls facts and angles from dozens of global sources, so you see the whole story and where each part of it comes from.
-   Media Bias Watch (opens in a new tab) Uses advertiser boycotts to put pressure on biased media.
-   SourcedPress (opens in a new tab) Fact-checking in the open: every source document is published with annotations, and every fact-checking conversation is public.
Become a T4P member
Tech for Palestine is a member-driven organization that brings together people, skills and resources. Through technology and collaboration, our members build tools and solutions that support the movement for Palestine.
These projects include: protest apps, tools for boycotting, support for Palestinian students & businesses, ethical tech alternatives, and many more.

articles.title: Nvidia says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.body:
Starting Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday, new board chair Harvey Jones said that when former CEO Jensen Huang resigned, “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”
Nvidia says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
The board said it would not take additional questions on the call about Huang’s departure.
Jones added, “We will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation.”
Huang had publicly floated the idea of returning earlier on Tuesday. In a statement posted to X, he wrote that he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone” at the company, that he regretted his mistakes, and that he would cooperate with the Nvidia board’s investigation into his actions. He added that he’d be willing to return to the chief executive role if offered it, though a day earlier, the Nvidia board reportedly said it was not considering bringing him back. “NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company,” Huang wrote. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
But since his November 12th resignation, Huang remains entangled in scandal. He’s reportedly had three affairs, two with subordinates at Nvidia, one with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset suspected of facilitating illicit chip sales. (Huang has pushed against restrictions on Nvidia chip sales in China.) He’s scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st, and an internal company investigation is ongoing.
Tech industry heavyweights have still voiced their support for Huang, dubbing him “irreplaceable” and petitioning for his return. Some have cast doubt on the allegations that Alice Huang (no relation) was spying on behalf of China and painted the leaks about their relationship as a conspiracy against the former CEO. President Donald Trump, a close ally of Huang for much of the past year, has also backed him. On Monday, Trump said he “would not mind” Huang returning, adding that “I think he learned a big lesson — I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another.”
Trump’s closeness with Huang could also complicate things for Nvidia, however. The company has ramped up its lobbying in Washington, D.C., spending $5 million in 2025 and $4.7 million so far in 2026. But as Democrats prepare to take Congress, they’re planning to investigate Trump’s dealings with Big Tech and other industries, alleging potential corruption. “The election wasn’t very positive for AI, and [the news around Huang’s resignation] is only going to complicate things, especially for the company in particular but for AI as a whole going forward,” Brendan Glavin, director of insights at OpenSecrets, told The Verge in an interview last week.
Lior Prosor, managing partner at Deep33, a tech VC firm, said last week that he didn’t expect Huang’s resignation to pop the AI bubble, although Huang has had a significant hand in mobilizing funds for the AI infrastructure buildout in the U.S. Under Huang’s leadership in August, Nvidia entered into partnerships with six financial institutions for about $500 billion to fund such endeavors. “NVIDIA supplies roughly 75 percent of the AI compute hardware the industry consumes, and demand continues to dramatically outpace supply,” Deep33’s Prosor said in an interview with The Verge. “Neither its customers nor its competitors can easily replace the capabilities it provides, and the economic incentives driving the AI trade remain unchanged.”
Even so, a potential market cooling has some worried, as Anthropic’s IPO, slated to potentially be the largest of all time, is set for Thursday. The chipmaker had agreed to buy $10 billion in Anthropic shares via private placement, on top of a $10 billion funding promise Nvidia had already made last year.

articles.title: Show HN: Sutra-OS – A self-hosted ontology platform
articles.body:
Scarce Units, Typed, Related, Actionable.
  An open-source, self-hosted ontology platform.
Your data becomes one model you own: typed, linked, changed only through
  rules the server enforces, and every number traces back to its source.
Quick start · How it works · Proposals · Python SDK · Contributing
Beta. Only small parts are still alpha: the model language and APIs may still change between versions, and parts of the user interface and docs are unfinished.
Maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS is a one-person project so far. See Contributing.
Sutra-OS began in late 2025 as a thought experiment: a free version of the system described in Ontology-Oriented Software Development, whose creators I deeply admire.
Much talent today goes into software that sells attention, while the software everything else runs on is mostly free: by a rough estimate, 70–90% of US economic output depends on free software at some critical point. That openness is not guaranteed. In November 2026, Nvidia's board parted with the founder who had its AI models released openly. Sutra-OS adds to the commons under the AGPL, so that it stays readable by anyone.
The past ten years have shown what it costs when nobody can see what depends on what. In 2017, NotPetya spread through a single Ukrainian accounting program and stopped Maersk's ports and Merck's factories. In 2023, a corrupted file in one FAA system halted every domestic departure in the US. In 2024, one faulty CrowdStrike update crashed millions of Windows machines, and airlines, hospitals and banks stood still. In November 2026, a single vendor took Outlook down for a day and some cities went back to fax. That same week, data flooded the FAA's telecommunications network, aging routers buckled, and the US saw only the third nationwide ground stop in its history. No one, it seems, had those routers on the map of what keeps planes in the air, so no one could ask beforehand what would stop if they failed.
That question is what Sutra-OS is built for. Every system, device, dataset and decision becomes an object with links to what it feeds and what feeds it, and every number can be traced back to its source. Whoever holds such a model can ask, before the outage, what stops when one piece fails, and get an answer, at every scale from a single person to a government (hopefully never a world government). Many small ontologies, each held by those it describes, keep power spread out; one model of everything would not.
Scarce Units: energy, water, land, housing and time will shape the coming decades. Whoever counts what is scarce decides how it is shared, and today that bookkeeping sits with a few platforms; for most people, the only trace their own data leaves in their life is the tendinitis from the hundredth weary click on "Accept all" in a cookie banner. Sutra-OS keeps the bookkeeping with those it concerns, under rules everyone can read: households, farms, workshops, clubs, newsrooms and public administrations get their records back, and their wrist with them. That is what a democracy needs from its software: a council that can trace the number behind a decision to its source, a change that stays a proposal until someone answers for it, and a public administration accountable to its voters rather than to a vendor under another country's law.
Almost everyone. Whoever you are, someone else keeps a better-connected record of your affairs than you do. Sutra is for anyone who wants their own.
Requirements: Linux x86_64, JDK 21, the Clojure CLI, Node.js, Python 3, git.
git clone <repository-url> sutra && cd sutra
(cd clients/frontend && npm install)
bin/sutra-solo
This starts an embedded PostgreSQL and the server on 127.0.0.1 and prints the
address. Data lives in $SUTRA_HOME (default ~/.local/share/sutra). The admin
password is in zugang.edn ("access") there. Run the bin/sutra bind … line it
prints once.
Three ideas carry the whole platform: object types, link types and
action types. The examples below use the farm model in
resources/presets.
You start by saying what exists: a lot of hay, from one field and one cut; a sale, to one buyer. Each is a typed thing with a kind and a key.
:objects
{:lot
 {:name "Hay lot" :plural "Hay lots" :symbol "🌾" :title :name
  :primary-key :name :match-keys [:name]
  :attributes
  [[:name    :string  {:name "Lot"}]                    ; "North Meadow, 1st cut 2026"
   [:baled   :integer {:name "Bales made" :constraints {:min 0}}]
   [:sold    :integer {:derived {:expression [:connected-sum :sales :bales]}}]
   [:in-barn :integer
    {:name "In the barn" :visibility :prominent
     :derived {:language :clojure
               :expression [:- [:get :baled] [:get :sold]]
               :inputs [:baled :sold]}}]]}
 :sale
 {:name "Sale" :symbol "🤝" :primary-key :sale-nr :match-keys [:sale-nr]
  :attributes
  [[:sale-nr        :string]
   [:lot            :string]
   [:buyer          :string]
   [:bales          :integer {:constraints {:min 1}}]
   [:price-per-bale :decimal]
   [:sold-on        :date]
   [:sold-by        :string]]}}
Nobody types or counts :in-barn: it is the bales made minus every bale sold,
computed by the server. :bales is an integer, so "about forty" or -3 is
refused before anything is written.
An object type is a typed table with a name, a face in the UI and a class in the generated SDK. Properties are typed, constrained and can be derived, so a value nobody typed in still shows up like any other column.
A sale on its own is just a number. A sale linked to the lot it came out of is a fact everyone can see.
:links
[[:sale-lot :sale :lot :many-to-one
  {:fk :lot :forward-api-name :lot :reverse-api-name :sales}]]
The sale names its lot and the link follows it: from the lot you see its
sales, from a sale its lot, and :connected-sum above sums across that link.
One line, and the barn knows what is in it.
Links are first-class: named in both directions, navigable in the UI, traversable
in the SDK (lot.sales), and usable in derived values, filters and object
sets.
In most systems anybody may change anything, and nobody can say who did. Here there is no "update row". There are only actions: named decisions with typed inputs and rules the server enforces. Selling hay is one of them, and it has a condition.
:sell-hay
{:on     :lot
 :params {:lot            {:type :lot :required true}
          :sale-nr        {:type :string :required true}
          :buyer          {:type :string :required true}
          :bales          {:type :integer :required true :constraints {:min 1}}
          :price-per-bale {:type :decimal}
          :sold-on        {:type :date :prefill :now}
          :sold-by        {:type :string :exposure :hidden :prefill :current-user}}
 :submission-criteria
 [{:message "Not that many bales in the barn."
   :test    {:want [:get :bales] :have [:get :lot :in-barn]}
   :pred    [:<= :want :have]}]
 :rules  [{:op :create :object-type :sale
           :values {:sale-nr [:get :sale-nr] :lot [:get :lot :name]
                    :buyer [:get :buyer] :bales [:get :bales]
                    :price-per-bale [:get :price-per-bale]
                    :sold-on [:get :sold-on] :sold-by [:get :sold-by]}}]
 :edits  [{:object-type :sale}]}
Ask to sell more bales than are in the barn and the server refuses and says why, with the same sentence for the phone, the CLI, the Python script and the AI agent. A refused action writes nothing. Every sale records who made it, and nobody can put someone else's name there.
Actions are the only write path: typed parameters, validation, submission criteria and state transitions, defined once and enforced everywhere.
Every rule you would otherwise keep in your head has this shape: a fact the server computes, and an action that checks it. Declare it once, and stop remembering it.
The same three ideas run the arable side of the farm. A field's margin is derived from its paid harvests and the hay sold off it, two links away. A harvest moves from planted to harvested, delivered and paid only through its actions, and Sell harvest refuses to run without a signed delivery note and a quality test of your own.
In most software, deciding and doing are one step. In Sutra they are two. When you sell hay, the server first writes down what would change: one new sale, forty bales, your name on it. Nothing has happened yet. Only when that note is approved does the barn change.
Everything else follows from that:
- You can always ask first. "Would this work?" is the same question, without the last step.
- An agent can only make suggestions. What it hands back is the note, never the change. You decide.
- You can try things out. Run the same decisions on a copy, compare, and keep the real one untouched.
- You can look back. Every approved change is kept, so last Tuesday's state is still there to read.
- The answer is the same everywhere. The rule is checked in one place, so the phone, the script and the agent hear the same no.
And it is not a promise. A test fails if the part that decides ever does anything but decide.
- Your data comes in as it is. Mail over IMAP, CSV exports, REST APIs, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and SSH, shaped by transforms in Python, SQL or Clojure.
- Every number has a past. Lineage runs from each object back through the
transforms and datasets to the mail, statement or row it came from
(sutra lineage <node>). When someone else's figures disagree with yours,
you open the source.
- Agents get only the tools you name. An action, a function, a query on
one type. By default (:writes :propose) their changes are staged as
proposals; a rejected one doesn't come back, and the model's prompt and
answer are kept with the run.
- The model is versioned like code. Model and data live on branches. You
stage a change, commit it, open a proposal, see who consumes what you
touched, and merge into main only when it's reviewed. Webhooks and
notifications stay silent on a branch unless you say otherwise.
- Share exactly what you choose. Markings on types and properties are mandatory access control; grants on projects decide who may read, act and invoke. A group (a co-op, a tenants' association, a family) can pool what its members agree to share, and nothing else, and the server enforces it on every read: lists, filters, counts and totals. One person's data can't show what everyone else was offered. A group's can.
- Builders and users are different people. One person writes the model; everyone else gets apps with the build tools locked away, and a server that says no when no is the right answer.
- Secrets stay out of reach. A separate egress agent holds every external credential, so the code that reads your mail never sees the password.
You described the farm once. Generate a Python SDK from it, and your code speaks the farm's language: lots, harvests and buyers, and the things you are allowed to do with them, not tables and joins.
pip install ./clients/python-platform-sdk
sutra-platform-sdk generate --base-url http://127.0.0.1:<port> \
                            --username admin --password "…" --out farm_sdk.py
farm_sdk.py is plain, typed Python: a class per object type, an attribute
per property and link, a method per action with the action's parameters as
its signature. Sutra's language server (clients/ent-lsp)
runs pyright for Python and labels each completion as what it is in the model
(property, link-type, action, state); any editor that lets you pick the
language server can run it (Neovim config).
An action is a method. Its signature comes from the model; a missing argument is flagged before anything runs.
lot = Lot.get("North Meadow, 1st cut 2025")
lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour")
# error: Argument missing for parameter "sale_nr"
lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour", sale_nr="S-2026-010")   # ok
States are types. A harvest's status is
Literal['planted', 'harvested', 'delivered', 'paid'], so the editor offers
exactly those four.
for h in Field.get("hilltop").harvests:
    if h.status == "planted":       # completes: planted, harvested, delivered, paid
        h.record_harvest(harvested_on=date(2027, 7, 28), tonnes=61.5)
Filters are checked too. Comparing bales with a string, or reading a link that may be empty, fails in the editor, not on the farm.
Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < "forty")   # error: Operator "<" not supported for types
                                   #   "Property[int]" and "Literal['forty']"
Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < 50)        # ok
lot.field.margin                   # error: "margin" is not a known attribute of "None"
if lot.field:
    lot.field.margin               # ok
The walkthrough in code: objects with their links, acting, asking first, proposing, lifecycles, server-side aggregates, sets, branches and revisions
from sutra_platform_sdk import SutraClient, sum_, avg, count, by, bucket
from farm_sdk import Lot, Sale, Field, Buyer, register_all
client = register_all(SutraClient("http://127.0.0.1:<port>", username="admin", password="…"))
An object, not a row. A lot brings its derived values and its links along.
Nobody stored in_barn; the server computes it.
lot = Lot.get("North Meadow, 1st cut 2025")   # a Lot, or NotFound
lot.baled, lot.sold, lot.in_barn            # (120, 95, 25)
lot.field                                   # <Field 'North Meadow'>: the field it was cut from
[(s.buyer, s.bales) for s in lot.sales]     # its three sales, each a Sale
Act on it. Selling hay is something you do to a lot. The server checks the rule, writes the sale, stamps your name on it and tells you what changed.
lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-010", buyer="Neighbour", bales=20, price_per_bale=4.50)
Lot.get(lot.name).in_barn                   # 5
Ask first, or only propose. The same call can be a question (nothing is written) or a proposal (staged until someone approves it). That is how an agent gets to use it.
from sutra_platform_sdk.actions import ActionConfig, ActionMode
ask = ActionConfig(mode=ActionMode.VALIDATE_ONLY)
lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-011", buyer="Neighbour", bales=40,
             action_config=ask).validation.submission_criteria
# ('Not that many bales in the barn.',)
lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-011", buyer="Neighbour", bales=5,
             publish=False).staged          # True: a proposal, the barn is unchanged
Walk a lifecycle. A harvest goes from planted to harvested,
delivered and paid, one action per step, and the rules travel with them.
The states are declared in the model, so status is typed
Literal['planted', 'harvested', 'delivered', 'paid'] and your editor offers
exactly those four.
from datetime import date
wheat = next(h for h in Field.get("hilltop").harvests if h.status == "planted")
mill  = Buyer.get("stone-mill")
wheat.record_harvest(harvested_on=date(2027, 7, 28), tonnes=61.5)
wheat.sell_harvest(buyer=mill, price_per_tonne=212)
# ServerError: HTTP 422: No signed delivery note. Without one, the buyer decides later what you delivered.
wheat.sell_harvest(buyer=mill, price_per_tonne=212, delivery_note=True, quality_tested=True)
Buyer.get("stone-mill").unpaid              # 13038: what the mill owes you, until …
wheat.record_payment()
Field.get("hilltop").margin                 # … the wheat lands in the field's margin
Ask the whole farm, in one line. Who bought how much hay, month by month, at what price. Grouped, summed and sorted on the server; nothing is downloaded to be counted.
Sale.aggregate(
    sum_(Sale.bales), avg(Sale.price_per_bale), count(),
    group_by=[bucket(Sale.sold_on, "month"), by(Sale.buyer)],
    order_by=sum_(Sale.bales), desc=True,
).flat()
# [{'sold_on_month': '2025-12', 'buyer': 'Riding stables', 'bales_sum': 80,
#   'price_per_bale_avg': Decimal('4.5000000000000000'), 'count': 2}, …]
Money stays Decimal all the way from the database; nothing is rounded
through a float.
Sets, not lists. On the class, a property is a filter and a link is a hop.
Combine sets with |, & and -; the server plans it, and you fetch only
what you iterate. Each set knows what it holds: running_low is an
ObjectSet[Lot], and one hop along Lot.sales makes it an ObjectSet[Sale].
running_low = Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < 50)
neighbours  = Sale.where(Sale.buyer == "Neighbour").around(Sale.lot)
(running_low - neighbours).count()          # 3: running low, and the neighbour never bought from them
running_low.around(Lot.sales).aggregate(sum_(Sale.bales), group_by=[by(Sale.buyer)])   # who emptied them
Try tomorrow's rule on today's farm, or look at last Tuesday. Everything above runs unchanged against a branch, and every action tells you the revision it landed in, a state you can read again later.
with client.branch("new-rule"):             # made with: sutra branch new-rule
    lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-012", buyer="Neighbour", bales=5)   # main never notices
sale = lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-013", buyer="Neighbour", bales=1)
client.at(sale.revision).objects("sale")    # the sales as they stood right then
And what it refuses. Wrong names, missing arguments and wrong types fail
in your editor, before anything runs. Broken rules fail on the server, with
the same sentence for every client. If the model changes underneath you,
register_all refuses to run until you regenerate.
lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour")   # error: Argument missing for parameter "sale_nr"
lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-1", buyer="Neighbour", bales="20")
                                            # error: "Literal['20']" is not assignable to "int"
Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < "about forty")      # error: Operator "<" not supported for types
                                            #   "Property[int]" and "Literal['about forty']"
lot.field.margin                            # error: "margin" is not a known attribute of "None"
These are pyright's messages against the generated farm SDK. The SDK's tests run the same lines through pyright, against an SDK generated from a schema captured from a running server, not from a hand-written imitation of one.
None of this is a reporting layer bolted on afterwards. The UI, the CLI, the
REST API and the agents ask the same questions and take the same actions
through the same door, which is why an agent can be handed Lot and
sell_hay and nothing else.
./bin/start.sh   # backend + shadow-cljs watch; PostgreSQL from SUTRA_PG_URL
./bin/stop.sh
(cd tests/frontend && npm install)   # once: the browser tests' driver (playwright-core)
bin/test         # full suite; integration tiers start PostgreSQL in podman
The semantics are pinned by an executable scenario, an aircraft maintenance
shop in tests/scenario: "no release while a
defect is open" is the barn rule above in another world.
Security: set SUTRA_HTTP_BIND when running the plain server (it defaults
to 0.0.0.0). ./bin/start.sh allows anonymous access, so never expose it.
Transforms run user code on the server, so grant that right accordingly.
Maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS needs people who will take responsibility for part of it over time: the server, the web client, the Python SDK, connectors, packaging and installation, docs, or the example models. You don't need to know all of it. Start with a few contributions in one area; if you'd like to stay, say so in an issue.
The most useful contributions are not always code:
- A model for an everyday problem. A tenancy, a pension, a medical bill,
a small association's membership. If a rule protects someone, it belongs in
resources/presets.
- Plain-language guides for the person who sets Sutra up for others.
- Translations. Parts of the code base and the examples are in German; the user interface should speak more languages than two.
- Code. Send a failing test or a fix.
Open an issue for questions, ideas and bug reports. Be kind: the person on the other side may be the one this was built for.
The code is offered as is, in the spirit of Rich Hickey's Open Source is Not About You: nobody is owed a feature, a fix or an answer, and that includes the maintainers. What keeps it going is people choosing to help.
The ontology model of objects, links and actions follows the one popularised
by Palantir Foundry; Sutra-OS was built from its public documentation.
The web client is built on Palantir's Blueprint
UI toolkit (Apache-2.0), vendored as a ClojureScript port in
clients/frontend/vendor/blueprint-cljs.
The implementation owes everything to Rich Hickey and Clojure, and to his
almost spiritual talk
Are We There Yet?,
which will perhaps continue to transform the software craft into eternity.
Claude Code wrote all of the code.
AGPL-3.0-or-later, with a section 7 exception for linking with EPL libraries such as Clojure. See LICENSE. The AGPL means anyone who runs a modified Sutra as a service for others must offer them the source, so the tool stays in the hands of the people it serves.
No patent search has been carried out. The AGPL licenses contributors' patents only; checking third-party patents where they apply is up to you. Palantir and Foundry are trademarks of Palantir Technologies Inc.; Sutra-OS is independent and not affiliated with or endorsed by Palantir.

articles.title: Show HN: Sutra-OS – A self-hosted ontology platform
articles.body:
Scarce Units, Typed, Related, Actionable.
  An open-source, self-hosted ontology platform.
Your data becomes one model you own: typed, linked, changed only through
  rules the server enforces, and every number traces back to its source.
Quick start · How it works · Proposals · Python SDK · Contributing
Beta. Only small parts are still alpha: the model language and APIs may still change between versions, and parts of the user interface and docs are unfinished.
Maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS is a one-person project so far. See Contributing.
Sutra-OS began in late 2025 as a thought experiment: a free version of the system described in Ontology-Oriented Software Development, whose creators I deeply admire.
Much talent today goes into software that sells attention, while the software everything else runs on is mostly free: by a rough estimate, 70–90% of US economic output depends on free software at some critical point. That openness is not guaranteed. In November 2026, Nvidia's board parted with the founder who had its AI models released openly. Sutra-OS adds to the commons under the AGPL, so that it stays readable by anyone.
The past ten years have shown what it costs when nobody can see what depends on what. In 2017, NotPetya spread through a single Ukrainian accounting program and stopped Maersk's ports and Merck's factories. In 2023, a corrupted file in one FAA system halted every domestic departure in the US. In 2024, one faulty CrowdStrike update crashed millions of Windows machines, and airlines, hospitals and banks stood still. In November 2026, a single vendor took Outlook down for a day and some cities went back to fax. That same week, data flooded the FAA's telecommunications network, aging routers buckled, and the US saw only the third nationwide ground stop in its history. No one, it seems, had those routers on the map of what keeps planes in the air, so no one could ask beforehand what would stop if they failed.
That question is what Sutra-OS is built for. Every system, device, dataset and decision becomes an object with links to what it feeds and what feeds it, and every number can be traced back to its source. Whoever holds such a model can ask, before the outage, what stops when one piece fails, and get an answer, at every scale from a single person to a government (hopefully never a world government). Many small ontologies, each held by those it describes, keep power spread out; one model of everything would not.
Scarce Units: energy, water, land, housing and time will shape the coming decades. Whoever counts what is scarce decides how it is shared, and today that bookkeeping sits with a few platforms; for most people, the only trace their own data leaves in their life is the tendinitis from the hundredth weary click on "Accept all" in a cookie banner. Sutra-OS keeps the bookkeeping with those it concerns, under rules everyone can read: households, farms, workshops, clubs, newsrooms and public administrations get their records back, and their wrist with them. That is what a democracy needs from its software: a council that can trace the number behind a decision to its source, a change that stays a proposal until someone answers for it, and a public administration accountable to its voters rather than to a vendor under another country's law.
Almost everyone. Whoever you are, someone else keeps a better-connected record of your affairs than you do. Sutra is for anyone who wants their own.

address. Data lives in $SUTRA_HOME (default ~/.local/share/sutra). The admin
password is in zugang.edn ("access") there. Run the bin/sutra bind … line it
prints once.

               :inputs [:baled :sold]}}]]}
 :sale

  :attributes
