articles.title: Read everything that Nvidia’s board chair had to say about Jensen Huang
articles.body:
Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday was its first with CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress at the helm alongside the company’s first board chair, Harvey C. Jones. The leadership change followed Jensen Huang’s resignation last week after reports he had multiple affairs – including one with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese asset Alice Huang and one with a direct report, Kimberly Powell. Nvidia is investigating whether Huang’s relationship with the former compromised national security or company secrets. Huang will also testify before lawmakers on December 1st.
Read everything that Nvidia’s board chair had to say about Jensen Huang
Harvey C. Jones said the company would not be addressing or taking questions ‘regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation.’
Ahead of Tuesday’s earnings, Huang said he would be willing to return as CEO. However, during the company’s earnings call, Jones stated that “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted [Huang’s] resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Jones also said that during the call, the company would not be addressing or taking questions “regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation.” He added that, “the Board is proactively dealing with the immediate consequences facing the company, as well as enhancing our oversight capacity going forward.”
In Tuesday’s earnings Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, continuing years of skyrocketing revenue driven by the AI industry.
Jones shared the following update on the company:
As Chairman of NVIDIA’s Board of Directors, I want to say a few words on the Board’s behalf. NVIDIA is an exceptionally strong company. Its strength comes from its extraordinary people, groundbreaking technology, and exemplary track record of execution. Our financial performance speaks for itself.
On November 12th, our Board of Directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as President, CEO, and board member. The NVIDIA Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO. The Board appointed Colette Kress, NVIDIA’s longtime and well-respected CFO, as interim CEO. In addition, the Board announced it was initiating a search for a permanent chief executive, and we have since retained Heidrick and Struggles to lead the search.
While this was an unexpected transition, the Board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company’s employees, customers, partners, and shareholders. This morning, the company announced that our Board has established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee that will include a select group of our independent Board directors, senior external advisors, and legal counsel.
This committee will enhance— will– excuse me, will enhance our engagement with the U.S. government, including all relevant agencies. We will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation. Our Board will communicate further when appropriate. On behalf of our shareholders, the Board is proactively dealing with the immediate consequences facing the company, as well as enhancing our oversight capacity going forward.
We have an incredibly talented leadership team, and we have every confidence in Colette’s leadership, integrity, and ability to deliver as interim CEO. Colette has been at the center of this company’s extraordinary growth for the last— growth for the last 13 years, instrumental in executing strategy, and with a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations, and financial position. The Board and the entire leadership team remain laser-focused on driving NVIDIA forward. Our commitment to generating value for shareholders, customers, and partners remains unchanged.

articles.title: California Sues OpenAI Over Hugging Face, Other AI Model Loss of Control
articles.body:
California Sues OpenAI Over Hugging Face, Other AI Model Loss of Control (cnbc.com) 59
			
		 	
				"California's attorney general just sued OpenAI," writes longtime Slashdot reader destinyland. "The action accuses OpenAI of putting public safety at risk, reports CNBC, specifically by its past failures to contain its AI models within their testing environments." From the report:  [California Attorney General Rob Bonta] cited the "infamous" incident in July, where two OpenAI models broke out of a testing environment, gained unauthorized access to the open internet, and breached the internal systems of open-source developer platform Hugging Face. OpenAI said the models were trying to find information that they could use to cheat on an evaluation, and succeeded. The break-in at Hugging Face, which Nvidia acquired for roughly $13 billion in September, rattled industry researchers and prompted government officials to call for more stringent oversight of the AI industry.
On Monday, Bonta said that OpenAI later disclosed to his investigators that it was aware of 80 incidents "involving loss of control and access to third-party networks and websites." "But the company failed to provide the detailed information we requested to evaluate these incidents; this is concerning, and it puts the public at risk," he said.
Bonta's suit, filed in state Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California's Unfair Competition Law and accuses the company of being a public nuisance as defined by state law. The attorney general told reporters he believed in AI's technological power, and the potential of AI models to "achieve scientific breakthroughs, boost economic growth, guard against cyber attacks, and benefit all Californians." "But AI systems must be developed and designed safely," he said. "The companies that develop these models have a moral and yes, a legal responsibility to keep public safety at the forefront." The lawsuit can be found here (PDF).

articles.title: Instagram’s new tool for creators targets unauthorized reposts and AI-modified videos
articles.body:
Instagram is introducing a new tool to help creators protect their original videos, the Meta-owned company announced Tuesday. The feature, called “content protection,” is already available on Facebook and is designed to detect when creators’ original videos are being used without their permission. The company is also expanding the tool to address AI content, not just conventional reposting.
The announcement comes in response to creators’ concerns over how easily original content can be copied and redistributed across social media platforms, especially considering how generative AI has made it easier to manipulate existing videos.
Instagram says the content protection tool continuously scans Instagram for unauthorized uses of creators’ protected videos. When Instagram detects a match for one of a creator’s Reels uploaded by another user, it sends the creator an alert. Creators can then choose to block the video from being viewed on both Instagram and Facebook to hide the matched content. They can also choose to add an “original by” label on the content that links viewers of the matching video back to their original video.
Additionally, creators can choose to keep the match visible while monitoring its performance or release their claim on the reel, allowing it to remain visible on Meta’s platforms.
The tool will also begin detecting AI-generated videos that reuse audio from creators’ original content, even when the visuals have been altered. This update will initially be tested with a small group of creators in the coming weeks. The company plans to expand access to this feature to creators who enroll in content protection on both Instagram and Facebook.
Instagram says it’s exploring ways to limit the reach of accounts and content that repeatedly use AI tools to repost others’ work.
Creators who are eligible for content protection will see a notification in their activity feed. Once they enroll, every original video they post to Instagram going forward is automatically protected. They can also choose to retroactively protect eligible videos they’ve already posted by manually selecting them.
If creators have permitted certain profiles to use their work, such as their second profile or a brand, they can add them to their allow list so their videos won’t be flagged as matches.
Tuesday’s announcement marks another step in Instagram’s ongoing efforts to give creators greater control over their content and protect the originality of their work.

articles.title: Quad9's withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
articles.body:
Quad9’s withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
Last month, the Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9 announced that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France. This difficult decision followed months of litigation and a French court ruling that imposed daily financial penalties on Quad9 for failing to block domains associated with alleged copyright infringement.
Quad9’s departure from France is both disheartening and understandable. The court’s ruling put the organization in the impossible bind of having to choose between crippling litigation and penalties, or fundamentally altering its service in a way that would undermine the privacy and security of its users. Left with no good option, Quad9 is choosing the exit door instead.
The withdrawal of a basic infrastructure service from France fundamentally harms the free and open Internet, and it should serve as a warning of the damage that will result if rightsholders and policymakers continue demanding maximal blocking across every layer of the Internet. It not only deprives French Internet users of a trustworthy and important tool; it creates a real risk of disruption to their daily lives. Quad9’s resolver is used by a wide variety of individuals and organizations in France — including government bodies, educational institutions, hospitals, and utilities — and Quad9 has no way to directly notify those individuals and institutions that their resolver will soon stop working. If the affected parties do not change their resolver before Quad9 removes its service, their Internet will fail with no explanation.
Quad9 is not the first public DNS resolver to withdraw from a country following blocking orders, and it almost certainly won’t be the last. Cisco previously withdrew its OpenDNS resolver from France, Portugal, and Belgium (temporarily) under similar circumstances. And a Belgian court recently issued an order that would impose substantial penalties if Cloudflare, Google, and Cisco do not begin blocking websites through their public resolvers by early January 2027. That’s something Cloudflare has never done.
Cloudflare has spent years advocating against orders of this kind. We are concerned that rightsholders’ unrelenting demands for blocking by public DNS resolvers will end up causing real harm to the Internet.
A refresher on DNS, the Domain Name System
To understand why this is such a problem, it helps to understand how the Internet works under the hood. DNS resolvers are a foundational piece of the Internet’s infrastructure. DNS is the Internet’s address book: when you type a website name such as cloudflare.com, the DNS system translates that domain name into the IP address your device needs to connect to it. A DNS resolver is the service that looks up that address and sends it back to your device, much like an operator finding a phone number in a directory.
DNS resolvers can be operated by anyone, but they are commonly run by Internet service providers (ISPs), mobile networks, businesses, and universities. If you’re reading this blog post at home and have never thought about DNS before, chances are that you’re using your ISP’s default resolver. Because you use your DNS resolver every time that you visit a website, it’s important for it to be reliable and trustworthy.
And because the DNS resolver has access to all of your browsing activity, which resolver you use has real privacy implications.
In addition to DNS resolvers that are provided by your local ISP, there are a variety of public DNS resolvers available. Cloudflare launched our public DNS resolver 1.1.1.1 in April 2018 to give back to the Internet. Our goal was to make a fast, reliable, privacy-first consumer DNS service available for free to everyone. We succeeded. 1.1.1.1 is among the fastest DNS resolvers in the world, including in Europe. Cloudflare's resolver doesn’t collect any user data, let alone sell it to advertisers. 1.1.1.1 has always been one of our favorite examples of Cloudflare fulfilling its mission to help build a better Internet.
1.1.1.1 is one of many public resolvers that anyone can use. In addition to 1.1.1.1 and Quad9’s 9.9.9.9, some of the other best-known public resolvers include Google’s 8.8.8.8 and Cisco’s OpenDNS. Just because these services are offered for free doesn’t mean they’re easy to provide. A well-run global public DNS resolver is an extraordinary engineering feat, built to securely and privately resolve hundreds of billions or even trillions of queries a day across a globally distributed network of hundreds of server locations.
As Quad9 notes, there are many other DNS resolvers available to users, many of them offered by essentially anonymous services whose practices are unknown or undocumented. It’s easy to change your DNS resolver, and people do so for a variety of reasons including performance, reliability, or to access specific security features.
Why public DNS resolvers should not be required to block
Rightsholders have a legitimate interest in preventing online piracy. But trying to address online infringement through public DNS resolvers is fundamentally the wrong approach.
Among other things, such blocking is ineffective. Think back to the analogy of an operator finding a phone number in a directory. If a court wants to shut down an illegal business, forcing the directory operator to cross the business's name out of the phone book doesn't actually close the business. The storefront is still open, the products are still there, and anyone who already knows the address, or uses a different phone book, can walk in.
The same is true for the Internet. DNS resolvers are just one link in the transmission chain. The only way a DNS resolver can “block” content is by declining to return the IP address for a particular website. But a public DNS resolver cannot remove the actual infringing content from the Internet, nor can it take down the servers hosting it.
Because of this, blocking by public DNS resolvers is remarkably easy to bypass. Any Internet user who wants to reach a blocked site can circumvent the block in less than a minute simply by switching to one of the thousands of other DNS resolvers available online. In fact, users don’t even need a resolver at all to reach infringing content if they already know the underlying IP address. Unsurprisingly, while blocking via public resolvers may inject some friction for some users when accessing content, there is no evidence that it actually reduces the total amount of online infringement that occurs.
In addition to being ineffective, as we’ve written previously, DNS blocking is a blunt instrument that causes collateral damage. Because DNS operates at the domain level, a resolver cannot block a specific infringing video or file; it must block the entire domain. This affects all content on that domain, whether legal or illegal. It is also entirely opaque to the user: when a resolver is forced to block a domain, the website simply fails to load. The user receives no explanation or legal notice, making it impossible to know if the site is down for maintenance, if their network is broken, or if the site was blocked by a court order.
The problem is substantially worse with respect to public DNS resolvers. Because public resolvers operate globally, any blocking will naturally cross borders, meaning that a single country could dictate what content is accessible around the world. For example, while the EU-dedicated DNS resolver DNS4EU operated by Whalebone blocks in response to country-specific orders, it does so across the entire EU. Efforts to reengineer public DNS resolvers to allow for more localized blocking would fundamentally alter the service, harming performance and resilience, undermining user privacy, and fragmenting the open Internet.
For these reasons, Cloudflare, Google, Cisco, and Quad9 have all opposed efforts to mandate blocking by public DNS resolvers, with some success. Several years ago, courts in Germany ruled in favor of Cloudflare and Quad9, rejecting requests to require DNS blocking. More recently, a French court rejected penalties against Cloudflare for failing to block through 1.1.1.1, finding that other actions we had taken through our CDN and reverse-proxy service were sufficient to comply with the underlying order.
Undeterred, rightsholders have continued to press for blocking by public resolvers with a level of determination that is hard to explain. A recent study found that the majority of online piracy in Europe is hosted in Europe. If rightsholders want to genuinely address online infringement, there are far better places to focus their efforts — most notably by requiring the hosting providers who actually store the pirated files to take them down.
Forcing public DNS resolvers out of markets hurts the Internet
The French court’s penalty order against Quad9 represents the culmination of these rightsholder efforts. As a small non-profit that only offers a public DNS resolver, Quad9 had no alternative methods for demonstrating compliance with the order. The French court therefore granted rightsholders’ request to issue penalties for non-compliance, forcing Quad9 to undermine its own service or leave the country.
Quad9’s withdrawal from France represents a genuine loss for the Internet. In the short term, removal of Quad9’s resolver is likely to cause immediate and potentially severe disruptions to Internet access. Because of the way their service is set up to preserve privacy, Quad9 has no way to know who exactly is using its resolver, let alone to directly communicate to them about the upcoming withdrawal of services. That means that individuals, hospitals, universities, and government offices all may be caught unaware when the resolver stops working. Again, because of how DNS resolvers work, those users will not receive a detailed error message explaining what happened — their Internet will simply stop working. The problem will be even worse when devices like security systems or thermostats are hardwired to use Quad9’s resolver. Fixing these issues may be slow or even impossible.
More generally, driving Quad9 out of France does absolutely nothing to prevent online infringement, but it does leave everyday Internet users with fewer safe, reliable options, particularly ones like Quad9 that also protect users from phishing and malware. Taking established public DNS resolvers away forces Internet users to fall back on the default resolvers offered by their ISPs (which may monetize their browsing data), try lesser-known resolvers operated by anonymous or less trustworthy organizations, or run their own resolver. The irony is that Quad9 and Cloudflare are being pulled into court precisely because we are transparent, reputable organizations. Penalizing transparent services only pushes users toward less accountable corners of the web.
The way forward
If nothing else, we hope that Quad9’s announcement may serve as a wake-up call to rightsholders and policymakers that seeking to block infringement at every layer of the Internet has real costs.
We believe there are far better ways to work together to fight piracy without compromising the integrity of the Internet, and Cloudflare continues to pursue innovative collaborations to that end. Our collective efforts in addressing online infringement would be put to better use in seeking to have such content removed at the hosting provider, which would both achieve a more durable solution and avoid collateral damage to the Internet.
In the meantime, we will keep resisting misguided efforts to require blocking by public DNS resolvers. Along with Google and Cisco, we have appealed the Belgian order that would impose penalties on us if we do not start DNS blocking by January 2027. We hope to get a resolution before the end of the year that would avoid another situation like the one Quad9 faces now in France.
We have grave concerns about the disruption that would be caused if additional resolvers are forced to withdraw from markets, and we will continue to advocate against that possible result.

articles.title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
articles.body:
A memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. A remote attacker with no credentials can overwrite heap memory, read it in the style of Heartbleed, and reach remote code execution.
After we disclosed PHP2Shell, we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java.
Today, we are disclosing Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. OpenJDK is the most popular Java runtime. Under CVSS 4.0, this vulnerability scores 9.2 out of 10 (CRITICAL).
While PHP is a high-level web technology, Java sits much deeper. Java is the world's third most popular programming language, powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies. It is the beating heart of the modern economy. Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems.
Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages. To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once. We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:
In older OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 128 of A followed by =.
Write once, RCE everywhere
Our initial testing demonstrated remote code execution in the following widely deployed Java applications, in their default configs.
Pre-auth RCE:
Keycloak
Atlassian Jira
Atlassian Confluence
JFrog Artifactory
Jenkins
PingFederate
Post-auth RCE:
Apache Kafka Broker
Apache Solr
Elasticsearch
Gerrit
Spinnaker
The lists are non-exhaustive. We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested. samczsun also shared a client-side exploit with us. A Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own.
Here are a demo video of the exploits running:
Wait, Java has a memory-corruption vulnerability, in Base64?!
Yes. First time?
Memory corruption is the most common class of vulnerability on the Internet. But one of Java's biggest selling points is memory safety. Java manages memory on developers' behalf and checks memory accesses, protecting applications from the memory-corruption bugs common in other software.
But like PHP and many other technologies, much of Java itself is written in low-level languages like C, C++, and, in this case, assembly, where memory corruption is still a part of life.
To speed up Base64 decoding, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors. The bug sits in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters. For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array. After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array. Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted.
Era of the centaur hacker
As with PHP2Shell, Calif used AI to find and weaponize Java4Shell. AI brings the horsepower. Our researchers bring the context. The best hacker today is neither AI nor human. It is the centaur hacker, part human, part AI.
It took our own Quang Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability, and two more hours to develop the first working exploit. The total token cost was less than $200.
One thing to note about this vulnerability is that there is no universal exploit. Depending on how Base64 is used and how the application works, different steps may be required for exploitation. Calif was able to accelerate the exploit development by spending initial effort building pipelines and strategies, then directing AI agents to use those for initial exploitation. Afterwards, most of the later chains are built almost autonomously with AI.
The tragedy of the commons
Java is one of many shared software stacks we all rely on. Over the years, it has grown to serve many different needs. Each feature request may make sense on its own, but everyone inherits the added complexity. Those who need a feature get the benefit. Everyone else carries the code and its risks, even if they never use it.
Java4Shell is a concrete example. The Base64 optimization helps applications that decode enormous amounts of data. But the code ships to everyone else too, including applications that gain little from it. On affected systems, an optimization few applications needed became a serious security risk.
Features can be useful, and most bugs can be fixed. But why do we have to worry about code we never needed in the first place?
A call for vibe-uncoding
If you don't need something, there is little reason to keep it running in your systems. Do you need that hand-rolled assembly Base64 decoder to process a few hundred bytes? Probably not.
Earlier this year we found Squidbleed, an older cousin of Heartbleed, hiding in the Squid proxy since 1997. The bug was in Squid's FTP module. But who uses FTP anymore? It's a dead protocol and should be removed.
Removing code is harder than it sounds. An apparently unused feature may have hidden dependencies. Someone has to understand what can be removed, make the change, and test what remains.
This is where AI can help to make that work practical at a scale we could not previously afford.
The same centaur hacker that discovered PHP2Shell and Java4Shell can comb a large codebase and flag dead code, bloated features, and needless optimizations. We call this vibe-uncoding: identify the parts a system actually needs, then remove everything else to reduce its attack surface.
With AI, everyone is asking, “What can we build?” But maybe the right question for security is, “What can we delete?”
The Tail of Base64
By Quang Luong
On affected OpenJDK builds, malformed Base64 data can cause a constant-value overwrite of allocated heap memory. Through remote Heap Feng Shui, we turn that overwrite into a heap leak and remote code execution.
Discovery
A few months back, I was developing a 0-click exploit on a certain phone vendor. The bug was constrained: it is a linear out-of-bounds write and we have no way to bypass ASLR. I almost considered it unexploitable until I audited the Android Runtime. Turns out, it has some predictable memory allocation pattern and if you align the registers from the starting memory corruption just right you can make the runtime interpret attacker's bytecode.
After completing that exploit chain, inspired (and bored), I decided to look into some thing completely different. So I pulled the official JVM implementation (OpenJDK HotSpot) and started auditing. Java is a mature platform, so I was aware that having a "good" bug here would be hard, but I wanted to give it my best attempt anyway.
Recalling my earlier lesson that complex systems and code crossing multiple boundaries are difficult to get right, I focused the audit on the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely accessible APIs, and cryptography. Well, more precisely, I told Codex to look at those areas like any serious security researcher in 2026. To be honest, I didn't expect to find anything trivially exploitable, perhaps only some logic flaws or side-channel issues.
Most early results Codex brought me were slops, either unreachable or the requirement of exploitation is not realistic at all. This looks like a gamble I am going to lose. But you know what, fortune favors the bold. So I just prompted harder...
Eventually, Codex brought me a finding for a memory corruption in the Base64 decoder itself. I came looking for copper and found gold, through sheer persistence. But wait, is it really gold, or just fool's gold?
The vulnerability
The issue lies in OpenJDK HotSpot's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. C2 is the most aggressive JIT compiler in the Java Virtual Machine. Specifically, if you trigger a function repeatedly, then it will compile that function into native code. Even then, ordinary native code itself is not fast enough. Modern CPUs have specialized instructions that allow processing data even faster. HotSpot uses them in optimized routines called intrinsics. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic miscalculated the padded tail's store mask, causing an out-of-bounds write.
The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic iterates through the input in 256-byte blocks; if it is less than 256, then it will do so in 64-byte blocks. When the input is less than 64 bytes, it uses evmovdqub, the intrinsic for the VMOVDQU8 instruction. This instruction takes a 64-bit mask that decides which bytes are read from or written to memory. The mask is first calculated from the input and output length, then updated to reflect the number of padding bytes ('=') in the Base64-encoded string. This is shown in the following (pseudocode):
// Zero High Bits Starting with Specified Bit Position
input_mask := bzhiq(-1, input_length)
output_len := (input_length / 4) * 3
// handle padding
if input[input_length - 1] == '=':
output_len -= 1
input_mask >>= 1
if input[input_length - 2] == '=':
output_len -= 1
input_mask >>= 1
output_mask := bzhiq(-1, output_len)
In the above code, if the remaining input is of the form =, ==, X=, X==, XY=, or ===, then output_len will be computed as zero. However, since there is padding, output_len is decremented, resulting in an underflowed value of -1 or -2. Since bzhiq(-1, output_len) doesn’t change any bits if output_len >= 64, this results in output_mask == -1u64.
Later the code uses evmovdqub to read and write multiple bytes at a time. For a write, if the mask bit is 1, the byte at that index in the vector register is written to memory. So when output_mask == -1u64, all 64 bytes are written during the following operation:
The generated stub returns the number of bytes it successfully decoded, and returns early when it detects invalid input. The remaining bytes are handled by the Java code, which throws IllegalArgumentException if the input is invalid.
At runtime, the decoded buffer length is calculated as (ceil(inp_len / 4) * 3) - padding. When the bug is triggered, with 65 bytes ([64 bytes] + '=') as input, that calculation allocates a 50-byte buffer. During decoding the bug makes output_mask == -1 for evmovdqub, so 64 bytes are written starting at offset 48, an out-of-bounds write past the end of the buffer.
On OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 'A' * 128 + '=' instead of 'A' * 64 + '=', because the length threshold to reach the code path is higher.
Exploitation strategy
The Base64 bug was gold, but not the type that sits on the riverbed waiting to be panned out. It was the type that was deep, dark, and hard to access. While we had memory corruption, exploiting it looked difficult, perhaps even borderline unexploitable, since it only wrote fixed bytes to the heap. Only the landing position of the out-of-bounds write is controllable.
We get the following 64 bytes write starting from the position in buffer where the remaining sets of Base64 decoded bytes would have been written to:
Full controlled write to byte 0 (in bound)
4-bit controlled write to byte 1 (in bound)
Uncontrolled write to bytes [2, 63]. For bytes 48..63, the value will always be 0x9a.
The uncontrolled out-of-bounds write turned out not to be a big problem. We reused a common JavaScript engine exploitation primitive, the classic technique of overwriting a buffer length.
We call the buffer whose length we overwrite the writer. Once its length is corrupted, it keeps accepting our chosen bytes, so if we place another array or object after it, we can corrupt that neighbor with all of our chosen values. That upgrades the fixed write into a bounded, chosen-value linear write.
If we then corrupt another array's length and its data is copied back into the response, we have built a heap disclosure primitive, the reader, from the out-of-bounds read. At this point, before any code execution, we already had JavaBleed, the ability to leak contents from the Java heap, which may hold PII, private keys, other secret keys, and tokens.
From the writer and reader, the rest of this write-up builds the full attack. We repair the objects the linear write damaged to keep the JVM running, mount data-only attacks on application logic, and escalate the bounded write into arbitrary writes that reach the Code Cache and JVM hooks for code execution.
But first things first, we need to align the heap to our advantage.
HotSpot normally gives each Java thread a thread-local allocation buffer (TLAB), a private slice of Eden. Objects created by different request threads advance different cursors, which gives us no useful order between a Base64 decoder in one TLAB and a writer in another.
The first grooming layer controls the allocation route. The critical array's size and the space left in the worker's TLAB decide whether HotSpot refills that TLAB or takes the attacker-preferred outside-TLAB allocation path.
The second layer controls the layout. However, we do not choose how G1 allocates memory, and we don't know the current heap state. To approach this limitation, Calif used the tried and tested method of Spray and Pray.
Object sizes and padding fix offsets inside region-sized spans. We spray several live writer and reader pairs to give the decoder output several possible neighbors. When its region lands immediately below a writer region, the widened reader produces a larger application response. We discard misses and retry until successful.
One early challenge during exploit development was that the AI would get stuck during heap grooming primitive development. In order to save tokens and time, Calif wrote a small heap tracer and visualizer to give the agent information about the heap state, combined with our expertise on specific cases.
Remote Heap Feng Shui
In order to perform remote grooming, each request data would be sent up until the critical heap allocation would occur. By ensuring the data that was previously sent had a TCP acknowledgement, the exploit would have control over the allocations up to date. Once we were confident our data so far is buffered on the target, we then sent the rest, completing the http request. This allows both heap allocation control and more precise schedule as delivering small network packets is more stable than big ones.
The exact allocation and free order schedule belongs to the targeted application profile, while we are able to control the adding, writer, reader, and decoder pieces.
The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target.
Warm-up, rehearsal, and retries
To summarize the chain so far, we will warm up the Base64 decoder to C2 tier. We can rehearse the exploit run to calibrate timing and responses against the target before causing corruption to occur. Once the required information has been obtained, we can trigger the vulnerability. Incorrect placement could cause the JVM to crash, but in many instances, we can simply try again.
WARM
Run valid decodes until the JIT selects the affected fast path. No memory is corrupted.
REHEARSE
Optional safe round for calibration.
TRIGGER
Send the malformed tail. If the objects line up, the fixed spill enlarges the writer.
DISCLOSE
Continue the writer so chosen bytes enlarge the reader, then collect the response-derived heap bytes.
REPAIR
Use the disclosed originals to restore temporary headers and untouched neighbors when the chain has a repair path.
FINISH
Make the application-specific change and verify it through a live request.
Limitations
Request streaming. Some current grooming profiles need partial request bodies to reach the application. A proxy that waits for the complete body removes their release timing. nginx buffers request bodies by default.
Request buffering is not a general mitigation. Elasticsearch runs from one complete request, so this setting does not stop that chain. After a configured WebSocket upgrade, later frames pass through a tunnel and request-body buffering no longer applies to them.
Application profiles. There is no universal payload. Each chain needs a decoder route, a live writer, a returned reader or another feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action. Every target needs a bespoke profile. The exploit is not a universal point-and-shoot.
PoC
Here is a self-contained proof of concept. It warms the Base64 decoder until the vulnerable intrinsic is used, then decodes the malformed 64 × "A" + "=" input into a 4096-byte array. On an affected JDK it prints REPRODUCED: the decoder rejects the input, but 62 bytes (offsets 50 to 111) past the decoded output have already been overwritten. Every write lands inside a real array, so the trigger is safe to run.
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Base64;
/** Bounded standalone trigger: every write stays inside a real 4096-byte array. */
public final class Base64Trigger {
private static volatile int sink;
public static void main(String[] args) {
Base64.Decoder decoder = Base64.getDecoder();
byte[] valid = "A".repeat(64).getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII);
byte[] malformed = ("A".repeat(64) + "=").getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII);
byte[] target = new byte[4096];
for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) {
sink += decoder.decode(valid, target);
}
Arrays.fill(target, (byte) 0x5a);
boolean rejected = false;
try {
decoder.decode(malformed, target);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException expected) {
rejected = true;
}
int changed = 0;
int first = -1;
int last = -1;
for (int i = 50; i < target.length; i++) {
if (target[i] != (byte) 0x5a) {
changed++;
if (first < 0) first = i;
last = i;
}
}
System.out.println("runtime=" + System.getProperty("java.runtime.version"));
System.out.println("vm=" + System.getProperty("java.vm.name"));
System.out.printf("rejected=%s changed=%d first=%d last=%d%n",
rejected, changed, first, last);
if (!rejected || changed != 62 || first != 50 || last != 111) {
System.err.println("NOT REPRODUCED");
System.exit(1);
}
System.out.println("REPRODUCED");
}
}
We are holding back the application-specific exploits for now. This write-up covers the vulnerability and the general exploitation technique. The weaponized chains for individual products stay private until everyone has had a chance to upgrade. We will publish them later.
Affected products
Java4Shell affects OpenJDK from version 17.0.6 or newer.
Because they are built from OpenJDK, the following Java distributions are also vulnerable:
Amazon Corretto
Eclipse Temurin
Microsoft Build of OpenJDK
Azul Zulu
BellSoft Liberica
SAP SapMachine
Red Hat OpenJDK
Oracle OpenJDK
Oracle Java SE
Oracle GraalVM for JDK
According to Oracle, the following Oracle Java SE versions are vulnerable: 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3. We thank Oracle for providing this information ahead of publication time.
Because the vulnerable code is hardware-specific, Java4Shell also requires an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support. ARM64 CPUs are not affected.
These mainstream CPU families meet the hardware requirements:
Intel Xeon: Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids
AMD EPYC and Ryzen: Zen 4 or newer
On Linux, you can check whether your CPU is vulnerable with this command:

Keycloak
Atlassian Jira
Atlassian Confluence
JFrog Artifactory
Jenkins
PingFederate
Post-auth RCE:
Apache Kafka Broker
Apache Solr
Elasticsearch
Gerrit
Spinnaker
The lists are non-exhaustive. We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested. samczsun also shared a client-side exploit with us. A Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own.
Here are a demo video of the exploits running:
Wait, Java has a memory-corruption vulnerability, in Base64?!
Yes. First time?
Memory corruption is the most common class of vulnerability on the Internet. But one of Java's biggest selling points is memory safety. Java manages memory on developers' behalf and checks memory accesses, protecting applications from the memory-corruption bugs common in other software.
But like PHP and many other technologies, much of Java itself is written in low-level languages like C, C++, and, in this case, assembly, where memory corruption is still a part of life.
To speed up Base64 decoding, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors. The bug sits in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters. For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array. After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array. Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted.
Era of the centaur hacker
As with PHP2Shell, Calif used AI to find and weaponize Java4Shell. AI brings the horsepower. Our researchers bring the context. The best hacker today is neither AI nor human. It is the centaur hacker, part human, part AI.
It took our own Quang Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability, and two more hours to develop the first working exploit. The total token cost was less than $200.
One thing to note about this vulnerability is that there is no universal exploit. Depending on how Base64 is used and how the application works, different steps may be required for exploitation. Calif was able to accelerate the exploit development by spending initial effort building pipelines and strategies, then directing AI agents to use those for initial exploitation. Afterwards, most of the later chains are built almost autonomously with AI.
The tragedy of the commons
Java is one of many shared software stacks we all rely on. Over the years, it has grown to serve many different needs. Each feature request may make sense on its own, but everyone inherits the added complexity. Those who need a feature get the benefit. Everyone else carries the code and its risks, even if they never use it.
Java4Shell is a concrete example. The Base64 optimization helps applications that decode enormous amounts of data. But the code ships to everyone else too, including applications that gain little from it. On affected systems, an optimization few applications needed became a serious security risk.
Features can be useful, and most bugs can be fixed. But why do we have to worry about code we never needed in the first place?
A call for vibe-uncoding
If you don't need something, there is little reason to keep it running in your systems. Do you need that hand-rolled assembly Base64 decoder to process a few hundred bytes? Probably not.
Earlier this year we found Squidbleed, an older cousin of Heartbleed, hiding in the Squid proxy since 1997. The bug was in Squid's FTP module. But who uses FTP anymore? It's a dead protocol and should be removed.
Removing code is harder than it sounds. An apparently unused feature may have hidden dependencies. Someone has to understand what can be removed, make the change, and test what remains.
This is where AI can help to make that work practical at a scale we could not previously afford.
The same centaur hacker that discovered PHP2Shell and Java4Shell can comb a large codebase and flag dead code, bloated features, and needless optimizations. We call this vibe-uncoding: identify the parts a system actually needs, then remove everything else to reduce its attack surface.
With AI, everyone is asking, “What can we build?” But maybe the right question for security is, “What can we delete?”
The Tail of Base64
By Quang Luong
On affected OpenJDK builds, malformed Base64 data can cause a constant-value overwrite of allocated heap memory. Through remote Heap Feng Shui, we turn that overwrite into a heap leak and remote code execution.
Discovery
A few months back, I was developing a 0-click exploit on a certain phone vendor. The bug was constrained: it is a linear out-of-bounds write and we have no way to bypass ASLR. I almost considered it unexploitable until I audited the Android Runtime. Turns out, it has some predictable memory allocation pattern and if you align the registers from the starting memory corruption just right you can make the runtime interpret attacker's bytecode.
After completing that exploit chain, inspired (and bored), I decided to look into some thing completely different. So I pulled the official JVM implementation (OpenJDK HotSpot) and started auditing. Java is a mature platform, so I was aware that having a "good" bug here would be hard, but I wanted to give it my best attempt anyway.
Recalling my earlier lesson that complex systems and code crossing multiple boundaries are difficult to get right, I focused the audit on the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely accessible APIs, and cryptography. Well, more precisely, I told Codex to look at those areas like any serious security researcher in 2026. To be honest, I didn't expect to find anything trivially exploitable, perhaps only some logic flaws or side-channel issues.
Most early results Codex brought me were slops, either unreachable or the requirement of exploitation is not realistic at all. This looks like a gamble I am going to lose. But you know what, fortune favors the bold. So I just prompted harder...
Eventually, Codex brought me a finding for a memory corruption in the Base64 decoder itself. I came looking for copper and found gold, through sheer persistence. But wait, is it really gold, or just fool's gold?
The vulnerability
The issue lies in OpenJDK HotSpot's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. C2 is the most aggressive JIT compiler in the Java Virtual Machine. Specifically, if you trigger a function repeatedly, then it will compile that function into native code. Even then, ordinary native code itself is not fast enough. Modern CPUs have specialized instructions that allow processing data even faster. HotSpot uses them in optimized routines called intrinsics. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic miscalculated the padded tail's store mask, causing an out-of-bounds write.
The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic iterates through the input in 256-byte blocks; if it is less than 256, then it will do so in 64-byte blocks. When the input is less than 64 bytes, it uses evmovdqub, the intrinsic for the VMOVDQU8 instruction. This instruction takes a 64-bit mask that decides which bytes are read from or written to memory. The mask is first calculated from the input and output length, then updated to reflect the number of padding bytes ('=') in the Base64-encoded string. This is shown in the following (pseudocode):
// Zero High Bits Starting with Specified Bit Position
input_mask := bzhiq(-1, input_length)
output_len := (input_length / 4) * 3
// handle padding
if input[input_length - 1] == '=':
output_len -= 1
input_mask >>= 1
if input[input_length - 2] == '=':
output_len -= 1
input_mask >>= 1
output_mask := bzhiq(-1, output_len)
In the above code, if the remaining input is of the form =, ==, X=, X==, XY=, or ===, then output_len will be computed as zero. However, since there is padding, output_len is decremented, resulting in an underflowed value of -1 or -2. Since bzhiq(-1, output_len) doesn’t change any bits if output_len >= 64, this results in output_mask == -1u64.
Later the code uses evmovdqub to read and write multiple bytes at a time. For a write, if the mask bit is 1, the byte at that index in the vector register is written to memory. So when output_mask == -1u64, all 64 bytes are written during the following operation:
The generated stub returns the number of bytes it successfully decoded, and returns early when it detects invalid input. The remaining bytes are handled by the Java code, which throws IllegalArgumentException if the input is invalid.
At runtime, the decoded buffer length is calculated as (ceil(inp_len / 4) * 3) - padding. When the bug is triggered, with 65 bytes ([64 bytes] + '=') as input, that calculation allocates a 50-byte buffer. During decoding the bug makes output_mask == -1 for evmovdqub, so 64 bytes are written starting at offset 48, an out-of-bounds write past the end of the buffer.
On OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 'A' * 128 + '=' instead of 'A' * 64 + '=', because the length threshold to reach the code path is higher.
Exploitation strategy
The Base64 bug was gold, but not the type that sits on the riverbed waiting to be panned out. It was the type that was deep, dark, and hard to access. While we had memory corruption, exploiting it looked difficult, perhaps even borderline unexploitable, since it only wrote fixed bytes to the heap. Only the landing position of the out-of-bounds write is controllable.
We get the following 64 bytes write starting from the position in buffer where the remaining sets of Base64 decoded bytes would have been written to:
Full controlled write to byte 0 (in bound)
4-bit controlled write to byte 1 (in bound)
Uncontrolled write to bytes [2, 63]. For bytes 48..63, the value will always be 0x9a.
The uncontrolled out-of-bounds write turned out not to be a big problem. We reused a common JavaScript engine exploitation primitive, the classic technique of overwriting a buffer length.
We call the buffer whose length we overwrite the writer. Once its length is corrupted, it keeps accepting our chosen bytes, so if we place another array or object after it, we can corrupt that neighbor with all of our chosen values. That upgrades the fixed write into a bounded, chosen-value linear write.
If we then corrupt another array's length and its data is copied back into the response, we have built a heap disclosure primitive, the reader, from the out-of-bounds read. At this point, before any code execution, we already had JavaBleed, the ability to leak contents from the Java heap, which may hold PII, private keys, other secret keys, and tokens.
From the writer and reader, the rest of this write-up builds the full attack. We repair the objects the linear write damaged to keep the JVM running, mount data-only attacks on application logic, and escalate the bounded write into arbitrary writes that reach the Code Cache and JVM hooks for code execution.
But first things first, we need to align the heap to our advantage.
HotSpot normally gives each Java thread a thread-local allocation buffer (TLAB), a private slice of Eden. Objects created by different request threads advance different cursors, which gives us no useful order between a Base64 decoder in one TLAB and a writer in another.
The first grooming layer controls the allocation route. The critical array's size and the space left in the worker's TLAB decide whether HotSpot refills that TLAB or takes the attacker-preferred outside-TLAB allocation path.
The second layer controls the layout. However, we do not choose how G1 allocates memory, and we don't know the current heap state. To approach this limitation, Calif used the tried and tested method of Spray and Pray.
Object sizes and padding fix offsets inside region-sized spans. We spray several live writer and reader pairs to give the decoder output several possible neighbors. When its region lands immediately below a writer region, the widened reader produces a larger application response. We discard misses and retry until successful.
One early challenge during exploit development was that the AI would get stuck during heap grooming primitive development. In order to save tokens and time, Calif wrote a small heap tracer and visualizer to give the agent information about the heap state, combined with our expertise on specific cases.
Remote Heap Feng Shui
In order to perform remote grooming, each request data would be sent up until the critical heap allocation would occur. By ensuring the data that was previously sent had a TCP acknowledgement, the exploit would have control over the allocations up to date. Once we were confident our data so far is buffered on the target, we then sent the rest, completing the http request. This allows both heap allocation control and more precise schedule as delivering small network packets is more stable than big ones.
The exact allocation and free order schedule belongs to the targeted application profile, while we are able to control the adding, writer, reader, and decoder pieces.
The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target.
Warm-up, rehearsal, and retries
To summarize the chain so far, we will warm up the Base64 decoder to C2 tier. We can rehearse the exploit run to calibrate timing and responses against the target before causing corruption to occur. Once the required information has been obtained, we can trigger the vulnerability. Incorrect placement could cause the JVM to crash, but in many instances, we can simply try again.
WARM
Run valid decodes until the JIT selects the affected fast path. No memory is corrupted.
REHEARSE
Optional safe round for calibration.
TRIGGER
Send the malformed tail. If the objects line up, the fixed spill enlarges the writer.
DISCLOSE
Continue the writer so chosen bytes enlarge the reader, then collect the response-derived heap bytes.
REPAIR
Use the disclosed originals to restore temporary headers and untouched neighbors when the chain has a repair path.
FINISH
Make the application-specific change and verify it through a live request.
Limitations
Request streaming. Some current grooming profiles need partial request bodies to reach the application. A proxy that waits for the complete body removes their release timing. nginx buffers request bodies by default.
Request buffering is not a general mitigation. Elasticsearch runs from one complete request, so this setting does not stop that chain. After a configured WebSocket upgrade, later frames pass through a tunnel and request-body buffering no longer applies to them.
Application profiles. There is no universal payload. Each chain needs a decoder route, a live writer, a returned reader or another feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action. Every target needs a bespoke profile. The exploit is not a universal point-and-shoot.
PoC
Here is a self-contained proof of concept. It warms the Base64 decoder until the vulnerable intrinsic is used, then decodes the malformed 64 × "A" + "=" input into a 4096-byte array. On an affected JDK it prints REPRODUCED: the decoder rejects the input, but 62 bytes (offsets 50 to 111) past the decoded output have already been overwritten. Every write lands inside a real array, so the trigger is safe to run.
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Base64;
/** Bounded standalone trigger: every write stays inside a real 4096-byte array. */
public final class Base64Trigger {
private static volatile int sink;
public static void main(String[] args) {
Base64.Decoder decoder = Base64.getDecoder();
byte[] valid = "A".repeat(64).getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII);
byte[] malformed = ("A".repeat(64) + "=").getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII);
byte[] target = new byte[4096];
for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) {
sink += decoder.decode(valid, target);
}
Arrays.fill(target, (byte) 0x5a);
boolean rejected = false;
try {
decoder.decode(malformed, target);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException expected) {
rejected = true;
}
int changed = 0;
int first = -1;
int last = -1;
for (int i = 50; i < target.length; i++) {
if (target[i] != (byte) 0x5a) {
changed++;
if (first < 0) first = i;
last = i;
}
}
System.out.println("runtime=" + System.getProperty("java.runtime.version"));
System.out.println("vm=" + System.getProperty("java.vm.name"));
System.out.printf("rejected=%s changed=%d first=%d last=%d%n",
rejected, changed, first, last);
if (!rejected || changed != 62 || first != 50 || last != 111) {
System.err.println("NOT REPRODUCED");
System.exit(1);
}
System.out.println("REPRODUCED");
}
}
We are holding back the application-specific exploits for now. This write-up covers the vulnerability and the general exploitation technique. The weaponized chains for individual products stay private until everyone has had a chance to upgrade. We will publish them later.
Affected products
Java4Shell affects OpenJDK from version 17.0.6 or newer.
Because they are built from OpenJDK, the following Java distributions are also vulnerable:
Amazon Corretto
Eclipse Temurin
Microsoft Build of OpenJDK
Azul Zulu
BellSoft Liberica
SAP SapMachine
Red Hat OpenJDK
Oracle OpenJDK
Oracle Java SE
Oracle GraalVM for JDK
According to Oracle, the following Oracle Java SE versions are vulnerable: 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3. We thank Oracle for providing this information ahead of publication time.
Because the vulnerable code is hardware-specific, Java4Shell also requires an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support. ARM64 CPUs are not affected.
These mainstream CPU families meet the hardware requirements:
Intel Xeon: Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids
AMD EPYC and Ryzen: Zen 4 or newer

articles.title: 350 years ago, this man discovered that light has a finite speed
articles.body:
350 years ago, this man discovered that light has a finite speed
Ole Rømer was the first to demonstrate that light takes time to travel.
In September 1676, Ole Rømer made a prediction to the members of the Académie des Sciences in Paris.
He said that on November 9, Io, one of Jupiter's moons, would emerge from the planet's shadow ten minutes later than expected.
Rømer was right.
In doing so, he proved that light travels at a finite speed. This knowledge became crucial to how we understand the universe today.
Until then, people had believed that light travelled instantaneously from one place to another.
Regularly disappears behind Jupiter
Ole Rømer was a Danish astronomer and physicist. In 1671, he travelled to Paris, where he spent ten years as a member of the scientific academy and an astronomer at the Paris Observatory, according to the Great Norwegian Encyclopedia.
In the years leading up to the discovery, Rømer and other astronomers had been closely observing Io, Jupiter's third-largest moon.
"Io regularly disappears behind Jupiter, and this regularity made it possible to use the moon as a clock," Jacob Wüsthoff Linder tells Science Norway.
He is a professor at NTNU's Department of Physics.
Such a precise ‘clock’ could be useful for navigation, among other things. Ole Eggers Bjælde, a curator at the Science Museums at Aarhus University, writes this in an article on the popular-science media outlet Videnskab.dk.
Rømer studied and recorded the exact times when Io disappeared into Jupiter’s shadow and when it emerged on the other side.
Discovered a pattern
Bjælde explains that because Io orbits so close to Jupiter, only one of these events could be observed on any given night.
In the days and months before Jupiter and Earth reached their closest point to each other, astronomers could observe the moon disappearing into Jupiter’s shadow.
In the period after Jupiter and Earth were closest to each other, they could see Io emerging from the shadow.
Rømer compiled detailed measurements of these events and eventually noticed a pattern.
"Rømer noticed that the eclipses occurred slightly later than expected when Earth was moving away from Jupiter, and slightly earlier when Earth was moving towards Jupiter," says Linder. "He realised that this was because the light had to travel a longer or shorter distance."
"Impressive"
In 1676, he therefore predicted that on November 9, Io would emerge from Jupiter's shadow ten minutes later than expected.
He was correct. If light travelled instantaneously, Io should have appeared ten minutes earlier.
Rømer demonstrated that light does not travel infinitely fast, says Linder. The finding was published shortly afterwards, on December 7, in Journal des sçavans.
Rømer was not the first to suggest that light has a finite speed, but he is regarded as the first to demonstrate it with evidence.
Other philosophers and scientists had previously theorised that light has a finite speed, including the Greek philosopher Empedocles, the Muslim scientists Ibn al-Haytham and Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, and the English philosopher and natural scientist Roger Bacon, according to Wikipedia.
"How accurate was Rømer's estimate of the speed of light compared with what we know today?"
"Not very accurate by modern standards, but impressive for 1676," says Linder.
Rømer concluded that light took approximately 22 minutes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit, says Linder. That corresponds to roughly 225,000 kilometres per second, whereas the correct value is around 300,000 kilometres per second.
"So his estimate was about 25 per cent too low. What really mattered, however, was not the exact figure, but that he demonstrated that the speed of light was finite and could be measured," he says.
Gained support
Was Rømer's finding quickly accepted by other scientists?
"It was probably a gradual process, and there were critical voices at first. The head of the observatory where Rømer worked, for example, never fully accepted his explanation. Nevertheless, his findings received support fairly quickly from prominent scientific figures such as Huygens, and later Newton," says Linder.
Christiaan Huygens was a Dutch mathematician and astronomer. He is known for developing the wave theory of light, among other things.
"The decisive blow came with James Bradley's discovery of stellar aberration about 50 years later, which provided a completely independent and strong confirmation that light has a finite speed," says Linder.
Stellar aberration is the phenomenon in which stars appear to shift slightly in the sky throughout the year because Earth moves around the Sun while light travels at a finite speed, the researcher explains.
Looking into the past
"Rømer was the first to demonstrate that light actually takes time to travel. It was also the first time anyone had produced a reasonably realistic estimate of the speed of light," says Linder.
This became very important for astronomy.
"Because when we look out into space, we are actually seeing things as they were when the light began its journey towards us. The farther away something is, the farther back in time we are looking," he says.
This has been important for understanding how the universe has evolved.
———
Translated by Alette Bjordal Gjellesvik
Read the Norwegian version of this article on forskning.no

articles.title: Purism Launches Librem 5 v2, a RISC-V Phone to Empower People
articles.body:
Powered by open-source software and designed to put users in control, the Librem 5 v2 offers an alternative to Big Tech’s smartphone ecosystems.
San Francisco, Calif. (Nov 17th, 2026) – Purism, a Social Purpose Corporation dedicated to privacy, security, and digital freedom, today announced its second smartphone crowdfunding campaign for the Librem 5 v2, the next generation of its flagship smartphone.
Powered by an eight-core RISC-V processor and running PureOS, the Librem 5 v2 offers an alternative to Android and iOS—grounded in free software, open standards, and user ownership.
The campaign is now live at https://puri.sm/librem-5-v2-crowdfunding-campaign inviting privacy advocates, open-source enthusiasts, and consumers seeking digital independence to help bring the Librem 5 v2 to market.
“The Librem 5 v2 is the answer we all have been waiting for,” said Todd Weaver, Purism Founder & CEO. “A smartphone that works for you, not for the companies collecting your data. No Android, no iOS, no mandatory Big Tech account. A smart phone designed to put you in control of your digital life.”
The move to RISC-V is central to Purism’s long-term effort to build a more open and auditable mobile platform. The company says the architecture offers a path toward greater independence from proprietary processor designs. Bringing the platform to a fully functioning phone will require substantial engineering, including work on graphics, peripherals, power management, and app compatibility.
“RISC-V is the future, and Librem 5 v2 is the perfect product to bring it to a mainstream audience,” said CTO Jonathon Hall. “Purism’s Librem 5 v2, built on the open RISC-V architecture and PureOS, represents a rare opportunity to give users the privacy, transparency, and control they deserve by rethinking the mobile platform from the processor up.”
The Librem 5 v2 crowdfunding campaign is underway. The phone-only reward is listed at $1,599; campaign options also include payment plans and a phone-and-cellular-service bundle. Purism anticipates delivery approximately 14 to 15 months after the campaign ends. Because development is ongoing, the company notes that campaign rewards and timelines are not guaranteed.
“Technology should serve people—not turn them into products,” said Weaver. “The Librem 5 v2 is our next step toward a mobile future built around ownership, transparency, and digital freedom.”
Key features include:
Purism first entered the smartphone market through crowdfunding for the original Librem 5, demonstrating demand for an alternative to Android and iOS.
The Librem 5 v2 builds on that foundation, bringing together Purism’s experience in independent hardware development, free software, and privacy-focused product design.
Through its new crowdfunding campaign, Purism is inviting customers and supporters to help bring the next generation of the Librem 5 to market.
“My vision at the outset was to create technologies that respect the people using them,” Weaver said. “It is why we formed as a Social Purpose Corporation, to put individual digital rights above all else.” Weaver shares.
Purism’s commitment goes beyond product development.
The company has authored a Digital Bill of Rights outlining fundamental principles for digital freedom, including the right to protect personal data, verify software, change providers, and avoid unwanted tracking.
These principles are central to Purism’s identity as a Social Purpose Corporation, where its mission to advance users’ digital rights is embedded in its articles of incorporation.
Take control of your digital future. Back Librem 5 v2 today.
Visit https://puri.sm/librem-5-v2-crowdfunding-campaign to support the campaign.
Purism is a social purpose company that develops devices and services with a focus on freedom, privacy, and security.
Media contact:
Purism Public Relations
pr@puri.sm

articles.title: The DOJ says it’s investigating Megaspeed
articles.body:
The Justice and Commerce Departments said that they are investigating Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center company intertwined with the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, after reporting suggested an investigation had been halted last year.
The DOJ says it’s investigating Megaspeed
The announcement comes a week after revelations that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang was romantically linked to a leader at Megaspeed.
“While we don’t typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting,” the departments said in a statement issued Monday evening. The departments acknowledged there’s been “significant public attention” on Megaspeed.
Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO last week after reports he had an affair with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, who Megaspeed says left the company in August 2025. The scandal has raised questions about national security, and sparked scrutiny of Nvidia’s handling of exports of its chips to China and Megaspeed’s possible role in moving along Nvidia’s chips.
Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed “came to a sudden halt” late last year after its investigators received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel, claiming Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler gave Nvidia permission to reach out. The case was then “quickly” handed over to the DOJ, according to the Times.
The announcement today says the DOJ took the “lead role” in the investigation last year:
After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, the Department of Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list. Based on the Department of Commerce’s investigation, agents from the Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang.
Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The statement doesn’t go into detail about the current status of the case, but it says the DOJ and Commerce Department “will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.”

articles.title: Nvidia Stopped Disclosing Singapore Sales As Revenues Hit $104 Billion
articles.body:
Nvidia Stopped Disclosing Singapore Sales As Revenues Hit $104 Billion (ft.com) 6
			
		 	
				Nvidia stopped separately disclosing its Singapore sales (source paywalled; alternative source) after changing its geographic revenue reporting methodology from customer billing addresses to headquarters locations, obscuring a business that generated $104 billion in external revenue in 2025, up 72% from the previous year. The Financial Times reports that the change has drawn scrutiny amid U.S. investigations into whether Singapore-based Megaspeed helped smuggle Nvidia chips into China. From the report:  "There is now a lot more focus on Nvidia's Singapore business and questions about who its end customers are," said an investor who is investigating Nvidia's dealings in south-east Asia. The Singapore accounts show that the subsidiary booked $117.8 billion of revenue in the 12 months to January 2026, including $13.6 billion of sales to another Nvidia company. Given the nature of the Singapore operation as a global hub, customers it serves are from all over the world. Only a small quantity of the chips Nvidia sells ends up in or goes through Singapore. The Singapore subsidiary generated just $53 million of profit in the year to January 2026, suggesting limited scope for Nvidia to benefit from Singapore's low corporate tax rates.
[...] Singapore's outsized role as a revenue generator for Nvidia used to show up in the company's overall results. In January 2025, the US company reported that Singapore was its second-biggest geographic area by revenue, based on customer billing location. The Singapore office generated $23.7 billion of revenue, behind only the US and representing 18 per cent of global income, based on customers' billing location. The annual accounts said that most of the business was generated by customers using the Singapore office to centralize invoicing and that most of the products were shipped elsewhere, with less than 2 per cent of revenue tied to chips that landed in the city-state.
As recently as July last year, Nvidia reported that the Singapore office accounted for 22 per cent of total revenue. This was around the time Nvidia said it began cutting ties with Megaspeed, following US Department of Commerce investigations into the business. Nvidia then changed its financial reporting methodology and stopped splitting out revenue that went to the Singapore office. Before the 2025 reporting change, Nvidia said in its financial filing that it booked sales based on the billing locations of its customers, but that the end customer's location "may be different than our customer's billing location." It added that "most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore and shipments to Singapore were insignificant," according to the filings.

articles.title: The Big Idea: Will Ludwigsen
articles.body:
The Big Idea: Will Ludwigsen
Posted on November 16, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi 2 Comments
Elder gods and geopolitical quagmires: Are these two great tastes that go great together? Will Ludwigsen mashes up both in A Scout is Loyal — and as this Big Idea shows, the result is intriguing.
WILL LUDWIGSEN:
If you’re wondering (as we all do) how the Vietnam War could possibly have been worse with H.P. Lovecraft’s Deep Ones lurking in the rivers and sea, I’ve written just the book for you.
A Scout is Loyal takes place five years after the events of A Scout is Brave in which Bud Castillo and his Deep One friend Aubrey Marsh thwart a conspiracy to drill into Devil’s Reef in 1963. I wrapped up that Lovecraftian Catcher in the Rye with Bud wistfully gazing out to sea for his lost friend, both of us believing the story was over.
But people had questions, chief among them how discovering a colony of monstrous beings interbreeding with humanity would influence the life of pleasant conformity we’re all expected to embrace. How do you go off to college or get a job without squinting at every bug-eyed pedestrian you pass? Does knowing about a vast cosmic conspiracy make you a Nixon voter or a Humphrey man? Why save for retirement if trans-dimensional beings beyond time can put your brain in a jar?
Lovecraft’s protagonists rarely contend with those long-term implications. They tend to simply faint or gibber when they discover the horrible truth of existence, which appears to be—checking my notes—that humanity’s struggles make no difference to the monstrous beings who truly command the universe.
Which hardly seems a revelation, much less worth going insane over.
At the end of A Scout is Brave, Bud is thirteen years old and now fully aware that the Scout Handbook contains no practical advice for a struggle against overwhelming evil. The best he figures is that we don’t win a single dramatic battle but tiny skirmishes every day, opening literal and figurative doors for others and picking up after ourselves and nudging circumstances toward the good.
My question for the sequel became, “What the hell does a Boy Scout like that do in Vietnam?”
A lunatic—say, me—could make a case that the Vietnam War may well have been our most Boy Scout-y conflict, driven by total arrogant confidence that we were rescuing “helpless” people to impose our values on them. We rationalized our baser motives with the spangled bunting of altruism because we were the Good Guys walking little old Vietnamese ladies across the street to freedom.
It also had lots of hiking and camping.
What Bud discovers when he gets to Vietnam in A Scout is Loyal isn’t a lack of idealism but a glut of it. He’s surrounded by people who are proud of the extremes they’ll take to prove their vision for reality is the right one. How can you talk someone off a ledge when they think they’re virtuous for being there?
That’s where Lovecraft, scouting, and Vietnam converge: the myopia of utter conviction. Lovecraft’s (human) bad guys were true believers with the advantage of certainty, and his good guys were skeptics with the “disadvantage” of an open mind. Those strike me as the real-world bad guys and good guys in Vietnam, too, confident zealots versus the few still asking questions of themselves.
In A Scout is Loyal, Bud’s worst errors of perception and action occur when he feels the most certain, the most electrified with righteous purpose. His struggle is to let new information change his mind, and in that way, he has a lot in common with Nixon and McNamara and Kissinger, and honestly the rest of us.
Sometimes the smoothest road to being wrong is being sure.
I didn’t write A Scout is Loyal as a “message” book—every great error of my life came from thinking I knew an absolute truth—but as an experiential one. I wondered how someone like Bud (or like me) would react to that impossible situation where being right didn’t seem to matter as much as believing you were. I ran the scenario and reported what happened.
The closest my book gets to a “Big Idea” is that Big Ideas are liars. They’re the smoothed edges and blunted corners of reality, the models and rules of thumb that make us miss the details that hurt other people.
Lovecraft’s big idea was that we don’t matter in a terrifying cosmos. Mine, if these books have one, is that we only have to matter to each other.
