Even when witnesses or victims do report abuse, investigators rarely conclude that it occurred. As of 2022, less than 10% of allegations against Bureau of Prisons employees were substantiated, meaning investigators found it more likely than not that the abuse happened in those cases. In some instances, investigators decided there was evidence the abuse didn’t occur. But more than 75% of the time, they said there wasn’t enough evidence to make a determination either way.
Officers accused of abuse face an internal disciplinary process that can take years. In many cases, they can simply retire or resign, knowing that the agency will no longer have jurisdiction to punish them once they leave. They could still face criminal charges — but bureau insiders say that many cases don’t reach that point because investigators abandon the criminal probes when an officer resigns. “Staff would know that if they were having sex with inmates, the worst that would happen is that you would have to find a new job,” one former prison official said.
The landmark law intended to combat sex abuse, the 2003 Prison Rape Elimination Act — widely known as PREA — mandates employee training and regular audits but lacks a serious enforcement mechanism. Auditors are primarily looking for policy compliance, not signs of abuse. “A facility may have widespread sexual abuse, but they’re still meeting compliance on the things they’re required to do,” said Kendra Prisk, a PREA auditor who has evaluated several federal prisons, including Aliceville.
Do You Have a Story to Share About This Topic?
Beth Schwartzapfel and I are continuing to report on this issue and want to hear from any prisoners or prison staff who have been sexually harassed or abused in the Federal Bureau of Prisons.
Keri Blakinger
I welcome any tips leading to tough accountability stories about the legal system. Right now, I’m particularly interested in hearing from federal prison employees and federal prisoners with information about untold and revelatory stories.
At Dublin, Ana said she watched the officer who’d been bringing in burritos get walked off the job by investigators. He was, according to an Associated Press investigation and several agency sources, one of about a dozen Dublin workers in the early 2010s who were quietly removed from their posts — but not prosecuted — over sex abuse allegations.
In September 2021, a new round of problems at Dublin burst into public view when the FBI arrested the facility’s warden, Ray Garcia. He was eventually charged with sexually abusing multiple women all over the compound — then lying to cover it up. In one instance, prosecutors say he abused a woman while PREA auditors were visiting. Though Garcia was later convicted and sentenced to nearly six years in prison, his attorney, Kevin Little, told ProPublica and The Marshall Project that Garcia maintained that he is not guilty.
The arrest of such a high-ranking official sent shockwaves through the system. Members of Congress began asking questions. The head of the agency, Michael Carvajal, announced that he would step down, a move he said in a recent interview was driven by concerns that Congress would not support the bureau until he left. Ultimately, 10 Dublin officers pleaded guilty or were convicted at trial, and one walked free after two hung juries.
While several of the Dublin officers could not be reached or did not respond to requests for comment, one did. John Bellhouse, who was a safety supervisor, emailed ProPublica and The Marshall Project from a federal prison in Louisiana, where he is serving a 63-month sentence after he was convicted of sexually abusing two women. Bellhouse insisted he is innocent and said the problem at Dublin was that the lower-ranking staff were “too comfortable” at the facility and too familiar with the prisoners. “It was very junior high school,” he wrote.
To Ana and the other women at Dublin, the rash of charges had made it seem for a moment like there might be change. But it soon became clear the problems were far more entrenched.
In the wake of the indictments at Dublin, prison officials were dispatched across the country beginning in 2022 to inspect other women’s prisons and generate internal reports.
That spring, at the low-security prison in Tallahassee, Florida, most of the women surveyed for the “Women’s Institution Cultural Assessment” said they were afraid of reprisals if they spoke freely, according to a copy reviewed by ProPublica and The Marshall Project. The last time officials visited, they said, officers had punished the women with “shakedowns” — in which officers ransack cells and destroy belongings — and told them it was in retaliation for talking to the visitors. Despite noting this and “several concerning observations,” the bureau found that sexual safety was “not determined to be a problem” at the facility.
Since then, at least 10 prisoners have filed legal claims saying they were abused by Tallahassee officers in the same year as the assessment. Six said they were sexually assaulted by a single officer, Lenton Hatten, who had previously been reprimanded by prison officials at another facility for putting money in women’s commissary accounts, “which was a warning sign of inappropriate relations,” according to multiple lawsuits. He was ultimately sentenced to three months in prison for repeatedly abusing one woman after DNA tied him to the crime. In legal filings, attorneys for the prison system admitted that Hatten sexually abused that woman but denied that he assaulted any of the others. They also denied that officials had failed to train or supervise Hatten properly. Neither Hatten nor his attorney responded to requests for comment.
At Carswell, in the summer of 2022, multiple prisoners told officials that prison staff had held town hall meetings before the site visit, threatening repercussions if anyone reported their concerns, the assessment found. Nonetheless, the team concluded that women at Carswell overwhelmingly felt it was a “physically and sexually safe environment.”
But that year, at least seven women were sexually abused by four different Carswell employees, according to allegations in civil lawsuits they’ve since filed. In one case, a woman who was partially paralyzed and required a wheelchair said she was violently sodomized in the shower by an officer who attended her Bible study group. When he heard people coming, she said he dropped her on the floor, leaving her alone to crawl back to her wheelchair, crying and bloodied. Months later, when she finally reported the assault, the nurse on duty told her she’d reported that same officer for sexually harassing other prisoners and nothing had been done about it, according to her lawsuit.
All the suits are still pending. Among the staffers named in them, only Hatten has been prosecuted. In many cases, it’s not clear whether any of the employees were disciplined by the Bureau of Prisons. The prisons agency would not answer questions about the assessments’ findings, though a spokesperson said it has continued to visit prisons and conduct assessments, which it does not release to the public.
Later in 2022, a highly publicized Senate subcommittee investigation found the problem of prison sexual assault was more widespread than previously understood and, around the same time, the Justice Department’s inspector general issued a report criticizing the bureau’s handling of staff misconduct investigations.
Meanwhile, the Bureau of Prisons’ parent agency, the Justice Department, put together a working group that recommended prison officials “enhance prevention of sexual misconduct” by promoting “stronger leadership” at women’s facilities, improving staff training and installing more cameras.
In mid-2023, the department began dispatching its own teams to survey women’s prisons and make sure they were carrying out the working group’s recommendations. Nikhil Ramnaney, a former Justice Department attorney who participated in a visit to the SeaTac lockup in Washington state that summer, said the department notified prison officials in advance, giving them time to prepare. “BOP was putting on a show,” he said. And when Ramnaney and the other visitors interviewed women, the facility’s top officials stood nearby. When asked if they felt safe reporting abuse, the women offered “positive and lukewarm answers,” Ramnaney said. “In hindsight, what else were they going to say?”
Another Department of Justice attorney who visited Carswell offered a similar assessment, and both said the department never released findings from those site visits. Neither could identify any meaningful changes the agency made.
Since then, officials from the Bureau of Prisons and the Justice Department have repeatedly said the agency is working to implement the working group’s recommendations. But when asked a series of detailed questions about the status of specific recommendations, the Justice Department deferred to the prison agency. Giamusso, the prisons spokesperson, said in an email that information was “not readily available.” She added, “We have more work to do, and we are committed to doing that work.”
By the end of 2023, there were growing signs that women were being abused at other facilities. At the camp in Bryan, Texas, it was an open secret that officers were groping women and pressuring them into unwanted sex acts, according to women and staff previously interviewed by The Marshall Project and NBC News. At the federal jail in Chicago, an officer groped and sexually assaulted at least four women in December alone, according to an indictment. That officer pleaded not guilty, and the case is ongoing.
And perhaps most disturbingly, the abuse continued at Dublin, even while the prison was under the scrutiny of the courts and Congress in the wake of Warden Garcia’s arrest. In addition to the hundreds who said they were abused before 2021, at least 47 prisoners alleged abuse by staffers after that. Many of those allegations have not been previously reported, and many of the alleged abusers have not been prosecuted.
The abuse continued even after the agency replaced Garcia. And it continued after a sprawling legal team — including attorneys from the advocacy organization Rights Behind Bars, the law firm Rosen Bien Galvan & Grunfeld and the nonprofit legal group California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice — filed the class action lawsuit against the bureau in the summer of 2023 on behalf of Ana and hundreds of other Dublin women. They alleged the Bureau of Prisons’ systems for preventing and responding to sexual abuse were so inadequate that everyone at Dublin was at risk. The following year, the government claimed in court filings that sexual abuse was by then “virtually non-existent” at Dublin and that the facility was “not currently a sexualized environment.”
A few weeks before that claim, a Dublin officer had allegedly slammed Antonina Troyer against the wall of her cell and raped her, according to a lawsuit she filed later, which has since been stayed. Troyer said three years after she reported him, she received a letter stating that her allegation was not sustained but offering no further information. The officer, who did not respond to requests for comment, was not prosecuted and still worked for the agency as of November.
“You have a huge system that just steamrolls everybody, and you’re already considered to be not trustworthy,” Troyer said in an interview. “Our word means practically nothing.”
By March 2024, the federal judge overseeing the Dublin lawsuit had grown noticeably frustrated with what she called the prison agency’s sluggish response. Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers issued a scathing order and appointed a so-called “special master” to oversee promised reforms.
Days later, the bureau abruptly announced that it would shut down Dublin — then asked the judge to dismiss the case. The judge demurred, saying the idea that closure solved the agency’s problems “strains credulity.”
Ana and the other women at Dublin were shackled and taken to other facilities around the country in what seemed like an unusually torturous process. In letters and interviews, women recounted how some officers screamed at them, threatened to shoot them or left them without water for hours. “With their behavior and the noise of the cocked guns,” one woman wrote, “I was sure they were going to kill us.” An internal affairs investigation later determined that all the transport officers had acted “within policy” even though, in some cases, other prison staff corroborated the women’s accounts.
For Beaty and the other San Francisco-based attorneys heading up the legal team for the class action lawsuit, building a case against the federal government now became much more complicated. To interview dozens more survivors, they had to travel across the country to remote prisons.
That October, Beaty and fellow attorney Kara Janssen paid their first visit to Aliceville. They’d just come from a legal conference in Atlanta, where they’d given a presentation on their work at Dublin, then rented cars to drive four hours to a hotel in Tuscaloosa. After another hour on the road — once they’d nearly reached the Mississippi border — the bleak, boxy buildings of a federal prison rose up out of the endless forest.
When the lawyers walked through the front door, the prison staff seemed so unaccustomed to legal visitors that they weren’t sure how to sign them in. “It felt like nobody had come there in a long time,” said Janssen.
Over the next three days, she and Beaty took down statements from more than 70 women, most transfers from Dublin. Some described the rough move or their trouble getting basic medical care. But others told new stories of abuse, this time at Aliceville. The medical staff who forced them to dance. The officers who assaulted them in closets, and the other staff who pretended not to see.
One of the women who talked to them was Ela. She’d landed behind bars five years earlier, after FBI agents arrested her in a meth bust. It was the first time she’d been in real trouble. She was sentenced to seven years in federal prison and eventually ended up in Aliceville, where, in early 2022, an officer pulled her into a closet and pushed her to her knees, forcing her to perform oral sex on him before vaginally raping her, according to a tort claim filed on her behalf. When she reported the incident to prison officials, she said they yelled at her and fired her from her job in the prison’s safety department. Traumatized and distraught, she began cutting herself. Eventually, she asked to see a psychiatrist but left feeling worse after the psychiatrist made fun of her, according to the narrative laid out in her legal claim.
About a year later, Wilder — the officer in stylish jeans — started circling, according to the claim. He was flirtatious at first, talking about his own romantic encounters and asking about her family back home. Then, one day in the spring of 2023, she said he forced her into a utility closet and made her perform oral sex on him. A few months later, he locked her in that same closet for two hours, returning three times to rape her, according to the legal claim.
Ela wasn’t the only woman Wilder allegedly targeted. Other women had reported him for similar behavior, but his abuse continued until the fall of 2024, according to court filings and interviews. That September, investigators questioned Ela about her earlier abuser, who had by then pleaded guilty to assaulting two other women. But even though Ela had already confided in Ana about Wilder, she was reluctant to tell prison officials. “I was very scared to speak out,” she said in emails in Spanish to ProPublica and The Marshall Project.
Investigators paid another visit days later — and that time she told them everything. “I would not want the chain of victims to continue,” she said. “We had to put a stop to it.” Wilder was walked off the prison property that day. But officers threw Ela into solitary confinement for nearly two weeks. They told her it was for her safety — “which really wasn’t safe at all because it was a nightmare,” she said.
And while Wilder was eventually indicted for sexually abusing seven women, 11 others — including Ela — have also accused him of sexual assault in civil claims, including two lawsuits. In both of those cases, a court has paused the proceedings until the criminal charges against him are resolved. Apart from his not guilty plea, Wilder has not responded in court or to repeated requests for comment.
By the time Beaty and Janssen arrived at Aliceville, the women were skittish, rattled by the abuse, the retaliation, the prodding FBI agents.
“A lot of people were really scared,” Janssen said. “It felt just like another Dublin.” As she got in the car to leave, Janssen broke down crying.
In the months following the Aliceville trip, the lawyers traveled to prisons in California, Connecticut, Texas, Florida and Wisconsin to speak to Dublin victims. At almost every stop, women told them of abuse happening in that institution, too.
In early 2025, over the new Trump administration’s objections, Gonzalez Rogers, the judge in the Dublin class action suit, approved a sweeping consent decree — a first for the federal prison system. It included pathways to early release, increased protections against retaliation and two more years of court-mandated oversight for the Dublin survivors.
It would not be enough to protect those who were still incarcerated. Even as their lawyers prepared civil suits, Ana and the other Dublin women became targets for harassment at their new prisons. At some facilities, staff derisively referred to them as “Dublin girls” or “Dublin bitches” and refused to give them prison jobs, according to interviews and court papers. Elsewhere, other prisoners viewed them as snitches and held their decision to come forward against them.
The women also continued to face sexual abuse. After getting shipped out of Dublin, the survivors reported almost 40 instances of abuse at their new prisons during the first six months of the court-appointed monitoring, according to monthly reports filed in federal court.
Abuse allegations continue to extend far beyond Dublin survivors. In interviews and legal filings, ProPublica and The Marshall Project uncovered accusations of sexual abuse at a prison camp in California, a low-security prison in Wisconsin and a notoriously troubled facility in West Virginia.
And earlier this year, the FBI showed up at Carswell, a facility so troubled that one woman described it in court filings as “a federal prison that became a hunting ground.”
Investigators uncovered a cluster of allegations against paramedic Preston Emert, who was removed from his job after 18 women accused him of sexually abusive behavior, according to court filings and internal bureau correspondence. Emert targeted women with addiction issues and medical problems, demanding sex in exchange for drugs and medical treatments, according to several women, their attorneys and a top bureau official.
“I have seizures and would need help and in order to get it I would have to have sex with him,” Olivia Floyd said in a letter to reporters. Emert is one of 12 Carswell employees accused of sexual assault in the last five years. He has not been charged, and bureau officials said in November he is still employed as a paramedic at Carswell.
Last month, his boss — the health services supervisor who records show fielded at least one of the early complaints about the paramedic’s behavior — was arrested after he admitted to investigators that he was having sex with a woman incarcerated there. He has not yet entered a plea.
Despite evidence of persistent abuse throughout the system, the Bureau of Prisons now appears poised to have less oversight than ever. The landmark consent decree is set to expire early next year. The Office of Inspector General, the Justice Department’s watchdog that has the power to investigate and recommend reforms, has suffered staffing shortages in recent years as the Trump administration has pushed to slash its budget. Meanwhile, hoping to shore up its staffing levels, the bureau recently announced it would allow new officers to start with fewer qualifications and lower pay.
“It’s almost as if they’ve learned nothing,” said Shanna Rifkin, general counsel for FAMM, a nonpartisan organization that advocates for criminal justice reform. “They need staff who are well-trained and well-compensated, and to lower the qualifications when you already have rampant sex abuse and drugs being brought in — what do they think is going to happen?”
Two years after Congress passed the Federal Prison Oversight Act, the ombuds office it mandated still does not exist. The Trump Department of Justice has failed to release a projected budget and progress report, even after both chambers of Congress directed it to do so by April of this year. And lawmakers have yet to appropriate any money for it.
Within the Bureau of Prisons, the effects of the intended reforms have been minimal. The agency has installed more cameras and restructured its Office of Internal Affairs, though under the new structure, staff at individual prisons typically still investigate their coworkers. “I think small things were changed — like the signage about how to report [abuse] needed fixing,” said former Justice Department attorney Marnie Shiels. “There were no substantive long-term changes from this that I know of.”
Lawyers say it’s also becoming harder for civil cases to succeed. So far, the federal government has agreed to pay $116 million to settle lawsuits with the first 103 victims of Dublin. Roughly 300 more cases are working their way through the legal system, including the one brought by Ana, who has since been released from prison. The man who abused her was never criminally charged, and he died while under investigation.
Trump’s Justice Department has offered paltry payouts in some cases and reneged on signed agreements that could have avoided protracted litigation in others, according to sources familiar with the situation. Lauren Bis, a spokesperson for the White House, referred questions to federal prison officials.
Legal experts also point to a recent, troubling precedent. In 2024, a federal judge in Alabama threw out a lawsuit brought by a woman at Aliceville who had been raped by an officer. The judge, Scott Coogler, sided with the Justice Department in ruling that the prison system wasn’t liable because the officer “was acting outside the scope of his employment” when he sexually assaulted her while on duty. The decision is pending appeal.
“This case could make it incredibly hard for anyone abused in government custody to seek accountability from the BOP,” said Deborah Golden, who is representing dozens of women in cases about their sexual abuse at federal prisons. “I hope that doesn’t happen.”
To the lawyers at the forefront of this fight, the fallout from Dublin has come to a disappointing conclusion. “It should not be hard to go to work and not force someone to give you a blow job,” Janssen said. “That is an extremely easy rule to follow. And I can only think that it’s just a complete lack of accountability.”
As for the Bureau of Prisons, it’s already returning to a familiar playbook. Earlier this year, the bureau announced plans to stop housing women at Aliceville and turn the facility into a men’s prison. Ela has since been released. But the rest of the women will, once again, be scattered across the country.
How We Counted Abuse Cases
Reporters searched federal court records and civil lawsuits and interviewed currently and formerly incarcerated survivors of sexual abuse, prison officials, and civil rights attorneys to compile a list of allegations that met the criteria for “sexual abuse” under the Prison Rape Elimination Act. They included only abuse allegedly committed by a BOP staffer against prisoners at women’s facilities operated by the Bureau of Prisons. There were 172 cases involving women and 15 in which the victims were transgender men. Allegations were sourced from an official record — including tort claims, lawsuits, criminal filings and internal agency documents — or the individual themselves, in which cases reporters corroborated their accounts with contemporaneous witness statements, journal entries, or letters; court filings; sworn statements; and other documentation.

articles.title: Daydream’s new AI agent acts as your personal stylist — and can shop for you, too
articles.body:
Can an AI agent serve as your personal stylist? That’s what e-commerce veteran Julie Bornstein’s fashion startup, Daydream, aims to find out.
On Tuesday, the company launched “Daydream Agent,” an AI agent that is described as a personal stylist that can help you plan a look, virtually try on clothes, surface relevant pieces based on your taste, and more.
The idea, the company explains, is to put a personal stylist in everyone’s pocket. This application of AI could be promising, given that early adopters of consumer AI agents like Meta’s Muse have found that online shopping is a key use case.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently noted that shopping was a top activity for Muse’s over 10 million users and that 25% of people who set up Muse now use it daily.
In Daydream’s case, the fashion startup has been focused on using AI to deliver personalized shopping results to its users. Its new AI agent builds on its earlier work with an AI chatbot that could help users find outfits and make suggestions, but not complete purchases.
Now the company says its Daydream Agent expands on that experience by remembering each shopper’s own personal style, fit preferences, and budget to refine its recommendations. Shoppers can also upload a photo to have the agent reuse that image to virtually try on any item they’ve saved. When they find something they like, the agent can complete a purchase through a one-click checkout process.
The agent can also handle other fashion-related tasks, like keeping an eye on when items go on sale or when brands have a new drop, or providing weekly updates or spotting new fashion trends.
Also, instead of leaving items in their cart, shoppers can save pieces they’re interested in to a persistent “clothing rack” so they can compare options and think about their purchases before deciding what to buy. Shoppers can also connect their own closet and their calendar to the agent, helping them to build outfits around what they already own and plan what to wear for upcoming events.
The tech works by pulling real-time pricing and availability information from its catalog of over 10,000 brands, then combines that with its fashion-focused artificial intelligence. It’s powered by a combination of OpenAI, Gemini, and Claude models, which it fine-tuned, along with its own trained models designed for particular use cases.
However, considering that fashion is more of an art than a science, the company says it’s keeping humans in the loop. To do so, this month it brought on its first stylist in residence, Francesca Salih, an international fashion stylist and the founder of StyleGrid. Salih provides the startup with styling content that helps shape how the agent pulls together outfits and offers advice. This advice is part of the company’s fashion knowledge database, which the agent experience relies on.
Bornstein, formerly Stitch Fix’s COO and the founder of The Yes (exited to Pinterest in 2022), started Daydream in 2023 as an AI search engine. The company, backed by $50 million in funding from Forerunner Ventures, Index Ventures, GV, and True Ventures, says more than 2 million shoppers have used Daydream to discover apparel and accessories since its June 2025 launch.

articles.title: Show HN: Win98 PE Interpreter in WebAssembly – StarCraft and Diablo on Phones
articles.body:
Wine-Assembly: run real Windows 98 apps and games in your browser
Wine-Assembly is a Windows 98 emulator that runs the original, unmodified .exe files in a browser tab: 3D Pinball Space Cadet, SkiFree, Solitaire, FreeCell, Minesweeper, Notepad, Paint, Calculator, Winamp, the Windows Entertainment Pack, DirectDraw and Direct3D games, and 16-bit Windows 3.1 programs.
There is no operating-system image and no source port. An x86 interpreter and a reimplementation of the Win32 API are written directly in WebAssembly Text, and the guest program's machine code runs on them. Nothing is installed and nothing leaves your browser; a program's settings and scores stay in this browser's local storage.
Double-click an icon on the desktop to launch a program. On a phone, one tap opens it and games that need keys get on-screen controls.
- Every program on the desktop, with a page each: Pinball, Solitaire, Winamp, Paint, SkiFree and more
- How it works: articles on the x86 interpreter, lazy flags, real DLLs, software GDI, DirectX and Win16, plus the design docs and reverse-engineering notes
- How Wine-Assembly was built
- Source code on GitHub (MIT)

				A software bug at JPMorgan Chase has disrupted online banking services Monday, triggering transaction delays for thousands of customers at Chase and other major U.S. banks. "JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system -- it is not cyber-related," said Joe Evangelisti, spokesman for the bank. "This is not a systemic issue -- other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us," he added. The Associated Press reports:  Monday's technical issues seem to be centered at Chase customers and customers at other banks trying to transact with Chase. Those banks, including Bank of America and Citigroup, were not having issues with their banking services. A spokesman for U.S. Bank said its systems are not directly impacted but that "clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays." articles.title: Human.md
articles.body:
BRIANA (MAZZIO) MAY · APR 28, 2026
HUMAN.md
          > a working manifesto. notes-to-self, mostly.
> not a thinkpiece. not a thread. not a deck.
> last edited at the kitchen table, coffee #2.
## what this file is
A reminder, in plain text, of what I think humans actually bring to the table now that the machines are very good and getting better every day.
I keep coming back to the word "taste" and I keep finding it too small. Taste is the surface. There is a whole engine underneath it, and that engine is the part the model can't have. Yet. Maybe ever. I don't know. I'm not in that argument. I'm in this one:
## the actual job
### 1. break the rule on purpose
Models are trained on the average. The average is the floor, not the ceiling. Our job is not to conform a little better than the last person who conformed. Our job is to know the rule cold, and then break it on purpose, in public, with a reason.
Symmetry is a rule. Break it.
Three-act structure is a rule. Break it.
"Don't shoot into the sun" is a rule. Break it.
If you can't say why you broke it, you didn't break it, you just missed.
### 2. find the thing in the weird place
Inspiration does not live in the first ten image-search results. It lives in:
- a misprinted parking ticket
- the way your grandfather folded a napkin
- an obscure Victorian zoetrope of a cat
- the back of a menu in a town you can't pronounce
- the tension in Rene Magritte's "The Son of Man", 1946
A model averages the internet. A human walks somewhere strange and brings back something unexpected.
### 3. advocate for the human and humanity
Every brief now has an invisible third party at the table. Someone has to keep saying "and what does this feel like for the person on the other end of it." Someone has to keep saying "how is humanity better through the birthing of this idea?" That's the job. Not "is it on-brand." Not "does it convert." What does it feel like? what good does it do?
If you aren't there saying it, no one will. The model certainly won't.
### 4. design for emotional resonance, not correctness
Tension. Surprise. Restraint. The pause before the punchline. The photograph that's almost in focus. The sentence that ends one beat earlier than you expected.
These are not bugs. These are the entire reason anyone remembers anything. "Correct" is the lowest bar in the building. Step over it and keep walking.
### 5. seek delight, not delivery
I would rather make one thing that makes someone laugh out loud on a train than ten things that "meet the brief." At the very least, it needs to make ME laugh. This is a personal bias.
If it's not at least a little bit fun, why are we here?
### 6. experiment ruthlessly, ship more than you opine
A working sketch beats a confident take. Every time.
A bad first draft beats a brilliant unwritten one. Every time.
A weird little prototype beats a slide deck about prototyping.
Every. Time.
Make 50 things. Throw away 47. Talk about the 3.
Do not, under any circumstances, become a person who mostly posts opinions about other people's work.
### 7. own the output. fully.
If the AI output is bad, the AI did not fail you. You failed it. You picked the tool. You wrote the prompt. You accepted the result. You shipped it.
The fix is not a better model, or a return to tools of the past. The fix is a sharper you. Sharpen yourself. Sharpen your ideas. Sharpen the way you say what you mean, because the gap between what you wanted and what came back is almost always a gap in you, not in the tool.
Powerful tools reward the people who showed up sharp, iterate, spend extra time on the vision. They expose the people who didn't. AI is not the great equalizer, it is the great amplifier.
### 8. design with it, not next to it
Watching the generation happen is not the work.
Prompting once and accepting the result is not the work.
The work is the back-and-forth. The push. The loop. The "again, but tweak is this way..." The hundredth iteration where the thing finally clicks.
If you're a spectator to your own output, you are not the author of your own output. Get your hands in.
### 9. play with purpose. and play for play.
Both. At the same time.
Some days the play is in service of a thing.
Some days the play is the thing.
A practice that only ever has goals is a job. A practice that never has goals is a hobby. The good work lives in between. Play doesn't result in burnout. It results in excitement, happiness, experiment, the unexpected, and an urge to play more.
### 10. be a builder and an ideas person
The split is fake. It was always fake. It's especially fake now. The people who can think of the thing and make the thing are going to eat. The people who can only do one half are going to be very busy explaining why the other half is hard, or blame the processes or tools.
Don't be that person. Learn the other half. It's never been cheaper to learn it.
## things I am trying to stop doing
- waiting until it's "ready"
- editing in my head instead of on the page
- making but not sharing publicly
- taking briefs that secretly bore me
- pretending taste is an innate quality
- treating "AI" like a noun instead of a verb
## things I am trying to do more
- finish the bad version first
- show people the in-between, mess, experiments
- write the thing I'd want to read
- dig deeper, get help
- stop pretending I know stuff, ask dumber questions

33% cheaper than GitHub Actions
Volume discounts available
Everything you need to evaluate StarSling for your CI.
StarSling is AI-native CI for GitHub Actions: drop-in Ubuntu runners plus agents that open optimization PRs for your workflows. The runners replace ubuntu-latest and ubuntu-24.04 and run up to 33% cheaper than equivalent GitHub-hosted runners. Together with agent PRs, they made GitHub Actions up to 10x faster in public benchmarks, and the agents continuously analyze your workflows to keep the pipeline improving.
Agent-native CI is CI that improves itself. Beyond running your workflows on faster hardware, AI agents continuously analyze your jobs, run logs, and machine telemetry, then open pull requests that optimize your pipeline: caching, parallelization, dependency installs, test sharding, and workflow structure. Traditional CI is static; agent-native CI gets faster the longer you use it. Read more about AI-native CI.
Two things move the needle: faster hardware and removing redundant work. Swap ubuntu-latest for a runner with stronger CPUs, then let AI agents find dead steps, cache fixes, and parallelization opportunities your team hasn't had time to fix (in StarSling's public benchmarks, runners plus agent PRs made CI up to 10x faster). For a deeper guide, read fast GitHub Actions. Usually the runner. GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest runs on older shared hardware, so even simple builds spend time waiting on CPU. Switching to faster CPUs (StarSling Runners use 5th Gen AMD EPYC) typically cuts wall-clock time significantly before any workflow optimization.
Yes. Change runs-on: ubuntu-latest to runs-on: starsling-ubuntu-26.04 (or ubuntu-24.04 to starsling-ubuntu-24.04) in your GitHub Actions workflow files. No other config changes required. See StarSling vs GitHub Actions and GitHub Actions alternatives.

$0.008 per minute for 4 vCPU Linux runners with 16 GB RAM, 33% cheaper than GitHub Actions' $0.012/min. New paid subscriptions are billed by the second, with no one-minute minimum. Queue time is never billed. New accounts get 2,000 free minutes in their first month. See StarSling pricing.
Yes. StarSling Disks are persistent directories mounted into StarSling Runners, so dependency stores and build output, such as pnpm's store or Rust's target/, are already in place when the next job starts. In a benchmark on Mastra's 4.5 GiB pnpm store, dependencies were ready in about 25 seconds, 4.5x faster than GitHub's actions/cache. Pull requests from the same repository read the default branch's published disk. Storage is $0.50 per GB-month.
StarSling Runners are x64 Linux, from 2 to 64 vCPU. Need ARM? Email founders@starsling.dev.
Building Docker images in CI? Email founders@starsling.dev to talk through caching layers on StarSling Runners.
Yes. StarSling GPU Runners are drop-in GitHub Actions runners backed by a dedicated NVIDIA GPU: RTX PRO 6000 at a normalized $0.06422 per minute, RTX 5090 at $0.03022, and RTX 4090 at $0.02522, with H100 coming soon. Set runs-on: starsling-ubuntu-26.04-gpu and pick a card in the label. The GPU is dedicated to that job for as long as it runs, so nothing reclaims it partway through your suite. Explore StarSling GPU Runners.
RTX PRO 6000 is the default, and it suits large-model and memory-heavy CI workloads. RTX 5090 suits fast inference tests and model evals. RTX 4090 covers everyday GPU tests at the lowest per-minute cost. You choose per job in the runs-on: label, so different jobs in the same workflow can use different cards. Explore StarSling GPU Runners.
Yes. StarSling Review Runners are code review agents you configure and run in your own CI. One workflow file, and every pull request is analyzed as a GitHub Actions job on a StarSling runner using your model key, review skills and scripts from your codebase, and team-defined reviewers. Skills and instructions load from the trusted base branch, so a pull request cannot rewrite its own reviewer. The output is a review comment on the pull request, before a human opens it. Explore StarSling Review Runners.
A review is a GitHub Actions job on a StarSling runner in the same account as the rest of your CI. It runs on starsling-review, a 4 vCPU runner with 16 GB of memory. Review Runner time has a normalized rate of $0.004 per minute. New paid subscriptions are billed in whole seconds from job start to finish. Partial seconds round up, with no one-minute minimum. Existing paid subscriptions remain billed in whole minutes with a one-minute minimum until migrated. Queue time is never billed. Concurrency is unlimited. Model tokens are billed by your own provider, on the account you already have. Explore StarSling Review Runners.
After installing the StarSling GitHub App, AI agents continuously analyze your workflows, jobs, run logs, and machine telemetry, then open pull requests that optimize your setup: cache fixes, faster install strategies, Docker health checks, test sharding, parallelization, workflow structure, and job ordering. You review and merge. Optimization PRs are on paid plans, off by default for new accounts.
Coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) push PR volume up several-fold, which compounds CI cost and queue times fast. The right fit is a runner with unlimited concurrency, continuous AI optimization (so the pipeline gets faster as PR volume grows), and per-minute pricing with no seat fees. StarSling Runners are built for this pattern.
Failed jobs are billed for the time they run: whole seconds on new paid subscriptions, with partial seconds rounded up; whole minutes on existing paid subscriptions until migrated. Queue time is never billed. New accounts get 2,000 free minutes in their first month.
Each job runs in its own single-use, hardware-isolated microVM that's destroyed after the run. That's the same isolation model GitHub-hosted runners use, so there's nothing for a later job or a fork PR to persist on or reach. Secrets pass directly from GitHub to your job and are never stored by StarSling. More details in our docs.
Sign up with GitHub and install the StarSling GitHub App, switch runners with one line, and run 2x faster on day one. StarSling agents keep finding the next speedup.

articles.title: Solid 2.0
articles.body:
Solid 2.0 - The Long Hold
Solid 2.0 reaches stable after five years: async in the reactive graph, server functions, diagnostics built for agents, and a smaller API.
5 years is a long time to work on anything. It took 5 years from my first commit of Solid to 1.0, and it's been another 5 since then.
A lot changes in 5 years. Solid 1.0 made a bet that fine-grained reactivity, signals, was the right foundation for building user interfaces. Back then it was an unusual position. Today signals are everywhere. In Angular, in Svelte's runes, in Vue Vapor, and in a proposal before TC39 to put them in the language itself. It even pushed the conversation into React's compiler.
More recently that conversation has shifted to AI, arguably an even larger change in how we build. But Solid has always been about building the right things; the performant things. So for us the mission hasn't really changed all that much. The things that we identified as standout about our approach still stand out now. But instead of living in the shadow of more popular solutions Solid 2.0 carves out a path that others can follow. Deliberately this time.
Today that solution reaches stable.
Async Graph
If fine-grained reactivity's greatest strength is knowing the shape of our application, that knowledge shouldn't end with the process, or the machine the code is running on. Real applications are distributed. Real applications are born from data that lives on a server. The coordination of these pieces should be intentional and by design.
This starts with bringing async into the graph. A computation can return a Promise or an async iterator, and everything downstream just understands:
This allows authoring by affordance while automating the handling of race conditions. The introduction of async doesn't cause an app refactor. Speculative state is automatically rolled back without manually written processes ensuring the server remains the authority on truth.
SolidStart introduce the world to server functions in early 2022, and now they have found their way home to Solid's core, better than ever. Not only do they support highly capable RPC calls over Request/Response but persistent connections over Server Sent Events. And consuming it remains as simple as the code below.
This is only the beginning of what can be done with Server Functions and we will be announcing some new features (like reactive Server Components) in coming weeks that leverage this capability.
Built to Be Written by Agents
"But, we aren't writing the code anymore!" We hear you. A system built on constraints by construction ends up with less code to maintain and less edge cases. What used to be considered a DX shortcoming of reactive frameworks are now their greatest strength. And Solid 2.0 goes all in.
Every framework now says it "works great with AI", and usually that means models have seen a lot of it. That's a statement about training data, not about the framework. The question that matters is what happens when the agent gets it wrong.
In most frameworks a reactive mistake is silent. The app runs, it's just wrong, and the framework can't tell you, because it can't see it either. Solid can. A fine-grained graph knows exactly what was read, where, and what will update. So Solid 2.0's development builds report mistakes as they happen, with a stable code, the location in your source, and the fix:
These handle everything from strict errors to helpful heuristics. Thanks to async in the graph we can detect waterfalls, poorly constructed effect loops, poorly scaling graph shapes like wide graph fanouts and fan-ins. Today along with linting rules we can provide the best in class direction for agents at compile and at runtime.
This area is still evolving as we learn more about how agents build applications with Solid. The hard part, defining the primitives and semantics, is done. We've integrated with new dev tooling, and Chrome's Performance Tracks. And this capability goes beyond development as this observability powers things like our updated Sentry plugin so you can get the same information on your production builds.
We've also been looking at alternative syntax. Solid 2.0 adds experimental support for ReactiveScript and TSRX, both aiming to use compilation to further improve agent authoring.
One Framework for All
I've always been a big believer that React's super power is its composability. That it allowed the ecosystem to build on its humble pieces. However, we've learned a lot since 2013. At that point composable state, async patterns, and server rendering lacked the primitives to build upon and the ecosystem came up with their own solutions. This was fine for a while but tied React's hands and fractured their ecosystem. Something only a framework as popular as React could survive.
Newer frameworks have taken more on themselves and tend to only have one metaframework, or one router. We respect React's original positioning but have updated it for 2026. It isn't about restricting the solution but giving developers the primitives to build upon in the way React originally did. Server functions are example of this. Supporting any router, and cache solution for Single-Flight Mutation is another.
We retired our metaframework SolidStart, since every primitive needed to build a Solid Metaframework is now provided by the core or by framework agnostic Vite plugins. We believe that building an opinionated layer like a metaframework shouldn't have you needing to re-implement everything again. We've taken care of the hard parts so you can focus on what you care about. And these days a lot of that work is going to be taken on by your agent. This means less to maintain but no loss in capability.
And this makes it easier for the ecosystem. Solid 2.0 only requires one Clerk or Sentry plugin since we provide the primitives for Request/Response (built on web standards) and the hooks for observability that work across any library. We've already seen success with TanStack Query and Router being as capable as anything we've built first party, bringing in Tanner's impeccable attention to detail for the APIs people love to use.
Less is More
Somehow even though Solid 2.0 brings more capability to Solid, we've collapsed the surface area at almost every point. There are less primitives needed to be learnt, less ceremony around handling async. createResource, batch, startTransition, on, produce, createComputed, createMutable are all gone, because we no longer need them.
The equivalent code written for Solid 2.0 is shorter and clearer on intent. It informs our ability observe the runtime, provide better compiler errors, and removes the need for as many escape hatches (like createEffect) that can get us in trouble. This is something we believe important in an age of AI. Safe by construction rather than by exhaustion. Reduce complexity by deriving(reducing) state rather than putting it in a reducer.
When the framework carries the guarantees, all loading state, race conditions, and cancellation logic disappears and what you are left with is the UI.
The Road Here
The first discussions of what a Solid 2.0 would look like started at the moment 1.0 was released. We saught feedback from the community on new reactivity ideas. The real effort started in late 2024. We announced the road to 2.0 in February 2025. Over a year of experiments followed, rewriting the reactive core from scratch until the async model held up to everything we threw at it. The beta landed in March, and the Release Candidate in August, with the API frozen.
Then 23 release candidates in 14 weeks. In that time alone, 971 pull requests were merged and 753 issues closed. We set one bar for stable. A full week with no regression in ordinary app code, and no crash or hang anywhere. It took a while to get there. By the end, the bug reports coming in were from people(agents) deliberately hunting edge cases in the deepest corners of the scheduler, and finding them.
So many people have touched the project over the past 5 years, from working on the initial reactivity prototypes, to testing the latest RC builds on their production apps. I've tried to thank as many of you as I can and attached hundreds of handles in the RC announcement. There are so many. There are also the many great organizations that have sponsored our development over the years: Sentry, Netlify, Google Chrome, JetBrains, Anomaly, Cursor, Code Rabbit, Anthropic, Tembo and so many more.
But mostly I want to thank everyone who has believed in the project. We've accomplished great things and there is much more to come. That isn't possible without all of you. Personally, the past 2 and half years have been some of the most difficult of my life, but knowing what we are building that impacts so many people leaves me with a sense of fulfillment. Solid has always been bigger than its core team, and 2.0 is the clearest proof of that yet.
Solid 2.0 is here. Let's build.
The Long Hold refers to a diagnostic warning in Solid 2.0. It fires when a hold has been shown(isPending) but sufficient time has passed since the last input. Holds were at the heart of our async work for 2.0, and we acknowledge it took a while for this all to land.

articles.title: Chorizo Cornbread Stuffing
articles.body:
Chorizo Cornbread Stuffing
A savory cornbread base stuffing with Mexican chorizo, softened lightly browned onions, tender vegetables, and warm spices, baked until golden and lightly crisp on top.
Serves6 to 8
Prep20 minutes
Cook50 minutes to 55 minutes
Why You’ll Love Chorizo Cornbread Stuffing
- A fun twist on a holiday classic. This stuffing brings bold Mexican-inspired flavors to the holiday table while keeping everything you love about traditional stuffing.
- The texture is irresistible. The stuffing bakes up soft and tender in the center with lightly golden crisp edges.
- It’s easy to make ahead. The cornbread can be toasted in advance, making assembly a breeze when you’re preparing a big holiday meal.
Chorizo was always a staple in our Mexican American household. Whether it was tucked into a warm tortilla for breakfast or cooked alongside potatoes, it was one of those ingredients that always brought so much flavor to the table. So when it came to putting my own spin on a classic Thanksgiving stuffing, adding Mexican chorizo just made sense.
This chorizo cornbread stuffing brings together slightly sweet, tender cornbread with smoky chorizo, softened vegetables, and warm spices. The chorizo adds the best smoky, salty, and spicy bite, while the cornbread soaks up all those delicious flavors and bakes until golden and lightly crisp on top (my favorite part!). It’s a fun twist on a classic that deserves a spot on your holiday table, but it also makes a wonderful weeknight side dish whenever you’re craving something smoky and slightly sweet. Truly, it’s the best of all the worlds combined into one baking dish.
Straight from Our Recipe Tester
“This recipe has me convinced that chorizo was destined for cornbread stuffing. The heavily spiced, super-savory sausage is the perfect complement to sweet cornbread. I used a tray of cornbread from the grocery store bakery and it was such an easy shortcut I’ll definitely be repeating.” —Rachel, October 2026
Why You Should Trust Me
As a Mexican American recipe developer with over a decade of experience in professional kitchens and food media, I love finding ways to bring the flavors I grew up with into classic American dishes. This chorizo cornbread stuffing combines my love for traditional holiday comfort food with the bold, savory flavors of Mexican chorizo.
Key Ingredients in Chorizo Cornbread Stuffing
- Cornbread: Creates a slightly sweet, tender base that absorbs the savory flavors while developing lightly crisp edges as it bakes.
- Mexican chorizo: Adds a rich, smoky, slightly spicy flavor while the rendered fat seasons the vegetables and cornbread.
- Jalapeño: Adds a gentle kick of heat that balances the sweetness of the cornbread.
- Eggs: Bind the stuffing together, helping it hold its shape.
How to Make Chorizo Cornbread Stuffing
- Toast the cornbread. Bake the diced cornbread until lightly browned and dried.
- Cook the chorizo. Brown the chorizo in a large skillet, breaking into small pieces.
- Cook the vegetables. Add the onion, carrot, celery, jalapeño, and salt. Cook until softened, then stir in the garlic and spices.
- Combine the stuffing. Stir the toasted cornbread, followed by the whisked broth, eggs, and melted butter.
- Bake the stuffing. Transfer to a greased baking dish, top with cheese if using, and bake until golden-brown and set. Garnish with cilantro and freshly ground black pepper.
Helpful Swaps
- Store-bought or homemade cornbread both work well in this recipe. Just make sure it’s thoroughly dried out before assembling the stuffing.
- Swap pepper Jack for Monterey Jack if you want a milder, creamier finish, if using cheese.
Chorizo Cornbread Stuffing Recipe
A savory cornbread base stuffing with Mexican chorizo, softened lightly browned onions, tender vegetables, and warm spices, baked until golden and lightly crisp on top.
Prep time 20 minutes
Cook time 50 minutes to 55 minutes
Serves 6 to 8
Nutritional Info
Ingredients
- Cooking spray
- 6 cups diced store-bought or homemade cornbread (18 ounces)
- 1 pound Mexican chorizo, casings removed
- 1 medium yellow onion, small dice (1 1/4 cups)
- 1 medium carrot, peeled and small dice (1/2 cups)
- 1 medium stalk celery, small dice (1/2 cup)
- 1 medium jalapeño pepper, stemmed, seeded, and small dice (1/4 cup)
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt
- 1/2 teaspoon smoked paprika
- 1/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, plus more for garnish
- 1 1/2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth
- 2 large eggs
- 2 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted
- 4 ounces pepper Jack or Monterey Jack cheese, shredded (1 cup, optional)
- Coarsely chopped fresh cilantro, for garnish (optional)
Instructions
- Heat the oven to 350ºF. Coat a 9x13-inch baking dish with cooking spray.
- Arrange 6 cups diced cornbread in an even layer on a rimmed baking sheet. Bake, stirring halfway through, until lightly brown, toasted, and dried out, 15 to 20 minutes total. Let cool slightly.
- Heat a large 12-inch skillet over medium heat. Add 1 pound Mexican chorizo and cook, breaking it up into small pieces and stirring occasionally, until browned and cooked through, 6 to 8 minutes.
- Stir in 1 small-diced medium yellow onion, 1 peeled and small-diced medium carrot, 1 small-diced medium celery stalk, 1 small-diced jalapeño pepper, and 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt. Cook until the vegetables are softened and the onion begins to brown, 8 to 10 minutes. Stir in 2 minced garlic cloves and cook until fragrant, about 40 seconds. Turn off the heat.
- Stir in 1/2 teaspoon smoked paprika and 1/4 teaspoon black pepper. Stir in the cornbread; it's OK if it begins to break or crumble up.
- Whisk 1 1/2 cups low-sodium chicken broth, 2 large eggs, and 2 tablespoons melted unsalted butter together in a medium bowl. Pour evenly over the cornbread mixture. Stir gently until combined and the broth mixture is absorbed.
- Transfer to the baking dish and arrange into an even layer. Sprinkle with 4 ounces shredded pepper Jack cheese if using.
- Bake until heated through and lightly browned on top, 20 to 25 minutes. Garnish with more black pepper and chopped fresh cilantro if desired.
Recipe Notes
Make ahead: The cornbread can be toasted up to 1 day ahead, cooled, and stored in an airtight container at room temperature.
Storage: Refrigerate leftover stuffing in an airtight container for up to 4 days.

our anniversary launch release in print at Defcon 33, HOPE, WHY25 and some
additional variations at several conferences around the world including
AlligatorCon, B-Sides Canberra, Out of the Box, Datenspuren, DistrictCon,
OffensiveCon, Recon, and Toorcamp. We included a CTF with exploit challenges
and had puzzles and easter eggs included in the zine. We threw parties and
had talks at Defcon and WHY25 to celebrate this milestone.
More importantly, we got new research into people's hands. The point of the
relaunch was to get people reading, researching, writing, and contributing
again. We wanted the next person picking up Phrack to find something that
made them sit down at a computer and start pulling a system apart.
We owe a huge thanks to the authors, editors, artists, publishing partners,
donors, and staff who made it happen. Writing the paper, working through
revisions, putting the print editions together, paying the bills, and
getting boxes of zines to the right places all take time and effort. Most of
that work is invisible when you are holding the finished issue. We
appreciate everyone who did it.
And to the readers: thank you for giving a shit. Seeing someone get excited
about an article, connect it to something they are working on, or realize
that they could contribute something themselves makes the effort worthwhile.
That exchange is how this thing keeps going. The relaunch worked, and this
issue is the follow-through.
--[ Present ]
This is the third release curated by the new staff, and we are not slowing
down. This issue is larger than last year's, with 23 main papers and eight
additional articles in Line Noise. The subjects range from exploitation and
reverse engineering to machine learning, hardware, and the history and
culture that grew around this work.
We have container escapes through the vDSO, use-after-free exploitation, QNX
userland shellcode, Linux kernel research, and a Chromium renderer sandbox
escape through Skia. Elsewhere, the issue takes on Windows smart card
architecture, static taint analysis in Binary Ninja, and autonomous
underwater vehicles.  There is also work examining backdoors in machine
learning and what it means to trust an AI system. One paper takes us from
PhrackCTF to two WinFSP zero-days, which is a pretty good argument for
continuing to put challenges in a zine.

of the infamous SSH1 CRC32 vulnerability featured in The Matrix Reloaded as
well as stories about blue boxing free phone calls, a confession of a hacker
who tried to backdoor Linux kernel in 2003, and an early discovery of
botnets for hire. Our Prophile features Halvar Flake, whose contributions to
reverse engineering and security research are legendary.

another five years. AI has moved well beyond completing a line of code into
agentic systems capable of analyzing source code and reverse engineering
binaries to find and exploit vulnerabilities.

ideas, create new tools, and push the boundaries of what is possible in the
face of new challenges and opportunities created by the advancement of AI
and automation systems. As the effort required to put ideas into practice
falls, creativity and human intuition forged through experience is valued
even higher.

articles.title: In 27,280 coding agent runs, 64% of inference spend went to runs that failed
articles.body:
TL;DR
We partnered with Baseten to build the largest-scale harness leaderboard using 83B tokens across 27,280 agent runs. We wanted to answer two questions: when you switch your model, should you consider switching the harness too? What is the best harness for each model?
Previously, our v1.0 FrontierHarness leaderboard ranked harnesses on a single model, Kimi K3.
V1.1 expands the benchmark to 22 harnesses × 5 models × 62 tasks × 4 attempts, 76× the size of v1.0.
Through our experiments, we found that you should consider switching harnesses when switching models to maximize your experience.
Each model had a different best-value (pass rate vs. cost) harness: Codex CLI with GLM-5.3, Pi with GLM-5.3 Flash, ZCode with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Oh My Pi with Muse and Alma with Kimi-K3. Cost ranks moved far between models.
By cost per task, the median harness moved 11 of 22 places, and Codex CLI went from 1st with GLM-5.3 to 16th with Kimi-K3.
Result
Figure 1. Cost per task and pass rate of each harness
Each point is one harness: further left is a lower average cost per task, and higher is a higher pass rate. The orange line joins the harnesses that no other harness beats in both cost and pass rate. Select a model to filter all figures of this post.
Over all models, four harnesses are on the line: OpenCode v2 (lowest cost per task, $0.561), Pi, Codex CLI and ZCode (highest pass rate, 61.9%). The others cost up to 1.6 times as much and passed 50.6% to 60.2%.
Each card names the best-value harness for one model: the lowest cost per pass, unless another harness costs at most 30% more per pass and passes at least 5 points more often. This rule picked ZCode over OpenCode v1 with DeepSeek (25% more cost, 7.7 more points) and Alma over Oh My Pi with Kimi-K3 (9% more cost, 6.5 more points).
Why We Built FrontierHarness Eval v1.1
V1.0 ran nine harnesses with one model. Their pass rates were within 17 points of each other, but the median cost per pass differed by 17 times. We thought that this came mostly from the pair of harness and model: a harness that is cheap with one model can be expensive with another.
V1.1 runs each harness with five models.
What We Tested
Harnesses. 18 harnesses. The four DeepSeek Harness profiles have different tool sets, and OpenCode ran at two versions. Each counts separately: 22 configurations. Table 2 in the appendix gives their versions.
Models. Baseten served all five: GLM-5.3 (zai-org/GLM-5.3), GLM Flash (zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash), DeepSeek (deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017), Muse (meta-models/muse-spark-open) and Kimi-K3 (moonshotai/Kimi-K3).
Tasks. 62 terminal tasks. The time limits are those of the tasks, from 15 minutes to 8 hours.
Setup and Scoring
Configuration and Runtime
We ran the Harbor evaluation with each harness’s default settings, because we think this is closest to how people use a harness every day. Each harness used the same version and settings with all models, at the maximum reasoning effort.
Figure 2. How Harbor and Runta divide the work in each trial
Each trial gets a new Runta runtime, which is deleted at the end. Thus no trial can see the files of an earlier trial.
Scoring Method
Table 1. Methodology
A cell is one harness and model pair. We use the two cost metrics of our dashboard:
- Average cost per task: the mean cost of the priced trials of each task, then the mean over the tasks. Figure 1 and the cost ranks use it (Figures 4 and 5).
- Cost per pass: the average cost per task divided by the pass rate. The best-value harness uses it (Figures 3, 6 and 7).
We pick the best value by cost per pass because we want harnesses at the top left of a chart of pass rate against cost per task: a high pass rate at a low cost. Draw a line from the origin to the point of a harness. Its slope, pass rate ÷ cost, is the passes per dollar. Cost per pass is the inverse of this slope, so the lowest cost per pass has the steepest line.
Audits of the trial logs flagged 216 trials for reward hacking, and 163 of them were online lookups. These trials score 0. Table 3 in the appendix gives the count for each harness and model.
Results by Model
Figure 3. Cost and pass rate of each harness with each model
A deeper cell costs less than the others in its column. Codex CLI was the cheapest per pass with GLM-5.3, $0.803, but 12th with Muse and 10th with Kimi-K3. Over all models, it cost the least per pass, $0.937, and Antigravity CLI the most, $1.63.
How Sure Are These Results?
We drew the 62 tasks again 4,000 times and chose the best-value harness each time. Codex CLI stayed first with GLM-5.3 in 99.6% of the draws. The other four winners are the most likely of several close harnesses: Oh My Pi with Muse (53%), ZCode with DeepSeek (47%), Pi with GLM Flash (42%) and Alma with Kimi-K3 (25%).
The Harness Changes the Cost
The model sets the general level of the cost, because the list prices of the models differ by 20 times or more (Figure 9). We took the average cost per task of the 110 cells on a log scale, so that a doubling counts the same with each model. A two-way analysis of variance divides the spread of these costs into three parts:
- Model, 92.8%: the differences between the five models.
- Harness, 2.3%: the part of the effect of a harness that is the same with every model.
- Pair, 4.9%: the rest. It also contains noise, because each cell has one value.
So with the model fixed, 68% of the variation between harnesses (4.9 of 7.2 points) depends on the pair, or is noise.
With the Model Fixed, the Harness Changes the Cost by 1.8 to 5.0 Times
Figure 4. Lowest-cost and highest-cost harness for each model
Each row is a model, on a log scale of average cost per task. The ratio divides the highest cost by the lowest.
To test for chance, we shuffled the trials between the harnesses of each model 300 times and calculated the ratio again. “Chance” is the median of these ratios, 1.2 to 1.8 times. All five real ratios are larger than every shuffle (p = 0.003), so the spread comes from the harnesses, not from the noise of reruns. The largest is with DeepSeek: Cline CLI cost 5.0 times as much as OpenCode v1, for 2.0 more points. With the other models, the cheapest harness per task was at most 0.4 points behind the most expensive one.
The Cheapest Harness per Task Changes With the Model
Figure 5. Cost rank of each harness with each model (1 = lowest cost per task)
Each line is a harness, with the cheapest at the top. The five highlighted lines are the cheapest harnesses per task with GLM-5.3, GLM Flash, DeepSeek, Muse and Kimi-K3.
Codex CLI was 1st with GLM-5.3 and 16th with Kimi-K3. DeepSeek Harness: Creator moved the most, from 1st with Muse to 21st with GLM Flash. OpenCode v1 was 1st with DeepSeek and 13th with Muse.
Reruns do not explain these moves. We divided the attempts into two halves and ranked the harnesses by cost in each half. With the same model, the two rankings had a mean rank correlation of 0.71. With two different models, it was 0.26.
A Higher Cost Does Not Give a Higher Score
Figure 6. Lowest and highest cost per pass for each model
This is Figure 4 for cost per pass. After each ratio is the rank correlation of the cost per task and the pass rate of the harnesses, from −0.39 to +0.22. A positive value means that the more expensive harnesses passed more often.
The harness with the highest pass rate was 5th to 20th of 22 in cost per task. With four of the five models, the most expensive harness per pass passed less often than the cheapest one.
Does a Simpler Harness Cost Less?
No. We compared four factors with the cost per pass. Prompt size, tool count and cache hit rate are not the main cost factors. Steps are.
- Start tokens: the input tokens of the first agent-loop request: the system prompt, the tool definitions and the task.
- Tools: the tools that the first request offers.
- Cache hit rate and steps: the mean over the passed trials. A step is one entry of the agent trajectory.
Figure 7. Four factors of each harness and the cost per pass
Over the 22 harnesses, the rank correlation of the steps per pass and the cost per pass was +0.51 (p = 0.015). For the other three factors, it was −0.03 to +0.02 (p ≥ 0.88). Within each model, tool calls tracked cost as well as steps. Table 4 below and Table 5 in the appendix give the values.
Each step sends the context again, so a trial used 2.0 to 4.8 million input tokens on average, by harness, and the largest first request, 21,365 tokens, is less than 1% of that. mini-SWE-agent has the smallest first request, 882 tokens, but took 38 steps per pass and was 17th of 22 in cost per pass.
Table 4. Start tokens, tools, cache hit rate, steps and cost per pass of each harness
Where the Cost Comes From
Figure 8. Inference cost of each harness, by token type or by trial outcome
All costs are inference estimates at list prices. The pass rate of the harness on the model card has an outline.
Over all trials, input from the cache was 42% of the cost, output 33% and other input 25%.
Tokens and the Cache
The cache makes repeated input much cheaper. Cached input costs 2% (DeepSeek) to 20% (GLM Flash) of the price of other input (Figure 9).
Figure 9. List prices of each model (USD for one million tokens)
One pair shows the effect of the cache. Cline CLI with DeepSeek (highest cost per task) read 86% of its input from the cache, and OpenCode v1 read 97%. It also sent twice as much input. Input that did not come from the cache was 57% of its cost.
Most of the Cost Goes to Trials That Do Not Pass
64.5% of the list-price cost of the scored runs went to trials that did not pass: 52.7% to failures and 11.8% to timeouts.
What the Best-Value Harnesses Share
The traces of the five best-value harnesses show three common design choices. These are observations, not tests.
One shell tool does most of the work. By harness, it got 61% to 93% of the tool calls. Pi’s default prompt has four tools and sends file searches to bash:
selectedTools: [...(input.selectedTools ?? ["read", "bash", "edit", "write"])],
addRule("Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find");
Each request only adds to the one before it. The start of the context does not change, so the provider reads it from the cache: 91.1% to 94.0% of input in passed trials (Table 4). But 18 of the 22 harnesses read 91% or more, so this does not separate the five. Each step pays the full input price for only about 500 new tokens:
# Pi, GLM-5.3, merge-diff-arc-agi-task (trial cd2f6dfd)
request  prompt tokens  cached tokens
   8        15,954         15,616
   9        16,351         15,936
  10        16,999         16,320
No subagents and almost no summaries. Each of the five used a subagent in at most 6 trials, too few to tell if subagents help. Of the five, only Codex CLI summarized, in 8 trials (the 11 Alma trials in Table 6 only drop old images and reminders). Codex CLI summarizes at 90% of the window (Table 6):
.map(|context_window| (context_window * 9) / 10);
The five also share a weakness. Failed runs end with a confident answer. About three in four failed trials ended with a final answer, not at the time limit: from 68% with Pi to 82% with Codex CLI. Few said that the work was incomplete:
# Codex CLI, GLM-5.3, cancel-async-tasks (trial 37182b0e)
Agent:    - Validated with system Python, including concurrency and
            cancellation-cleanup tests.
Verifier: FAILED test_tasks_cancel_above_max_concurrent
          assert stdout.count("Cleaned up.") == 2
          AssertionError: assert 0 == 2
Trials that did not pass took 60% (Codex CLI) to 69% (Alma) of the cost of each harness. A check before the harness stops could save part of it, but we did not test this.
Limitations and Future Work
- Open models, one provider. Closed models can give different results. The cache and the prices are those of Baseten, and another provider can change the cost ranks.
We plan two next steps:
- Closed models. We will add closed models, such as Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Carbon.
- Long-horizon work. We will study how a harness that runs continuously in the cloud improves itself during long work.
Conclusion
- When you change the model, think about changing the harness too. Test the candidate harnesses with your model on a private dataset of your own tasks, large enough to see past the noise.
- The model sets most of the cost, and the harness is second. The model explains 92.8% of the variance of cost per task. With the model fixed, the most expensive harness cost 1.9 to 4.9 times as much per pass as the cheapest (1.8 to 5.0 times per task), so compare the cost when you pick a harness.
- A higher cost does not buy a higher pass rate. For each model, the rank correlation of cost per task and pass rate was −0.39 to +0.22.
- Size does not predict cost. mini-SWE-agent, the smallest harness, was 19th of 22 by cost per task over all models.
- Most of the cost, 64.5%, went to runs that did not pass. With the five best-value harnesses, 68% to 82% of the failed runs ended with a confident final answer, not at the time limit.
- With a cheap model that has a wide range of pass rates, pick a harness with a high pass rate. Pass rates varied by harness, from 54.0% to 69.0% with DeepSeek. But each pass rate has a 95% interval of about ±10 points, so a gap of a few points is a tie.
- For harness developers: cut steps, not just prompt tokens. Prompt size, tool count and cache hit rate did not predict cost per pass. Steps did, because every step sends the whole context again.
Appendix: Reference Tables
Table 2. Harness configurations
Table 3. Reward-hacked trials of each harness
Table 5. Prompt and tools of each harness

- Harbor and Harbor Hub, where the ten jobs are stored
